topics.t: Types of solutions and percentage, ppm concentration
topics.h: The saline drip in an AIIMS ward and the sea breeze over Marina Beach are both solutions. Chemistry just asks: what dissolved in what, and how much?
p: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components. The component in larger amount is usually the solvent; the others are solutes. A binary solution has exactly two components.

By physical state of solute and solvent there are nine types: gas in gas (O₂ in N₂), liquid in gas (chloroform vapour mixed with N₂), solid in gas (camphor in N₂); gas in liquid (O₂ in water), liquid in liquid (ethanol in water), solid in liquid (glucose in water); gas in solid (H₂ in palladium), liquid in solid (amalgam of mercury with sodium), solid in solid (copper dissolved in gold).
Mass percentage (w/w) = (mass of component ÷ total mass of solution) × 100. Volume percentage (V/V) = (volume of component ÷ total volume of solution) × 100.
Mass by volume percentage (w/V) = mass of solute in grams dissolved in 100 mL of solution; common in medicine and pharmacy (normal saline is 0.9% w/V NaCl).
Parts per million (ppm) = (amount of component ÷ total amount of solution) × 10⁶; used for trace amounts such as fluoride in drinking water or pollutants in air.

ex.q: 0.0025 g of fluoride ions are present in 500 g of a water sample. Find the concentration in ppm and the mass percentage.

topics.rl: Packaged drinking water labels in India list dissolved solids and fluoride in ppm (mg per litre), and the BIS standard sets limits on them. Hospital IV bottles of normal saline are labelled 0.9% w/V sodium chloride.

topics.t: Mole fraction, molarity and molality
topics.h: A pharma lab in Hyderabad prepares the same solution in summer and winter. Why do chemists there prefer molality over molarity for precise work?
p: Mole fraction of component i: xᵢ = nᵢ ÷ (total moles). In a binary solution x₁ + x₂ = 1; it has no units.
Molarity (M) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres (mol L⁻¹). It changes with temperature because volume expands or contracts.
Molality (m) = moles of solute ÷ mass of solvent in kg (mol kg⁻¹). It does not depend on temperature because mass does not change.
Mass percentage, ppm, mole fraction and molality are temperature independent; molarity is temperature dependent.
To go from molarity to molality you need the density: mass of solution = density × volume; mass of solvent = mass of solution − mass of solute.

ex.q: A solution has 1.0 mol NaCl (58.5 g) in 1.000 L of solution. Its density is 1.0585 g mL⁻¹. Find its molality.
st: Mass of solution = 1000 mL × 1.0585 g mL⁻¹ = 1058.5 g

topics.rl: Doctors at AIIMS read blood glucose in mmol per litre (a molarity unit), while chemists making precise measurements over changing temperatures prefer temperature-independent units such as molality and mole fraction.

topics.t: Solubility of solids and Henry's law for gases
topics.h: Pop open a chilled bottle of soda on a hot Delhi afternoon and it fizzes wildly. William Henry worked out the rule behind that fizz in 1803.
p: Solubility is the maximum amount of a substance that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. 'Like dissolves like': polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar in non-polar.
In a saturated solution, undissolved solute is in dynamic equilibrium with dissolved solute (rate of dissolution = rate of crystallisation). An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.

For solids, if dissolving is endothermic (Δsol H > 0) solubility rises with temperature; if exothermic (Δsol H < 0) it falls (Le Chatelier). Pressure has no significant effect because solids and liquids are nearly incompressible.
Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: p = K_H x. Solubility of a gas rises with its pressure.
K_H depends on the gas and the temperature. A larger K_H at the same pressure means a smaller mole fraction, i.e. lower solubility.

ex.q: At 298 K, K_H for CO₂ in water is 1.67 kbar. Find the mole fraction of CO₂ in water when its partial pressure is 3.34 bar.

topics.rl: Soft-drink bottling plants in India seal the bottles under high CO₂ pressure; Henry's law tells them how much gas stays dissolved until you twist the cap.

topics.t: Henry's law in action: divers, mountaineers and temperature
topics.h: An Indian Navy diver surfacing too fast can feel crippling joint pain called 'the bends', while soldiers posted at Siachen battle breathlessness. Both stories are Henry's law stories.
p: Soft drinks and soda water are sealed under high CO₂ pressure to increase its solubility; opening the bottle lowers the pressure and CO₂ bubbles out.

Scuba divers breathe air at high pressure underwater, so more N₂ dissolves in blood. On rapid ascent the pressure falls, N₂ forms bubbles in the blood and blocks capillaries: 'the bends', which is painful and dangerous.
To reduce this, diving tanks use air diluted with helium (about 11.7% He, 56.2% N₂ and 32.1% O₂), since helium is much less soluble in blood.
At high altitudes the partial pressure of O₂ is low, so less O₂ dissolves in blood and tissues: climbers become weak and cannot think clearly (anoxia).
Gas solubility in liquids decreases as temperature rises (dissolving a gas is exothermic). K_H increases with temperature — for O₂ in water it rises from 34.86 kbar at 293 K to 46.82 kbar at 303 K.

ex.q: K_H for O₂ in water is 34.86 kbar at 293 K and 46.82 kbar at 303 K. At the same partial pressure, at which temperature is O₂ more soluble, and why do fish prefer cold water?
st: x = p/K_H, so a smaller K_H gives a larger mole fraction
So more O₂ dissolves at 293 K; cold water carries more dissolved oxygen for aquatic life
ex.a: More soluble at 293 K; cold water holds more dissolved O₂

topics.rl: In summer, fish kills are sometimes reported in shallow Indian ponds and lakes: warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, exactly as K_H increasing with temperature predicts.

topics.t: Raoult's law for liquid–liquid solutions
topics.h: Refineries at Jamnagar separate liquid mixtures by distillation. To predict what boils off first, you need François Raoult's law.
p: Raoult's law (volatile liquids): the partial vapour pressure of each component is proportional to its mole fraction in solution: p₁ = p₁° x₁ and p₂ = p₂° x₂, where p° is the vapour pressure of the pure liquid.
Dalton's law gives the total: p_total = p₁ + p₂ = p₁° x₁ + p₂° x₂ = p₁° + (p₂° − p₁°) x₂. A plot of p_total against x₂ is a straight line joining p₁° and p₂°.
Composition of the vapour: y₁ = p₁ ÷ p_total. The vapour is richer in the more volatile component (the one with higher p°).
Raoult's law is a special case of Henry's law: both say partial pressure ∝ mole fraction, and for Raoult's law the constant K_H equals p₁°.

ex.q: Liquids A (p_A° = 400 mm Hg) and B (p_B° = 600 mm Hg) form an ideal solution with x_A = 0.4. Find p_total and the mole fraction of A in the vapour.

topics.rl: Petrol is a blend of volatile hydrocarbons. Indian refiners adjust its vapour pressure for summer and winter grades so that engines start easily without too much fuel evaporating — a direct use of Raoult-type thinking.

topics.t: Ideal and non-ideal solutions, azeotropes
topics.h: Distil fermented sugarcane juice as long as you like, and the ethanol refuses to get purer than about 95% by volume. Meet the azeotrope.
p: Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law at all concentrations, with Δmix H = 0 and Δmix V = 0; A–B attractions equal A–A and B–B. Examples: n-hexane + n-heptane, bromoethane + chloroethane, benzene + toluene.

Positive deviation: A–B attractions weaker than A–A and B–B, so molecules escape more easily and vapour pressure is higher than Raoult's prediction; Δmix H > 0 and Δmix V > 0. Examples: ethanol + acetone, carbon disulphide + acetone.

Negative deviation: A–B attractions stronger, vapour pressure lower than predicted; Δmix H < 0 and Δmix V < 0. Example: chloroform + acetone (H-bond between CHCl₃ hydrogen and acetone oxygen); also phenol + aniline.
Azeotropes are binary mixtures that boil at a constant temperature with the same composition in liquid and vapour, so fractional distillation cannot separate them.

Minimum boiling azeotropes come from large positive deviation (ethanol–water at about 95% ethanol by volume). Maximum boiling azeotropes come from large negative deviation (nitric acid–water at about 68% HNO₃ by mass, boiling at 393.5 K).

ex.q: When acetone and chloroform are mixed, the mixture warms up slightly and the final volume is a little less than the sum of the volumes. Classify the solution.
st: Warming means heat is released: Δmix H < 0
Stronger A–B attraction (H-bond) means negative deviation
ex.a: Non-ideal solution with negative deviation from Raoult's law

topics.rl: India's ethanol-blended petrol needs nearly water-free ethanol, but simple distillation of molasses wash stops near the ethanol–water azeotrope; distilleries use extra dehydration steps (like molecular sieves) to break past it.

topics.t: Colligative properties: vapour pressure lowering and boiling point elevation
topics.h: Add salt to the pressure cooker water and the dal takes a tiny bit longer to start boiling. The salt is just counting particles.
p: A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent because fewer solvent molecules are at the surface to escape.

Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not their nature: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure.
Relative lowering of vapour pressure: (p₁° − p₁) ÷ p₁° = x₂. For dilute solutions x₂ ≈ n₂/n₁, so M₂ = (w₂ × M₁ × p₁°) ÷ (w₁ × Δp).

Boiling point elevation: ΔT_b = K_b m, where K_b is the ebullioscopic constant (unit K kg mol⁻¹; 0.52 for water, 2.53 for benzene). Molar mass: M₂ = (K_b × w₂ × 1000) ÷ (ΔT_b × w₁), with masses in grams.

ex.q: 1.28 g of a non-volatile solute in 50 g of benzene raises its boiling point by 0.506 K. K_b for benzene is 2.53 K kg mol⁻¹. Find the molar mass of the solute.

topics.rl: In Leh, water boils at a lower temperature because of low air pressure, which is why pressure cookers are essential there; dissolved salt nudges the boiling point up only a little, as ΔT_b = K_b m predicts.

topics.t: Depression of freezing point
topics.h: Every kulfi-wala knows the trick: pack the matka with ice and salt, and it gets colder than plain ice. That's freezing point depression at work.
p: A solution freezes at a lower temperature than the pure solvent because its vapour pressure is lower: ΔT_f = T_f° − T_f = K_f m.
K_f is the cryoscopic constant (unit K kg mol⁻¹): 1.86 for water and 5.12 for benzene. Molar mass: M₂ = (K_f × w₂ × 1000) ÷ (ΔT_f × w₁).
Both constants depend only on the solvent: K_b = R M₁ T_b² ÷ (1000 Δvap H) and K_f = R M₁ T_f² ÷ (1000 Δfus H), with M₁ in g mol⁻¹.
Uses: ethylene glycol is added to car radiators as antifreeze; salt (NaCl or CaCl₂) is spread on icy roads to melt the ice.

ex.q: How many kelvin will the freezing point of water drop if 62 g of ethylene glycol (M = 62 g mol⁻¹) is added to 500 g of water? K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.

topics.rl: Army vehicles in Ladakh and Sikkim run with antifreeze (glycol-based coolant) in their radiators so the water does not freeze in sub-zero nights.

topics.t: Osmosis, osmotic pressure and reverse osmosis
topics.h: That RO purifier humming in your kitchen pushes water the 'wrong way' through a membrane. To understand it, first understand osmosis.
p: Osmosis: net flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent (or dilute solution) into a more concentrated solution. Osmotic pressure π is the extra pressure that must be applied to the solution to just stop this flow.
van't Hoff equation: π = CRT = (n₂/V)RT, where C is molarity, R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T is in kelvin. Molar mass: M₂ = w₂RT ÷ (πV).

Osmotic pressure is the best method for macromolecules (proteins, polymers): it is measured at room temperature, uses molarity, and gives a large, measurable value even for very dilute solutions — useful for biomolecules that break down on heating.

Isotonic solutions have equal osmotic pressure. Blood cells are isotonic with 0.9% (w/V) NaCl (normal saline). In a hypertonic solution (more than 0.9%) cells lose water and shrink; in a hypotonic one (less than 0.9%) they swell and may burst.
Reverse osmosis: applying pressure greater than π on the solution side pushes pure solvent out through the membrane (e.g. cellulose acetate). It is used to desalinate sea water.

ex.q: A 0.25 L solution contains 2 g of a polymer and shows π = 0.00166 bar at 300 K. Find the molar mass (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

topics.rl: Chennai's Minjur and Nemmeli plants turn Bay of Bengal sea water into drinking water by reverse osmosis, and millions of Indian homes run small RO units under the kitchen sink.

topics.t: Abnormal molar masses and the van't Hoff factor
topics.h: Measure the molar mass of table salt by freezing point depression and you get about 29 g mol⁻¹, not 58.5. Is the experiment wrong, or is salt splitting up?
p: When a solute dissociates (electrolytes in water) or associates (e.g. ethanoic acid dimerising in benzene via H-bonds), the number of particles changes, giving an 'abnormal' molar mass.
van't Hoff factor: i = normal molar mass ÷ abnormal molar mass = observed colligative property ÷ calculated colligative property = total moles of particles after ÷ moles before.
Dissociation gives i > 1 (KCl ≈ 2, K₂SO₄ ≈ 3 at infinite dilution); association gives i < 1 (ethanoic acid dimer in benzene ≈ 0.5); no change gives i = 1.
Modified equations: Δp/p₁° = i n₂/n₁; ΔT_b = i K_b m; ΔT_f = i K_f m; π = i CRT.
Degree of dissociation α = (i − 1) ÷ (n − 1), where n ions form per formula unit. Degree of association α = (1 − i) ÷ (1 − 1/n), where n molecules join together.

ex.q: Ethanoic acid in benzene gives i = 0.6. Find its degree of association (it forms dimers).
ex.a: α = 0.8, i.e. 80% of the acid is dimerised

topics.rl: The ORS packets distributed in Indian health programmes are designed around total particle count: the salts dissociate, so their osmotic effect depends on the van't Hoff factor, not just the grams of salt.

topics.t: Electrochemical cells and the Daniell cell
topics.h: Your phone battery, the Ola electric scooter and the chrome plating on a bike handle all run on one idea: chemical energy and electrical energy can be swapped.
p: Electrochemistry studies the production of electricity from spontaneous chemical reactions and the use of electricity to drive non-spontaneous ones. It underpins batteries, fuel cells, electroplating and the industrial production of metals and chemicals such as NaOH and Cl₂.
A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to bring about a non-spontaneous reaction.
Daniell cell: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Zinc dips in ZnSO₄ and copper in CuSO₄, joined by a salt bridge; with 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions the cell gives 1.1 V.

If an opposing external voltage is applied: below 1.1 V electrons still flow from Zn to Cu; at exactly 1.1 V no current flows; above 1.1 V electrons flow from Cu to Zn and the cell works as an electrolytic cell (Zn deposits, Cu dissolves).
The salt bridge (e.g. KCl or KNO₃ in agar) completes the inner circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral.

ex.q: A Daniell cell (1.1 V) is connected to an external source of 1.5 V opposing it. What happens at each electrode?
st: External voltage 1.5 V > 1.1 V, so the reaction is reversed
Electrons now flow from Cu to Zn in the external circuit
Zn²⁺ is reduced: zinc deposits on the zinc electrode
Cu is oxidised: copper dissolves from the copper electrode
ex.a: The cell becomes electrolytic: zinc is deposited and copper dissolves

topics.rl: Hindustan Zinc and Hindalco produce zinc and aluminium electrolytically, and the chlor-alkali plants of Gujarat make caustic soda and chlorine — giant electrolytic cells in action.

topics.t: Galvanic cells: half-cells, notation and the SHE
topics.h: Cell notation is chemistry's shorthand. Zn|Zn²⁺||Cu²⁺|Cu tells an examiner the whole story in one line, if you know how to read it.
p: A galvanic cell has two half-cells (redox couples). Oxidation occurs at the anode, which is negative in a galvanic cell; reduction occurs at the cathode, which is positive.
Notation: anode on the left, cathode on the right, a single vertical line for a phase boundary and a double line for the salt bridge: Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq)||Cu²⁺(aq)|Cu(s).
E_cell = E_right − E_left = E_cathode − E_anode, using reduction potentials for both.
Single electrode potentials cannot be measured alone. The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), Pt(s)|H₂(g, 1 bar)|H⁺(aq, 1 M), is assigned 0.00 V at all temperatures.
Measured against SHE: Pt|H₂(1 bar)|H⁺(1 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu gives 0.34 V, so E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; the zinc cell gives E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.

ex.q: Write the cell for the reaction 2Ag⁺(aq) + Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) and find E°cell. E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.
st: Zn is oxidised, so it is the anode (left); Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode (right)

topics.rl: Chemistry labs at IISERs calibrate reference electrodes against the hydrogen electrode, the zero point on which every textbook E° value is built.

topics.t: Electrochemical series and predicting reactions
topics.h: Can you store copper sulphate solution in a zinc pot from the market? The electrochemical series answers in one glance.
p: Standard reduction potentials (1 M, 1 bar, 298 K) listed in order form the electrochemical series: F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V at the top, Li⁺/Li −3.05 V at the bottom.

The higher (more positive) E°, the stronger the oxidised form as an oxidising agent: F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent. The lower (more negative) E°, the stronger the reduced form as a reducing agent: Li is the strongest reducing agent.
A redox reaction is feasible if E°cell = E°(species reduced) − E°(species oxidised) is positive. A metal with negative E° can liberate H₂ from dilute acids; Cu (+0.34 V) cannot.
Inert electrodes such as platinum or gold carry electrons for couples with no solid metal, e.g. Pt(s)|Fe³⁺, Fe²⁺ or Pt(s)|H₂|H⁺.
Useful values: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44, H⁺/H₂ 0.00, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34, I₂/I⁻ +0.54, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V.

ex.q: Can CuSO₄ solution be stored in a zinc vessel? E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
st: Possible reaction: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
Positive E°cell means the reaction occurs, so zinc would dissolve
ex.a: No — zinc reduces Cu²⁺ and the vessel would be eaten away

topics.rl: Galvanised iron buckets and water tanks sold in Indian markets rely on zinc's lower E°: zinc corrodes first and protects the iron underneath.

topics.t: The Nernst equation
topics.h: Standard conditions are rare outside the textbook. Walther Nernst's equation tells you the real voltage when concentrations are anything but 1 M.
p: For a reduction Mⁿ⁺(aq) + ne⁻ → M(s): E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(1/[Mⁿ⁺]). At 298 K this becomes E = E° − (0.059/n) log(1/[Mⁿ⁺]).
For a whole cell aA + bB → cC + dD: E_cell = E°cell − (0.059/n) log Q at 298 K, where Q = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ (pure solids and liquids are left out).
For the Daniell cell: E_cell = 1.10 − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]). Raising [Cu²⁺] or lowering [Zn²⁺] increases E_cell.
Hydrogen electrode at 1 bar: E = −0.059 pH at 298 K.

ex.q: Find E_cell at 298 K for Zn|Zn²⁺(0.01 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu. E°cell = 1.10 V.

topics.rl: The pH meters used in Indian dairies and water-testing labs are electrochemical cells: their reading changes by 0.059 V for every pH unit, straight from the Nernst equation.

topics.t: Cell potential, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant
topics.h: A positive cell voltage is chemistry's green signal: it tells you the reaction is spontaneous and how far it will go before it stops.
p: Electrical work done by a cell = nFE_cell, so Δr G = −nFE_cell and Δr G° = −nFE°cell. F (Faraday constant) = 96487 C mol⁻¹, often taken as 96500 C mol⁻¹.
A positive E_cell gives a negative Δr G: the reaction is spontaneous.
At equilibrium E_cell = 0 and Q = K, so E°cell = (2.303RT/nF) log K_c = (0.059/n) log K_c at 298 K.
Also Δr G° = −2.303RT log K_c. A large positive E° means a very large K: the reaction goes nearly to completion.

ex.q: Find Δr G° for the Daniell cell (E°cell = 1.10 V). Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.

topics.rl: Electrochemists at CSIR-CECRI, Karaikudi, use exactly these relations to screen new battery chemistries: a bigger E° means more energy stored per mole.

topics.t: Conductance, conductivity and molar conductivity
topics.h: Tap water conducts electricity but distilled water barely does. Measuring that difference precisely is how labs check water purity.
p: Resistance R = ρ(l/A), where ρ is resistivity (Ω m). Conductance G = 1/R (siemens, S). Conductivity κ = 1/ρ (S m⁻¹, often S cm⁻¹; 1 S m⁻¹ = 0.01 S cm⁻¹).

Electronic (metallic) conduction depends on the metal's nature and structure and the number of valence electrons; it decreases as temperature rises. Electrolytic (ionic) conduction depends on the nature of the electrolyte, ion size and solvation, solvent viscosity, concentration and temperature; it increases as temperature rises.

Conductivity is measured in a conductivity cell (two Pt electrodes coated with Pt black) using a Wheatstone bridge with AC current, to avoid electrolysis and polarisation. Cell constant G* = l/A = R × κ.
Molar conductivity Λm = κ/c. In S cm² mol⁻¹: Λm = (κ in S cm⁻¹ × 1000) ÷ (molarity in mol L⁻¹). In SI it is S m² mol⁻¹.

ex.q: A conductivity cell filled with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹) has a resistance of 100 Ω. Find the cell constant and Λm.
ex.a: G* = 1.29 cm⁻¹; Λm = 129 S cm² mol⁻¹

topics.rl: Pharma companies in Baddi and Hyderabad monitor the conductivity of 'purified water' continuously; a rise warns that ions have crept in.

topics.t: Variation with concentration and Kohlrausch's law
topics.h: Dilute a salt solution and its conductivity falls, yet its molar conductivity rises. It sounds like a contradiction until you count ions properly.
p: Conductivity κ decreases on dilution because the number of ions per unit volume falls. Molar conductivity Λm increases on dilution because Λm = κV, and V (volume containing 1 mol) increases more than κ falls.
Limiting molar conductivity Λ°m is the value as concentration approaches zero.

Strong electrolytes: Λm = Λ°m − A c^½ (Debye–Hückel–Onsager). Λm rises slowly on dilution; a plot of Λm vs √c is a straight line whose intercept gives Λ°m and whose slope is −A. A depends on the solvent, temperature and type of electrolyte (charges of ions: NaCl 1-1, CaCl₂ 2-1, MgSO₄ 2-2).
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: Λ°m of an electrolyte = sum of limiting molar conductivities of its ions, Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.

ex.q: Find Λ°m of CaCl₂ using λ°(Ca²⁺) = 119.0 and λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹.

topics.rl: Water-treatment engineers at Indian municipal plants track conductivity to estimate total dissolved salts, using the fact that each ion contributes its own share — Kohlrausch's idea.

topics.t: Weak electrolytes: degree of dissociation and Ka from conductivity
topics.h: You cannot extrapolate acetic acid's conductivity curve to zero concentration — it shoots up wildly. Kohlrausch's law offers a clever detour.
p: Weak electrolytes (e.g. CH₃COOH) have low Λm at ordinary concentrations, which rises steeply on dilution as the degree of dissociation increases.
Their Λ°m cannot be obtained by extrapolation; instead use Kohlrausch's law with strong electrolytes: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(CH₃COONa) + Λ°(HCl) − Λ°(NaCl).
Degree of dissociation at concentration c: α = Λm ÷ Λ°m.
Dissociation constant: Ka = cα² ÷ (1 − α).

ex.q: Λ°m of HCl, NaCl and CH₃COONa are 425.9, 126.4 and 91.0 S cm² mol⁻¹. Find Λ°m of acetic acid.

topics.rl: Vinegar (about 5% acetic acid) used in Indian pickles is a weak electrolyte; its conductivity is far lower than that of an HCl solution of the same concentration.

topics.t: Electrolysis and Faraday's laws
topics.h: The silver-plated thali at a wedding and copper refined to 99.9% purity for wiring both depend on counting electrons — Faraday's way.
p: In electrolysis of CuSO₄ with copper electrodes, Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) while the copper anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻). This is the basis of electrorefining (impure Cu as anode) and electroplating.
In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode is negative (opposite of a galvanic cell); oxidation is still at the anode.
Faraday's first law: mass deposited m ∝ charge Q, so m = Z × I × t, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent, I is current (A) and t is time (s).
Faraday's second law: for the same charge, masses of different substances liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights (atomic mass ÷ number of electrons needed).
Charge on 1 mol of electrons = 1 F = 96487 C mol⁻¹ (≈ 96500). Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag needs 1 F per mol, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 F, Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al needs 3 F.

ex.q: A current of 2 A is passed through CuSO₄ solution for 965 s. What mass of copper is deposited? (Cu = 63.5 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
st: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles of Cu = 0.01 mol

topics.rl: Electrorefining at Hindustan Copper's plants produces high-purity copper for India's power cables, and Moradabad artisans electroplate brassware with silver and nickel.

topics.t: Products of electrolysis
topics.h: Electrolyse molten salt and you get sodium metal; electrolyse brine and you get hydrogen instead. Same ions, different stories.
p: Products depend on the state of the electrolyte, the nature of the electrodes (inert Pt or reactive Cu), the standard potentials of competing reactions and overpotential (extra voltage needed for some reactions, especially gas evolution).
Molten NaCl: cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(l); anode Cl⁻ → ½Cl₂(g) + e⁻.

Aqueous NaCl: at the cathode water is reduced instead of Na⁺ (E° of H₂O/H₂ = −0.83 V vs Na⁺/Na −2.71 V): H₂O + e⁻ → ½H₂ + OH⁻. At the anode Cl₂ is evolved rather than O₂ (although E° Cl₂/Cl⁻ 1.36 V > O₂ 1.23 V) because of the overpotential of oxygen. Net: NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) + ½H₂(g) + ½Cl₂(g).
Dilute H₂SO₄ (Pt electrodes): O₂ at the anode, 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (E° 1.23 V). At higher concentration, peroxodisulphate forms: 2SO₄²⁻ → S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻ (E° 1.96 V). H₂ is evolved at the cathode.

ex.q: Predict the products of electrolysis of aqueous NaCl using inert electrodes.
st: Cathode: compare Na⁺/Na (−2.71 V) with H₂O/H₂ (−0.83 V); water is reduced → H₂ + OH⁻
Anode: Cl₂ (1.36 V) vs O₂ (1.23 V); O₂ has a high overpotential, so Cl₂ forms
Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain in solution as NaOH
ex.a: H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode, NaOH in solution

topics.rl: This is the chlor-alkali process run at large plants in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu; the NaOH goes into soaps and paper, and the Cl₂ into water disinfection and PVC.

topics.t: Batteries and fuel cells
topics.h: The dry cell in a TV remote, the lead battery under an auto-rickshaw seat and the fuel cell that powered Apollo astronauts share the same physics but very different chemistry.
p: Primary batteries cannot be recharged. Dry (Leclanché) cell: zinc container anode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), carbon (graphite) rod cathode in MnO₂ + carbon, NH₄Cl/ZnCl₂ paste; cathode: MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃. About 1.5 V.

Mercury cell: zinc–mercury amalgam anode, HgO + carbon paste cathode, KOH + ZnO paste electrolyte. Anode: Zn(Hg) + 2OH⁻ → ZnO(s) + H₂O + 2e⁻; cathode: HgO + H₂O + 2e⁻ → Hg(l) + 2OH⁻. About 1.35 V, constant because no ion appears in the overall reaction Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l). Used in hearing aids and watches.
Secondary (rechargeable) lead storage battery: Pb anode, grid of lead packed with PbO₂ as cathode, 38% H₂SO₄. Discharge: Pb(s) + PbO₂(s) + 2H₂SO₄(aq) → 2PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l); charging reverses it.
Nickel–cadmium cell: Cd(s) + 2Ni(OH)₃(s) → CdO(s) + 2Ni(OH)₂(s) + H₂O(l); longer life than the lead cell but more expensive.

H₂–O₂ fuel cell (used in the Apollo programme): porous carbon electrodes with Pt/Pd catalyst in concentrated aqueous NaOH. Cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; anode: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻; overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Efficiency about 70%, versus about 40% for thermal power plants, and it is pollution free.

ex.q: Why does a mercury cell give a constant voltage throughout its life, unlike a dry cell?
st: Overall reaction: Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l)
No ion in solution appears in the overall reaction
So the reaction quotient, and hence E, does not change as the cell is used
ex.a: Its overall reaction involves no ions whose concentration changes, so the voltage stays about 1.35 V

topics.rl: Indian Oil and ISRO have tested hydrogen fuel-cell technology (ISRO demonstrated a fuel-cell power system on its POEM platform in space), and hydrogen fuel-cell buses have begun trials on Indian roads.

topics.t: Corrosion: an electrochemical enemy
topics.h: Mumbai's sea air is brutal on iron: railings, ships and bridges rust fast. Rusting is a tiny galvanic cell on the metal's surface.
p: Corrosion slowly destroys a metal by forming oxides or other salts; rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver and the green coating on copper are examples.

At an anodic spot on iron: 2Fe(s) → 2Fe²⁺ + 4e⁻ (E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V). Electrons move through the metal to a cathodic spot where O₂ is reduced in the presence of H⁺ (from H₂CO₃ formed by dissolved CO₂): O₂(g) + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (E° = 1.23 V).
Overall: 2Fe(s) + O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l), E°cell = 1.67 V. Fe²⁺ is further oxidised by air to Fe³⁺, forming rust, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

Prevention: barrier coatings (paint, oil, chemicals like bisphenol); covering with a more reactive metal that corrodes instead (galvanising with zinc); sacrificial electrodes of Mg or Zn connected to the iron; and anti-rust solutions.

ex.q: Calculate E°cell for the rusting reaction 2Fe + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + 2H₂O.

topics.rl: Indian Railways uses galvanised steel and special paints on bridges and overhead line masts in coastal areas, and ships docked at Visakhapatnam carry zinc or magnesium sacrificial anodes on their hulls.

topics.t: Rate of a reaction: average and instantaneous
topics.h: Diamond turning into graphite is thermodynamically favourable, yet your grandmother's diamond nose-pin is safe for millions of years. Feasibility is not speed — kinetics is.
p: Chemical kinetics studies reaction rates, the factors affecting them and the mechanism (the steps by which reactants become products). Thermodynamics tells whether a reaction is feasible; kinetics tells how fast it goes.
Average rate = change in concentration ÷ time interval: r_av = −Δ[R]/Δt = +Δ[P]/Δt. Units: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (for gases, atm s⁻¹).
Instantaneous rate is the average rate as Δt → 0: r = −d[R]/dt = d[P]/dt, found from the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that instant.
For aA + bB → cC + dD: rate = −(1/a) d[A]/dt = −(1/b) d[B]/dt = (1/c) d[C]/dt = (1/d) d[D]/dt, so that every species gives the same rate.

ex.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, hydrogen is used up at 0.03 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Find the rate of formation of NH₃ and the rate of the reaction.
ex.a: NH₃ forms at 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; rate of reaction = 0.01 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹

topics.rl: Food technologists at CFTRI, Mysuru, study how fast vitamins and colours in packaged foods break down to set 'best before' dates — that is reaction kinetics.

topics.t: Factors affecting rate; rate law and rate constant
topics.h: Milk curdles faster on a hot day in Chennai than in a cool Shimla kitchen. Concentration, temperature and catalysts are the three big dials of reaction speed.
p: Rate depends on concentration of reactants (pressure for gases), temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
Rate law (rate expression): rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ, where x and y are found by experiment and need not equal the stoichiometric coefficients.
k is the rate constant: the rate when all reactant concentrations are 1 mol L⁻¹. It is constant at a fixed temperature but changes with temperature.
Examples (experimental): 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), rate = k[NO]²[O₂]; CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl, rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½; CH₃CHO → CH₄ + CO, rate = k[CH₃CHO]^(3/2).

ex.q: For 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. How does the rate change if [NO] is doubled and [O₂] is halved?

topics.rl: Indian refineries use catalysts and high temperatures to speed up cracking of heavy oil — all about turning up the 'rate dials'.

topics.t: Order of reaction and units of k
topics.h: Exam favourite: a table of initial concentrations and rates. Spot how the rate responds and the order falls out like a puzzle.
p: Order of a reaction = sum of the powers of concentration terms in the rate law (x + y for rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ). It can be 0, 1, 2, 3 or even fractional.
Zero order: rate independent of concentration; first order: rate ∝ [A]; second order: rate ∝ [A]² or [A][B].
Units of k = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹ for order n: zero order mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; first order s⁻¹; second order L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Initial-rate method: change one concentration at a time. If doubling [A] doubles the rate, order in A is 1; if it quadruples the rate, order is 2; if the rate is unchanged, order is 0.

ex.q: For A + B → products: doubling [A] at fixed [B] doubles the rate; doubling [B] at fixed [A] makes the rate 4 times. Find the rate law and overall order.

topics.rl: Pharmacologists at Indian drug companies find the order of a drug's decomposition to decide shelf life: most tablets degrade by first-order kinetics.

topics.t: Molecularity, elementary and complex reactions
topics.h: Three molecules bumping into each other at exactly the same moment, in the right way? Rare — which is why termolecular reactions are so uncommon.
p: An elementary reaction occurs in a single step. A complex reaction occurs through a sequence of elementary steps (the mechanism).
The slowest step is the rate-determining step; it controls the overall rate.

Molecularity = number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) colliding at the same time in an elementary step: unimolecular (NH₄NO₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O), bimolecular (2HI → H₂ + I₂), termolecular (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂). Molecularity above 3 is very unlikely.
Molecularity applies only to elementary reactions and cannot be zero or fractional. Order applies to any reaction and can be zero or fractional; for a complex reaction, molecularity has no meaning.
Example: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ in alkaline medium with I⁻: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]. Step 1 (slow): H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻; step 2 (fast): H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + I⁻ + O₂.

ex.q: For the I⁻-catalysed decomposition of H₂O₂, the slow step is H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻. What are the order and the molecularity of this step?
st: Two species collide in this elementary step: molecularity 2
ex.a: Order 2, molecularity 2 (bimolecular) for the slow step

topics.rl: Traffic on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway moves only as fast as the narrowest toll booth — just as a reaction goes only as fast as its rate-determining step.

topics.t: Zero order reactions and half-life
topics.h: Ammonia decomposing on a hot platinum surface ignores how much ammonia you add — the surface is already full. That's a zero order reaction.
p: Zero order: rate = k[R]⁰ = k. Integrated form: [R] = [R]₀ − kt, so k = ([R]₀ − [R]) ÷ t. A plot of [R] vs t is a straight line with slope −k and intercept [R]₀.
Examples: decomposition of NH₃ on a hot Pt surface at high pressure, 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) (rate = k because the surface is saturated); thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface.
Half-life t½ is the time for the concentration to fall to half its initial value. Zero order: t½ = [R]₀ ÷ 2k, directly proportional to the initial concentration.
First order: t½ = 0.693 ÷ k, independent of initial concentration. For the zero order case, time for complete reaction = [R]₀ ÷ k.

ex.q: A zero order reaction has k = 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ and [R]₀ = 0.8 mol L⁻¹. Find the half-life and the time for completion.

topics.rl: Catalytic converters in BS-VI vehicles work on hot metal surfaces; when the surface is saturated with exhaust gas, the conversion behaves like a zero order process.

topics.t: First order reactions
topics.h: Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from Harappan sites, radioactive iodine therapy at Tata Memorial, and how quickly a medicine leaves your body: all follow first order kinetics.
p: First order: rate = k[R]. Integrated form: ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt, i.e. k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R]). Also [R] = [R]₀e^(−kt).
Plots: ln[R] vs t is a straight line with slope −k; log([R]₀/[R]) vs t is a straight line through the origin with slope k/2.303.
Half-life t½ = 0.693/k, independent of initial concentration. After n half-lives, the fraction left = (½)ⁿ.
Useful results: time for 75% completion = 2 t½; time for 99.9% completion ≈ 10 t½. Examples: hydrogenation of ethene, decomposition of N₂O₅ and N₂O, and all natural radioactive decay.

ex.q: A first order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. How long will it take for 75% of the reactant to react?

topics.rl: Archaeologists at the Birbal Sahni Institute, Lucknow, date ancient charcoal using the first order decay of carbon-14 (half-life about 5730 years).

topics.t: Gas-phase first order reactions and pseudo first order reactions
topics.h: When a gas decomposes in a sealed flask, chemists just watch the pressure gauge. And when water is in huge excess, a second order reaction behaves like first order.
p: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g) at constant volume: if pᵢ is the initial pressure and pₜ the total pressure at time t, then p_A = 2pᵢ − pₜ.
k = (2.303/t) log[pᵢ ÷ (2pᵢ − pₜ)]. The decomposition of N₂O₅ (2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂) is a classic first order gas-phase reaction studied this way.
Pseudo first order reactions are of higher molecularity/order but behave as first order because one reactant is in large excess, so its concentration barely changes.
Acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O →(H⁺) CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH; rate = k[CH₃COOC₂H₅] since water is in excess.
Inversion of cane sugar: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O →(H⁺) C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose); rate = k[C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁].

ex.q: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), pᵢ = 0.5 atm. After 100 s the total pressure is 0.95 atm. Find k.

topics.rl: Gur and jaggery makers in Kolhapur see sucrose slowly 'invert' when cane juice is acidic — the inversion of cane sugar is the textbook pseudo first order reaction.

topics.t: Temperature, activation energy and the Arrhenius equation
topics.h: Food in a refrigerator stays fresh for days; in a Rajasthan summer it spoils in hours. Svante Arrhenius explained why temperature has such a strong effect.
p: For many reactions, the rate constant nearly doubles for a 10 K rise in temperature. Temperature coefficient = k(T + 10)/k(T), usually about 2 to 3.
Arrhenius equation: k = A e^(−Ea/RT), where A is the pre-exponential (frequency) factor, Ea is the activation energy (J mol⁻¹) and R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Reactants must reach an unstable, high-energy activated complex at the top of the energy barrier before forming products. Ea is the energy needed to reach this complex from the reactants.

The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the fraction of molecules with each kinetic energy. At a higher temperature the curve broadens and shifts towards higher energy, and the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases a lot (the area beyond Ea roughly doubles for a 10 K rise).
The factor e^(−Ea/RT) is the fraction of molecules with kinetic energy equal to or greater than Ea.

ex.q: A reaction's rate constant doubles for every 10 K rise. By what factor does it increase from 300 K to 330 K?

topics.rl: Indian cold-chain logistics for vaccines (like the eVIN-tracked supply network) keep vials at 2–8 °C precisely because degradation rates climb steeply with temperature.

topics.t: Finding Ea and the effect of a catalyst
topics.h: Two rate constants at two temperatures — that's all you need to measure the height of a reaction's energy hill. And a catalyst simply digs a tunnel through it.
p: Taking logs: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, so a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope −Ea/R (or log k vs 1/T has slope −Ea/(2.303R)).
Two temperatures: log(k₂/k₁) = [Ea ÷ (2.303R)] × [(T₂ − T₁) ÷ (T₁T₂)].
A catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy (often via an intermediate complex), and is regenerated at the end.

A catalyst does not change ΔG of the reaction or the equilibrium constant; it speeds up forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster. It cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction occur.

ex.q: The rate constant of a reaction doubles from 300 K to 310 K. Find Ea. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, log 2 = 0.3010)

topics.rl: The Haber process at fertiliser plants like those of IFFCO uses an iron catalyst so that ammonia forms fast enough at a workable temperature — the catalyst changes speed, not the equilibrium yield.

topics.t: Collision theory of reaction rates
topics.h: Billions of collisions happen every second in a gas, yet only a tiny fraction cause a reaction. Like a perfect cover drive, it needs both power and the right angle.
p: Collision theory (Max Trautz and William Lewis): reactant molecules are hard spheres, and reaction happens only when they collide. Collision frequency Z is the number of collisions per second per unit volume.
Effective collisions need enough energy (at least the threshold energy, i.e. Ea above the ground state) and proper orientation.
Rate = Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT) for energy alone; including orientation, rate = P Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT), where P is the probability (steric) factor.
Example of orientation: CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻ happens only when OH⁻ approaches the carbon from the side opposite to Br.
Limitation: atoms and molecules are treated as hard spheres, ignoring their structure.

ex.q: In collision theory, which two conditions must a collision satisfy to be effective, and where do they appear in the rate expression?
st: Energy at least equal to the threshold (Ea): e^(−Ea/RT) term

topics.rl: A bowler at Eden Gardens needs pace and the right seam angle to take a wicket; molecules need energy and orientation to react.

topics.t: Position, definition and electronic configuration
topics.h: The iron in Delhi's Mehrauli pillar, the copper in your house wiring and the zinc on a galvanised bucket all sit in the same block of the periodic table, yet zinc is not called a transition metal. Why?
p: The d-block occupies groups 3–12, where d orbitals are progressively filled. It has four transition series: 3d (Sc to Zn), 4d (Y to Cd), 5d (La and Hf to Hg) and 6d (Ac and Rf to Cn).
The f-block (placed separately at the bottom) has two series: lanthanoids (4f, Ce to Lu) and actinoids (5f, Th to Lr).

A transition element has an incompletely filled d subshell in its ground state or in any of its common oxidation states. Zn, Cd and Hg have full d¹⁰ configurations in the ground state and in their common oxidation states, so they are not regarded as transition elements (though they are studied with them).
General configuration: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²; Pd is an exception with 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰.
Exceptions in the 3d series due to the extra stability of half-filled and fully filled d orbitals: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (not 3d⁴ 4s²) and Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (not 3d⁹ 4s²).

ex.q: Copper has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell in its ground state. Why is it still called a transition element?
st: 3d⁹ is incompletely filled in a common oxidation state
ex.a: Because Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has an incomplete d subshell

topics.rl: India's Hindustan Zinc and the stainless-steel industry of Jindal both work with d-block metals; nickel and chromium make the steel in your kitchen 'stainless'.

topics.t: Physical properties, atomic sizes and ionisation enthalpies
topics.h: Tungsten in an old filament bulb stays solid above 3600 K, while mercury in a thermometer is liquid at room temperature. Both are d-block metals.
p: Transition elements are typically hard, lustrous metals with high melting and boiling points, high densities and high enthalpies of atomisation, due to strong metallic bonding that involves (n−1)d as well as ns electrons. Melting points rise to a maximum around the middle (d⁵) of each series, apart from anomalous values for Mn and Tc.
Zn, Cd and Hg have no unpaired d electrons, weaker metallic bonding, and hence low melting points; Hg is a liquid.

Across a series, atomic radius decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant because each added d electron shields the outer electrons poorly while nuclear charge increases. Density increases from Ti to Cu.

4d and 5d elements of the same group have almost identical radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) because of lanthanoid contraction: the poorly shielding 4f electrons filled before the 5d series pull the 5d atoms in.

Ionisation enthalpy rises across a series but irregularly. The second ionisation enthalpies of Cr and Cu are unusually high (removing an electron from stable d⁵ and d¹⁰ ions), and the third ionisation enthalpies of Mn (Mn²⁺ is d⁵) and Zn (Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰) are high.

ex.q: Explain why Zr and Hf have almost the same atomic radius even though Hf has 32 more electrons.
st: Between Zr (4d) and Hf (5d) come the 14 lanthanoids, filling 4f
4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly
Effective nuclear charge rises, cancelling the expected increase in size: lanthanoid contraction
ex.a: Lanthanoid contraction makes their radii nearly equal (160 pm and 159 pm)

topics.rl: Zr and Hf are so alike that separating them for India's nuclear reactors (zirconium alloy tubes must be nearly hafnium-free) is a specialised job done at the Nuclear Fuel Complex, Hyderabad.

topics.t: Oxidation states and stability of higher oxidation states
topics.h: Manganese can show every oxidation state from +2 to +7. Potassium permanganate's purple and manganese dioxide's black are just two of its many faces.
p: Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the (n−1)d and ns electrons are close in energy, so different numbers can be lost or shared; oxidation states usually differ by one.
The number of oxidation states is greatest in the middle of the 3d series: Mn shows +2 to +7. At the ends there are few: Sc mainly +3, Zn only +2.
Highest oxidation states rise up to Mn (Sc +3, Ti +4, V +5, Cr +6, Mn +7) and then fall. Low oxidation states (0, +1) appear in complexes with π-acceptor ligands like CO, e.g. Ni(CO)₄ and Fe(CO)₅.
Fluorine and oxygen stabilise high oxidation states. Oxygen does it better because it can form multiple bonds to the metal: Mn's highest fluoride is MnF₄ but its highest oxide is Mn₂O₇.

Halides: Cu(II) halides exist except the iodide, because Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂. In water, Cu⁺ disproportionates (2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu) because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy.

ex.q: Find the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄, K₂MnO₄ and MnO₂.

topics.rl: The Mn in the MnO₂ of a dry cell (+4) and in KMnO₄ used to disinfect village wells in India (+7) shows how one element can play many redox roles.

topics.t: Electrode potentials and chemical reactivity
topics.h: Most 3d metals fizz in dilute acid, but copper sits calmly in it. The answer lies in a positive standard electrode potential and the energy accounting behind it.
p: E°(M²⁺/M) is generally negative across the 3d series (e.g. Mn −1.18, Fe −0.44, Ni −0.25, Zn −0.76 V), so these metals liberate H₂ from dilute acids.

Copper is unique with E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V: its high enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation enthalpies are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy, so it does not liberate H₂ from acids (only oxidising acids like HNO₃ react).
Values for Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than the general trend: Mn²⁺ (d⁵) and Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) are extra stable, and Ni²⁺ has a very negative hydration enthalpy.

E°(M³⁺/M²⁺): Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ = +1.57 V and Co³⁺/Co²⁺ = +1.97 V are high, so Mn³⁺ and Co³⁺ are strong oxidising agents. The comparatively low value for Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77 V) reflects the stability of Fe³⁺ (d⁵). Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ = −0.41 V, so Cr²⁺ is a strong reducing agent (it becomes stable d³).
Chemical reactivity: apart from copper, 3d metals are fairly reactive and are oxidised by 1 M H⁺, although some (like Ti and V) are passive due to protective oxide films.

ex.q: Cr²⁺ and Mn³⁺ are both d⁴. Why is Cr²⁺ reducing while Mn³⁺ is oxidising?
st: Cr²⁺ (d⁴) → Cr³⁺ (d³): loses an electron to reach the stable half-filled t₂g³ arrangement — acts as a reducing agent
Mn³⁺ (d⁴) → Mn²⁺ (d⁵): gains an electron to reach the extra-stable half-filled d⁵ — acts as an oxidising agent
This matches E°: Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V, Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V
ex.a: Cr²⁺ is oxidised to stable d³; Mn³⁺ is reduced to stable d⁵

topics.rl: Copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute non-oxidising acids, but in air sour foods slowly attack it; that is why traditional copper and brass cookware in Indian kitchens is lined with tin (kalai) before acidic dishes are cooked in it.

topics.t: Magnetic properties and coloured ions
topics.h: Copper sulphate crystals are blue, potassium permanganate is purple and zinc sulphate is white. Count the unpaired d electrons and much of the mystery melts away.
p: Substances with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic (attracted by a magnetic field); those with all electrons paired are diamagnetic (weakly repelled).
Spin-only magnetic moment: μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. n = 1 → 1.73, 2 → 2.83, 3 → 3.87, 4 → 4.90, 5 → 5.92 BM.
In a complex or hydrated ion, the d orbitals split into groups of different energy. An electron absorbs visible light to jump between them (a d–d transition), and we see the complementary colour.

Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations have no d–d transitions and are colourless in water: Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺. Coloured examples: Ti³⁺ purple, V³⁺ green, Cr³⁺ violet, Mn²⁺ pink, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ yellow, Co²⁺ pink, Ni²⁺ green, Cu²⁺ blue.

ex.q: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Fe²⁺ (Z of Fe = 26).

topics.rl: MRI scanners at AIIMS use contrast agents built around strongly paramagnetic ions (gadolinium complexes), the same idea of unpaired electrons responding to a magnetic field.

topics.t: Complexes, catalysts, interstitial compounds and alloys
topics.h: The urea made in Indian fertiliser plants starts with ammonia from the iron-catalysed Haber process, and sulphuric acid plants depend on vanadium pentoxide. Transition metals are chemistry's matchmakers.
p: Transition metals form many complexes, e.g. [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and [PtCl₄]²⁻, because their ions are small, highly charged and have vacant d orbitals of suitable energy to accept lone pairs from ligands.

They are good catalysts because they can show multiple oxidation states, form complexes with reactants, and (as solids) adsorb reactants on their surface. Examples: V₂O₅ in the Contact process (SO₂ → SO₃), finely divided Fe in the Haber process, Ni in hydrogenation of oils.
Fe³⁺ catalyses 2I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ → I₂ + 2SO₄²⁻ via 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ and then 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻.

Interstitial compounds form when small atoms (H, C, N) are trapped in the metal lattice, e.g. TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆, TiH₁.₇. They are usually non-stoichiometric, have higher melting points than the pure metals, are very hard, retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert.
Alloys form readily because transition metals have similar atomic radii (within about 15%), so one can replace another in the lattice: steels with Cr, V, W, Mo, Mn; brass (Cu + Zn); bronze (Cu + Sn).

ex.q: Explain how Fe³⁺ catalyses the reaction between iodide and persulphate ions.
st: Fe³⁺ is regenerated; both steps involve oppositely charged ions, unlike the slow direct reaction between two anions
ex.a: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ shuttles electrons, using its variable oxidation states

topics.rl: Vegetable ghee (vanaspati) is made by hydrogenating vegetable oils over a nickel catalyst, and the brass of a kitchen lota is an alloy of copper and zinc.

topics.t: Oxides, oxoanions and potassium dichromate
topics.h: The orange crystals used in old breath-analyser tests and as a primary standard in volumetric analysis are potassium dichromate. Turn the solution alkaline and it switches to yellow chromate.
p: Oxides: the higher the oxidation state, the more acidic the oxide. Mn₂O₇ (+7, a covalent green oil) and CrO₃ (+6) are acidic; V₂O₅ is amphoteric though mainly acidic; Cr₂O₃ is amphoteric; CrO and MnO are basic.

Preparation of K₂Cr₂O₇ from chromite ore: 4FeCr₂O₄ + 8Na₂CO₃ + 7O₂ → 8Na₂CrO₄ + 2Fe₂O₃ + 8CO₂ (fusion in air). Acidify: 2Na₂CrO₄ + 2H⁺ → Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2Na⁺ + H₂O. Then Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2KCl → K₂Cr₂O₇ + 2NaCl (K₂Cr₂O₇ is less soluble and crystallises as orange crystals).
Chromate and dichromate interconvert with pH: 2CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O; Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O.
Structures: chromate is tetrahedral; dichromate is two tetrahedra sharing one corner, with a Cr–O–Cr bond angle of 126°.

In acid, dichromate is a strong oxidant: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (E° = 1.33 V). It oxidises I⁻ to I₂, Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, H₂S to S and Sn²⁺ to Sn⁴⁺: e.g. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. K₂Cr₂O₇ is used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis.

ex.q: Balance the ionic equation for acidified dichromate oxidising iodide.

topics.rl: Analytical labs use K₂Cr₂O₇ as a primary standard to estimate iron(II) salts such as Mohr's salt; leather tanneries in Kanpur and Chennai use chromium(III) salts derived from dichromate.

topics.t: Potassium permanganate
topics.h: A pinch of 'lal dawa' turns a bucket of water pink and kills germs. That's potassium permanganate, one of the most versatile oxidising agents in the lab.
p: Preparation: fuse MnO₂ (pyrolusite) with KOH and an oxidant (like KNO₃ or air) to form dark green K₂MnO₄: 2MnO₂ + 4KOH + O₂ → 2K₂MnO₄ + 2H₂O. In neutral or acidic solution, manganate disproportionates: 3MnO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + MnO₂ + 2H₂O.

Commercially, MnO₂ is fused with alkali and oxidised to manganate (MnO₄²⁻), which is then oxidised electrolytically in alkaline solution to permanganate (MnO₄⁻). In the lab, Mn²⁺ can be oxidised by peroxodisulphate to permanganate.
Structures: both manganate (green, paramagnetic with one unpaired electron) and permanganate (purple, diamagnetic) are tetrahedral.

Acidic medium: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (E° = 1.52 V). It oxidises I⁻ to I₂, Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, oxalate to CO₂, H₂S to S, sulphite to sulphate and nitrite to nitrate. Dilute H₂SO₄ (not HCl) is used, since HCl would be oxidised to Cl₂.

Neutral or faintly alkaline medium: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻. Iodide is oxidised to iodate (2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O + I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻ + IO₃⁻), thiosulphate to sulphate, and Mn²⁺ to MnO₂ (in the presence of zinc sulphate or zinc oxide).

ex.q: Balance the reaction of acidified permanganate with oxalate ions.

topics.rl: Indian health workers have long used KMnO₄ ('lal dawa') to disinfect wells and rinse vegetables; in CBSE titrations it acts as its own indicator, turning pink at the end point.

topics.t: The lanthanoids
topics.h: The flint in a gas lighter and the rare-earth magnets in electric vehicle motors use lanthanoids — and India's Indian Rare Earths Ltd mines them from the monazite sands of Kerala.
p: Lanthanoids are the 14 elements Ce (58) to Lu (71) after lanthanum, filling 4f orbitals. General configuration 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s²; all Ln³⁺ ions are 4fⁿ (n = 1 for Ce³⁺ to 14 for Lu³⁺).

Lanthanoid contraction: atomic and ionic radii decrease steadily from La to Lu because 4f electrons shield one another imperfectly, so effective nuclear charge rises. Consequences: 4d and 5d elements of a group have similar radii (Zr/Hf), lanthanoids are hard to separate, and basicity of Ln(OH)₃ decreases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃.

+3 is the characteristic oxidation state. Ce⁴⁺ (4f⁰) is a strong oxidant (E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V) and Tb⁴⁺ (4f⁷) is also an oxidant; Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) and Yb²⁺ (4f¹⁴) are strong reducing agents. Stability comes from empty, half-filled or filled f subshells.

Lanthanoids are silvery-white soft metals that tarnish in air. Early members are about as reactive as calcium. They liberate H₂ from dilute acids, burn in halogens to form halides, react with water to form Ln(OH)₃ and H₂, form carbides (Ln₃C, Ln₂C₃, LnC₂) with carbon at 2773 K, and give LnN with N₂ on heating.

Uses: misch metal (about 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al) in magnesium alloys for bullets, shells and lighter flints; mixed oxides as cracking catalysts; some oxides as phosphors.

ex.q: Why is Ce⁴⁺ a good oxidising agent while Eu²⁺ is a good reducing agent?
st: Ce⁴⁺ is 4f⁰ but the common state is +3, so Ce⁴⁺ tends to gain an electron: Ce⁴⁺ + e⁻ → Ce³⁺ (E° = +1.74 V)
Eu²⁺ is 4f⁷ (half-filled) but it tends to reach the common +3 state by losing an electron
Both revert to the characteristic +3 state
ex.a: Ce⁴⁺ is reduced to Ce³⁺; Eu²⁺ is oxidised to Eu³⁺

topics.rl: Kerala's beach sands contain monazite; IREL processes it for rare earths now needed for the magnets in wind turbines and EV motors under India's clean-energy push.

topics.t: The actinoids
topics.h: Uranium fuels the reactors at Tarapur and Kudankulam, and thorium from Kerala's sands is the heart of India's three-stage nuclear programme. Both are actinoids.
p: Actinoids are the 14 elements Th (90) to Lr (103), filling 5f orbitals. General configuration 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s², with irregularities because 5f and 6d are close in energy (Th is 6d² 7s²).
Actinoid contraction (decrease in size across the series) is greater than lanthanoid contraction, because 5f electrons shield even more poorly than 4f electrons.

They show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids, because 5f, 6d and 7s levels are comparable in energy. The maximum rises from +4 (Th) to +5 (Pa), +6 (U) and +7 (Np), then falls in later elements; +3 is common but not as dominant.

All actinoids are radioactive; early members have long half-lives, later ones very short. They are reactive metals, especially when finely divided; HCl attacks all of them, but HNO₃ has little effect owing to a protective oxide layer.

Compared with lanthanoids: actinoids have wider oxidation states, larger contraction, lower ionisation enthalpies (early members), more complex magnetic behaviour and are all radioactive (among lanthanoids only promethium is radioactive).

ex.q: Why do actinoids show a larger number of oxidation states than lanthanoids?
st: In actinoids, 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals have comparable energies
So varying numbers of electrons can take part in bonding
In lanthanoids, 4f is buried deeper and rarely takes part, so +3 dominates

topics.rl: BARC's Advanced Heavy Water Reactor design is meant to use thorium, and India holds a large share of the world's thorium in its coastal monazite deposits.

topics.t: Applications of d- and f-block elements and reasoning on trends
topics.h: From the steel of the Chenab rail bridge to the TiO₂ that makes paint white, transition metals build modern India. Board exams love asking 'Give reasons' about them too.
p: Iron and steels are the most important construction materials, made by alloying iron with carbon and other transition metals (Cr, Ni, Mn, V, W, Mo).
TiO₂ is used as a white pigment; MnO₂ in dry cells; Zn and Ni/Cd in batteries; Cu, Ag and Au (group 11) are coinage metals.
Catalysts: V₂O₅ (SO₂ → SO₃ in the Contact process), TiCl₄ with Al(CH₃)₃ (Ziegler catalyst) for polythene, iron in the Haber process, nickel in hydrogenation of fats.
AgBr is used in photography because it is light-sensitive.

Typical 'give reasons': high enthalpy of atomisation (unpaired d electrons, strong metallic bonds); variable oxidation states (close ns and (n−1)d energies); coloured ions (d–d transitions); catalytic power (variable oxidation states, complex formation, surface adsorption); Zr/Hf similarity (lanthanoid contraction).

ex.q: Give reason: Transition metals and many of their compounds act as good catalysts.
st: They can show variable oxidation states, forming and breaking unstable intermediates
They can form complexes with reactants
Solid metals provide a large surface for adsorption, increasing reactant concentration and weakening bonds
ex.a: Because of variable oxidation states, complex formation and surface adsorption

topics.rl: The Chenab rail bridge in Jammu and Kashmir, the world's highest railway arch bridge, uses special steels; TiO₂ pigment made from Kerala's ilmenite sands at Kerala Minerals and Metals Ltd, Chavara, whitens paints across India.

topics.t: Werner's theory and double salts
topics.h: Haemoglobin carrying oxygen in your blood, chlorophyll capturing sunlight in a paddy leaf and the EDTA test for hard water all involve coordination compounds. Alfred Werner first made sense of them.
p: Coordination compounds are central to biology (chlorophyll, haemoglobin, vitamin B₁₂), analytical chemistry, metallurgy and industry (catalysts, electroplating, dyes).

Werner treated cobalt(III) chloride–ammonia compounds with excess AgNO₃: CoCl₃·6NH₃ (yellow) gave 3 mol AgCl, CoCl₃·5NH₃ (purple) gave 2, and CoCl₃·4NH₃ (green and violet forms) gave 1 each. He wrote them as [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ and [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]Cl.

Postulates: metals show primary valence (ionisable, equal to oxidation state, satisfied by negative ions) and secondary valence (non-ionisable, equal to coordination number, satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions). Secondary valence is fixed for a metal, and the groups bound by it have a definite geometry: octahedral, tetrahedral or square planar.

Double salts (e.g. carnallite KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O, Mohr's salt FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O, potash alum KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O) dissociate completely into simple ions in water. Complex ions such as [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ in K₄[Fe(CN)₆] do not give Fe²⁺ and CN⁻ ions.

ex.q: A solution of CoCl₃·5NH₃ gives 2 mol of AgCl per mole with excess AgNO₃. Write its Werner formula and state the number of ions it gives in solution.
st: 1 Cl and 5 NH₃ are bound to Co (coordination number 6)

topics.rl: Mohr's salt, a double salt, is the standard reagent in CBSE practical titrations, while K₄[Fe(CN)₆] is a complex used as an anti-caking agent in some salts.

topics.t: Ligands, coordination number and coordination sphere
topics.h: EDTA grabs a calcium ion like a hand with six fingers. That's why a few drops of it can tell how hard your tap water is.
p: A coordination entity is a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules, e.g. [CoCl₃(NH₃)₃] or [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻. The central atom acts as a Lewis acid; the ligands, which donate electron pairs, act as Lewis bases.
Ligands by number of donor atoms: unidentate (Cl⁻, H₂O, NH₃), didentate (ethane-1,2-diamine 'en', oxalate C₂O₄²⁻), polydentate (EDTA⁴⁻, hexadentate with 2 N and 4 O donors).

A di- or polydentate ligand binding through two or more atoms to the same metal forms a ring: a chelate ligand. Ambidentate ligands can bind through either of two atoms: NO₂⁻ (through N, nitrito-N, or O, nitrito-O) and SCN⁻ (through S or N).
Coordination number (CN) = number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal: [PtCl₆]²⁻ has CN 6, [Ni(NH₃)₄]²⁺ has CN 4, [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ and [Co(en)₃]³⁺ have CN 6.
The central atom and its ligands, written in square brackets, form the coordination sphere; ions outside it are counter ions, e.g. K⁺ in K₄[Fe(CN)₆].

ex.q: Find the coordination number of the metal in [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻.

topics.rl: The EDTA titration for water hardness used by state water-testing labs works because EDTA is a hexadentate chelating ligand that holds Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ tightly.

topics.t: Coordination polyhedra, oxidation number and types of complexes
topics.h: Board papers almost always ask: 'Find the oxidation state and coordination number of the metal.' Two quick sums and you have four marks.
p: The coordination polyhedron is the spatial arrangement of ligand atoms around the metal: octahedral ([Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺), square planar ([Ni(CN)₄]²⁻) or tetrahedral ([Ni(CO)₄]).
Oxidation number of the central atom = the charge it would carry if all ligands were removed with their electron pairs. Find it from: overall charge = x + sum of ligand charges.
Ligand charges: NH₃, H₂O, CO, en are 0; Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻, NO₂⁻ are −1; C₂O₄²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ are −2; EDTA⁴⁻ is −4.
Homoleptic complexes have only one kind of ligand ([Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺); heteroleptic complexes have more than one kind ([Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺).

ex.q: Find the oxidation state and coordination number of the metal in K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃].

topics.rl: The cisplatin given as chemotherapy at Indian cancer centres is a heteroleptic square-planar Pt(II) complex.

topics.t: IUPAC nomenclature of coordination compounds
topics.h: 'Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)' sounds like a tongue-twister, but it follows a handful of clear rules. Master them and naming questions become free marks.
p: Formulas: the central atom is written first, followed by ligands in alphabetical order; polydentate ligands are also listed alphabetically (abbreviations in parentheses). The whole entity is enclosed in square brackets, with the charge outside: K₃[Fe(CN)₆], [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃.
Names: cation first, then anion (for both positive and negative complexes). Within the complex, ligands are named in alphabetical order before the metal.
Anionic ligands end in -o: chlorido, cyanido, hydroxido, oxalato, nitrito-N. Neutral ligands keep their names, except aqua (H₂O), ammine (NH₃), carbonyl (CO) and nitrosyl (NO).
Prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- show the number of simple ligands; bis-, tris-, tetrakis- are used for ligands whose names already contain a numerical prefix, e.g. bis(ethane-1,2-diamine).

The oxidation state is given in Roman numerals in parentheses. If the complex is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate (cobaltate, zincate; Latin forms for Fe → ferrate, Cu → cuprate, Ag → argentate, Au → aurate). A neutral complex has no counter ion.

ex.q: Name [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)Cl]Cl₂.
st: Complex is a cation: Co is +3 (x + 0 + 0 − 1 = +2)
tetraammine + aqua + chlorido + cobalt(III), then the counter anion

topics.rl: Chemical suppliers in India label reagent bottles with IUPAC names such as potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III), so lab technicians never confuse the Fe(II) and Fe(III) salts.

topics.t: Stereoisomerism: geometrical and optical
topics.h: Cisplatin cures certain cancers; its trans isomer does not. Same atoms, same bonds, different arrangement in space — that's stereoisomerism.
p: Isomers have the same formula but different arrangements. Stereoisomers differ in spatial arrangement (geometrical, optical); structural isomers differ in bonds (linkage, coordination, ionisation, solvate).

Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism: square planar [MX₂L₂], e.g. [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], shows cis and trans forms; octahedral [MX₂L₄], e.g. [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺, also shows cis and trans. Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism.
Octahedral [MA₃B₃], e.g. [Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃], shows fac (three identical ligands on one face) and mer (on a meridian) isomers.

Optical isomers (enantiomers, d and l forms) are non-superimposable mirror images. Common in octahedral complexes with didentate ligands: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and cis-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ are optically active; trans-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ is not (it has a plane of symmetry).
So [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ has 3 stereoisomers: trans (optically inactive) and a pair of cis enantiomers.

ex.q: How many stereoisomers does [PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ have?
st: trans has a plane of symmetry: optically inactive
cis is chiral: exists as d and l forms

topics.rl: Cancer specialists at AIIMS and Tata Memorial use cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]; the trans isomer is far less effective as a drug.

topics.t: Structural isomerism: linkage, coordination, ionisation and solvate
topics.h: [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ comes in a red form and a yellow form. The only difference is which atom of NO₂⁻ holds on to cobalt.
p: Linkage isomerism arises with ambidentate ligands: [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ is red when NO₂⁻ binds through O (nitrito-O) and yellow when it binds through N (nitrito-N).
Coordination isomerism arises from interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic complexes: [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆].
Ionisation isomerism: a counter ion and a ligand swap places, so different ions are produced in solution: [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄.
Solvate (hydrate) isomerism: water is a ligand in one isomer and water of crystallisation in another: [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet), [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (grey-green), [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O (dark green).

ex.q: How can you tell [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br from [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ in the lab?
st: [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br gives free Br⁻: AgNO₃ gives a pale yellow AgBr precipitate
[Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ gives free SO₄²⁻: BaCl₂ gives a white BaSO₄ precipitate
ex.a: Test with AgNO₃ (for Br⁻) and BaCl₂ (for SO₄²⁻)

topics.rl: Pigment chemists working on paints and inks look for compounds with the right colour, and linkage isomers show how one atom's switch can change a compound from red to yellow.

topics.t: Valence bond theory and magnetic properties
topics.h: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is diamagnetic while [CoF₆]³⁻ is strongly paramagnetic, though both contain Co³⁺. Valence bond theory explains this with hybrid orbitals.
p: In VBT the metal uses hybrid orbitals to accept ligand electron pairs: CN 4 → sp³ (tetrahedral) or dsp² (square planar); CN 6 → d²sp³ (inner orbital) or sp³d² (outer orbital), both octahedral.

[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺: Co³⁺ (3d⁶); NH₃ causes pairing, freeing two 3d orbitals → d²sp³, inner orbital, low spin, diamagnetic. [CoF₆]³⁻: no pairing; uses 4d → sp³d², outer orbital, high spin, 4 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic.
[Ni(CN)₄]²⁻: Ni²⁺ (3d⁸); CN⁻ pairs the two unpaired electrons → dsp², square planar, diamagnetic. [NiCl₄]²⁻: no pairing → sp³, tetrahedral, 2 unpaired, paramagnetic.

The measured magnetic moment tells the number of unpaired electrons (μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM) and hence the hybridisation and geometry, e.g. [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (1 unpaired, d²sp³) vs [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (5 unpaired, sp³d²).

Limitations of VBT: it does not explain colour, gives no quantitative interpretation of magnetic data or thermodynamic/kinetic stability, does not distinguish weak and strong ligands, and cannot exactly predict whether a 4-coordinate complex is tetrahedral or square planar.

ex.q: Predict the hybridisation, shape and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻.
st: Strong-field CN⁻ forces pairing, leaving one 3d orbital empty

topics.rl: Research labs in India, such as those at IISc Bengaluru, measure the magnetic moments of newly made complexes to work out how their d electrons are arranged.

topics.t: Crystal field theory: splitting, spectrochemical series and spin
topics.h: Crystal field theory treats ligands as point charges that push d orbitals apart in energy. That simple idea explains colour and magnetism together.
p: In an octahedral field, the five degenerate d orbitals split: t₂g (dxy, dyz, dxz) are lowered by 0.4Δo and eg (dx²−y², dz²) are raised by 0.6Δo. Δo is the crystal field splitting energy.
Spectrochemical series (increasing Δo): I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO.
For d⁴–d⁷ ions, the fourth electron can pair in t₂g or enter eg. If Δo < P (pairing energy, weak field) → high spin, e.g. d⁴ as t₂g³eg¹. If Δo > P (strong field) → low spin, e.g. d⁴ as t₂g⁴eg⁰.

In a tetrahedral field the splitting is reversed (e lower, t₂ higher) and smaller: Δt = (4/9)Δo. Because Δt is small, pairing is rarely favoured and low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed.

ex.q: Write the d-electron configuration of a d⁶ ion in an octahedral field with (i) Δo < P and (ii) Δo > P, and count the unpaired electrons.
st: Weak field (Δo < P): t₂g⁴eg², four unpaired electrons
Strong field (Δo > P): t₂g⁶eg⁰, no unpaired electrons
ex.a: High spin t₂g⁴eg² (4 unpaired); low spin t₂g⁶ (0 unpaired)

topics.rl: The deep blue of the copper(II) ammonia complex that students see in Class 12 salt analysis comes from a crystal-field splitting that absorbs orange-red light.

topics.t: Colour in coordination compounds and limits of CFT
topics.h: Ruby and emerald both owe their colour to Cr³⁺ ions, yet one is red and the other green. The surrounding crystal field makes the difference.
p: A complex absorbs light whose energy matches a d–d transition (from t₂g to eg in octahedral complexes); we see the complementary colour of the absorbed light.

[Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) absorbs in the blue-green region and appears violet. Without ligands there is no splitting and no colour: anhydrous CuSO₄ is white but CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue; heating [Ti(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ to remove water makes it colourless.
Changing the ligand changes Δo and the colour: green [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ turns violet as en replaces water, forming [Ni(en)₃]²⁺.
Gemstones: ruby is Al₂O₃ with about 0.5–1% Cr³⁺; emerald has Cr³⁺ in beryl (Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈). The different surroundings give different splitting and colours.

Limitations of CFT: ligands are treated as point charges, so anionic ligands should give the greatest splitting, but they lie at the weak end of the spectrochemical series; CFT also ignores the covalent character of metal–ligand bonding.

ex.q: Explain why [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is violet, and why the compound becomes colourless when heated to remove the water ligands.
st: Ti³⁺ is 3d¹; in [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ the electron sits in t₂g
It absorbs blue-green light to jump to eg
The transmitted complementary colour is violet; without ligands there is no splitting and no d–d absorption
ex.a: Violet colour comes from a t₂g → eg transition caused by the water ligand field

topics.rl: Jaipur's gem-cutters prize rubies and emeralds; physicists explain both colours with crystal field splitting of Cr³⁺ in different host crystals.

topics.t: Bonding in metal carbonyls
topics.h: Nickel tetracarbonyl is so volatile that impure nickel can be purified by turning it into a gas and back. The trick lies in a special two-way bond.
p: Homoleptic carbonyls contain only CO ligands: Ni(CO)₄ is tetrahedral, Fe(CO)₅ is trigonal bipyramidal, Cr(CO)₆ is octahedral.
Mn₂(CO)₁₀ has two square pyramidal Mn(CO)₅ units joined by a Mn–Mn bond. Co₂(CO)₈ has a Co–Co bond bridged by two CO groups.

The metal–carbon bond has both σ and π character: the C atom of CO donates a lone pair into a vacant metal orbital (σ bond), and a filled metal d orbital donates electron density back into the vacant antibonding π* orbital of CO (π back-bond).
This synergic bonding strengthens the M–C bond and weakens the C≡O bond, which is why metals in very low oxidation states (such as 0) are stabilised by CO.

ex.q: Explain why the metal–carbon bond in Ni(CO)₄ is strong.
st: σ donation: lone pair on C of CO → vacant orbital of Ni
π back-donation: filled Ni d orbital → empty π* of CO
Each interaction strengthens the other (synergic effect)
ex.a: Because of synergic σ donation and π back-bonding

topics.rl: Mond's process uses Ni(CO)₄ to purify nickel, and metal carbonyl catalysts help make chemicals in Indian petrochemical plants.

topics.t: Importance and applications of coordination compounds
topics.h: From the haemoglobin in a cricketer's blood to the gold refined at Karnataka's Hutti mines and the cancer drug cisplatin, coordination chemistry is everywhere.
p: Analysis: many metal ions are detected or estimated through coloured complexes (e.g. Ni²⁺ with dimethylglyoxime). Hardness of water is found by titration with Na₂EDTA, which forms stable complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Biology: chlorophyll (photosynthesis) is a Mg complex, haemoglobin (oxygen carrier) is an Fe complex, and vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin, the anti-pernicious-anaemia factor) is a Co complex.
Metallurgy: Ag and Au are extracted as soluble cyanide complexes [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ and [Au(CN)₂]⁻, then recovered by displacement with zinc. Impure nickel is purified via volatile [Ni(CO)₄] (Mond process).

Catalysis and industry: Wilkinson's catalyst [(Ph₃P)₃RhCl] hydrogenates alkenes. Complexes like [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ and [Au(CN)₂]⁻ give smoother, more even electroplated deposits. In photography, undecomposed AgBr is dissolved by hypo as [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.
Medicine: chelate therapy removes toxic metals — EDTA for lead poisoning; D-penicillamine and desferrioxamine B remove excess copper and iron. cis-Platin and related complexes inhibit tumour growth.

ex.q: Which complex-forming reagent is used to estimate the hardness of water, and why does it work?
st: Na₂EDTA forms very stable complexes with them
The volume of EDTA needed to complex all the Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ gives their amount
ex.a: Na₂EDTA, by forming stable complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺

topics.rl: Gold mines such as Hutti in Karnataka extract gold by cyanide leaching, and today Indian hospitals use cisplatin for testicular, ovarian and other cancers.

topics.t: Classification and nomenclature of halo compounds
topics.h: PVC water pipes start from vinyl chloride, chloroquine treats malaria, and the halothane once used in operation theatres is a haloalkane. Naming and classifying them is step one.
p: By number of halogen atoms: mono-, di-, tri- or polyhalo compounds.

Compounds with an sp³ C–X bond: alkyl halides (1°, 2° or 3°, by the carbon bearing X), allylic halides (X on an sp³ carbon next to C=C, e.g. CH₂=CH–CH₂Br) and benzylic halides (X on an sp³ carbon attached to a benzene ring, e.g. C₆H₅CH₂Cl).
Compounds with an sp² C–X bond: vinylic halides (X on a C=C carbon, e.g. CH₂=CHCl) and aryl halides (X directly on an aromatic ring, e.g. C₆H₅Cl).
IUPAC names treat halogens as prefixes: CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)CH₃ is 2-chlorobutane, (CH₃)₃CBr is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, CH₂=CHCH₂Br is 3-bromoprop-1-ene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl is (chloromethyl)benzene.

Dihalides: geminal (gem) have both X on the same carbon, e.g. CH₃CHCl₂ (1,1-dichloroethane, ethylidene chloride); vicinal (vic) have X on adjacent carbons, e.g. ClCH₂CH₂Cl (1,2-dichloroethane, ethylene dichloride).

ex.q: Give the IUPAC name and classify (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl.
st: Longest chain containing C–Cl: 3 carbons, Cl on C-1, CH₃ on C-2
The carbon bearing Cl is attached to only one other carbon → primary

topics.rl: The antimalarial chloroquine and the antiseptic chloroxylenol are halogen compounds, and PVC pipes laid under Indian cities are polymers of chloroethene (vinyl chloride).

topics.t: Nature of the C–X bond and physical properties
topics.h: Chloroform is so dense that it sinks under water in a test tube. Halogens make molecules heavier, more polar and stickier.
p: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar (Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻). From F to I the halogen gets larger, so bond length increases (CH₃F 139 pm → CH₃I 214 pm) and bond enthalpy decreases (452 → 234 kJ mol⁻¹).
Dipole moments: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) > CH₃F (1.847 D) > CH₃Br (1.830 D) > CH₃I (1.636 D); CH₃F is lower than CH₃Cl because of its very short bond.

Boiling points: higher than hydrocarbons of similar mass (polarity, greater mass); RI > RBr > RCl > RF; for isomers, bp decreases with branching (1-bromobutane > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane).
para-Dihalobenzenes have higher melting points than ortho and meta isomers because their symmetry lets them pack better in the crystal lattice.

Bromo, iodo and polychloro compounds are denser than water. Haloalkanes are only slightly soluble in water (the energy needed to break water's hydrogen bonds is not recovered) but dissolve well in organic solvents.

ex.q: Arrange 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in decreasing order of boiling point.
st: All three have the formula C₄H₉Br (same mass)
More branching → more compact shape → smaller surface area → weaker van der Waals forces
