topics.rl: Mothballs used in Indian wardrobes are often 1,4-dichlorobenzene; being the symmetric para isomer, it is a solid that slowly sublimes.

topics.t: Preparation of haloalkanes
topics.h: Thionyl chloride is a chemist's favourite for turning alcohols into chlorides. Its by-products simply bubble away as gases, leaving a pure product behind.
p: From alcohols with HX: R–OH + HCl →(ZnCl₂) R–Cl + H₂O. ZnCl₂ is needed for primary and secondary alcohols; tertiary alcohols react with concentrated HCl at room temperature. Reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°.
With phosphorus halides: 3R–OH + PX₃ → 3R–X + H₃PO₃ (PBr₃, PI₃ generated in situ from red P and Br₂/I₂); R–OH + PCl₅ → R–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl.
With thionyl chloride: R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑. Preferred, because both by-products are gases that escape, leaving pure alkyl chloride.
These methods are not used for aryl halides because the C–O bond in phenols has partial double bond character and is hard to break.

Halogen exchange: Finkelstein reaction R–X + NaI →(dry acetone) R–I + NaX (X = Cl, Br); NaCl or NaBr precipitates in acetone, driving the reaction forward. Swarts reaction: CH₃–Br + AgF → CH₃–F + AgBr (also with Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃).

ex.q: Why is thionyl chloride preferred for converting ethanol into chloroethane?
st: Both by-products are gases and escape
No separation is needed, giving pure chloroethane
ex.a: Because its by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases, leaving the product pure

topics.rl: India's pharmaceutical industry, the 'pharmacy of the world', uses thionyl chloride and halogen-exchange reactions in many drug syntheses.

topics.t: Preparation of haloarenes
topics.h: You can't chlorinate benzene the way you'd chlorinate methane; it needs a Lewis acid helper, or a clever detour through a diazonium salt.
p: Electrophilic substitution: benzene + Cl₂ (or Br₂) with a Lewis acid catalyst (Fe or anhydrous FeCl₃/FeBr₃) in the dark gives chlorobenzene (or bromobenzene). Methylbenzene gives a mixture of ortho and para isomers, which can be separated (the para isomer has a higher melting point).
Iodination is reversible and needs an oxidising agent (HNO₃ or HIO₄) to remove the HI formed. Fluorination is too violent to control, so fluoroarenes are not made this way.
Sandmeyer reaction: an arenediazonium salt (from aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K) is treated with CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr, replacing –N₂⁺ by Cl or Br: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + CuCl → C₆H₅Cl + N₂.
Iodobenzene is made simply by shaking the diazonium salt with potassium iodide: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + KI → C₆H₅I + KCl + N₂.

ex.q: How would you prepare iodobenzene from aniline?
st: Diazotise: aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K → benzenediazonium chloride
ex.a: Diazotisation followed by treatment with KI

topics.rl: Chlorobenzene from plants in Gujarat's chemical clusters is a starting material for pesticides and dyes.

topics.t: Nucleophilic substitution: products and ambident nucleophiles
topics.h: A haloalkane is like a kabaddi raider with a weak hold: a nucleophile tags the carbon and the halide is pushed out. Swap the nucleophile and you get a whole family of products.
p: In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile (electron-rich species) attacks the partially positive carbon of C–X and the halide leaves: Nu⁻ + R–X → R–Nu + X⁻.

Products: OH⁻ (aq KOH) → alcohol; R′O⁻ → ether; I⁻ → alkyl iodide; NH₃ → amine; KCN → alkyl cyanide (nitrile); AgCN → isocyanide; KNO₂ → alkyl nitrite; AgNO₂ → nitroalkane; R′COOAg → ester; LiAlH₄ → hydrocarbon.

Ambident nucleophiles can attack through two different atoms. Cyanide: KCN is ionic, giving free CN⁻ that attacks through carbon (C–C bond is more stable), forming R–CN. AgCN is mainly covalent, so only nitrogen's lone pair is available, forming R–NC.
Nitrite: KNO₂ attacks through oxygen to give alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O; AgNO₂ attacks through nitrogen to give nitroalkane R–NO₂.
Reaction with KCN is useful for increasing the carbon chain by one carbon.

ex.q: What products form when bromoethane reacts with (i) KCN and (ii) AgCN?
st: KCN is ionic: CN⁻ attacks through C → CH₃CH₂CN (propanenitrile)
AgCN is covalent: N attacks → CH₃CH₂NC (ethyl isocyanide)

topics.rl: Many Indian drug syntheses use cyanide substitution to add one carbon to a chain, followed by converting the nitrile into an acid or amine.

topics.t: SN2 and SN1 mechanisms and reactivity
topics.h: Two routes, one goal: SN2 is a single swift tackle from behind; SN1 waits for the halide to leave first. Which route a molecule takes depends on its crowding.
p: SN2 (substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular): one step; the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to X (backside attack) as X leaves; the transition state has carbon partly bonded to both. Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (second order). Configuration is inverted (Walden inversion). Example: CH₃Cl + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Cl⁻.
SN2 reactivity: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°, because bulky groups hinder the backside approach (steric hindrance).

SN1 (unimolecular): two steps — slow ionisation of R–X to a carbocation (rate-determining), then fast attack by the nucleophile. Rate = k[RX] (first order). Favoured in polar protic solvents (water, alcohol, acetic acid). Example: (CH₃)₃CBr + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH + Br⁻.
SN1 reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°, following carbocation stability. Allylic and benzylic halides are very reactive in SN1 because their carbocations are stabilised by resonance.
For the same alkyl group, reactivity of the halide in both mechanisms: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (weaker C–X bond, better leaving group).

ex.q: Arrange CH₃Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr and (CH₃)₃CBr in order of increasing SN2 reactivity, and in order of increasing SN1 reactivity.
st: SN2 is slowed by crowding: (CH₃)₃CBr < (CH₃)₂CHBr < CH₃Br
SN1 depends on carbocation stability: CH₃Br < (CH₃)₂CHBr < (CH₃)₃CBr

topics.rl: Medicinal chemists in Indian labs choose SN2 routes when a drug molecule needs one specific inverted 3D arrangement, since enzymes in the body can tell mirror-image forms apart.

topics.t: Stereochemistry: optical activity, chirality and configuration
topics.h: Your left and right hands are mirror images that never superimpose. Many molecules are 'handed' too, and they twist polarised light in opposite directions.
p: Optically active compounds rotate the plane of plane-polarised light (measured in a polarimeter): dextrorotatory (d or +) to the right, laevorotatory (l or −) to the left.

A carbon bonded to four different groups is an asymmetric carbon (stereocentre); a molecule that is not superimposable on its mirror image is chiral. Butan-2-ol and 2-chlorobutane are chiral; propan-2-ol and 2-chloropropane are achiral.
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. They have identical physical properties (mp, bp, solubility) except the direction of rotation of plane-polarised light.

A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers and shows zero rotation (external compensation); it is written dl or (±). Converting an enantiomer into a racemic mixture is racemisation.

Retention: the spatial arrangement around the stereocentre is preserved. SN2 gives inversion of configuration; SN1 gives mostly racemisation, because the planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.

ex.q: Optically active 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed by aqueous KOH via (i) SN2 and (ii) SN1. What is the stereochemistry of butan-2-ol in each case?
st: (i) SN2: backside attack → inverted configuration, still optically active
(ii) SN1: planar carbocation → attack from both faces
Equal amounts of both enantiomers → racemic mixture, optically inactive
ex.a: SN2 gives inversion; SN1 gives racemisation

topics.rl: Some medicines are sold as a single enantiomer because one mirror form works better in the body; for example, the acid-reducer esomeprazole is the single-enantiomer form of omeprazole.

topics.t: Elimination, and reactions with metals
topics.h: Heat 2-bromopentane with alcoholic KOH and two alkenes form, but one wins by a big margin. Zaitsev's rule predicts the winner.
p: Dehydrohalogenation (β-elimination): a haloalkane with a β-hydrogen, heated with alcoholic KOH, loses H and X from adjacent carbons to form an alkene.
Zaitsev (Saytzeff) rule: the preferred alkene is the one with more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons. E.g. 2-bromopentane gives pent-2-ene (81%) rather than pent-1-ene (19%).

Substitution vs elimination: a strong, bulky base favours elimination; primary halides prefer SN2; secondary give SN2 or elimination depending on the base/nucleophile; tertiary give SN1 or elimination depending on carbocation stability and alkene substitution.

Grignard reagent: R–X + Mg →(dry ether) R–MgX. The C–Mg bond is highly polar, so R behaves as a carbanion and reacts with any proton source: RMgX + H₂O → R–H + Mg(OH)X. Hence it must be made under anhydrous conditions. (Victor Grignard, Nobel Prize 1912.)
Wurtz reaction: 2R–X + 2Na →(dry ether) R–R + 2NaX, doubling the alkyl group.

ex.q: Predict the major product when 2-bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH.
st: β-hydrogens are on C-1 and C-3
Loss of H from C-3 gives but-2-ene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃, more substituted)
Loss of H from C-1 gives but-1-ene (less substituted)
By Zaitsev's rule, the more substituted alkene is major

topics.rl: Grignard reactions are workhorses in API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) plants in Hyderabad, where moisture is kept out carefully because water destroys the reagent.

topics.t: Reactions of haloarenes
topics.h: Boil chlorobenzene with aqueous NaOH and almost nothing happens. Industry had to use 623 K and 300 atmospheres to make phenol from it — the Dow process.
p: Haloarenes are much less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophiles because: (i) resonance gives the C–X bond partial double bond character; (ii) the sp² carbon holds the bond more tightly (C–Cl 169 pm in chlorobenzene vs 177 pm in CH₃Cl); (iii) the phenyl cation is not resonance stabilised, so SN1 is ruled out; (iv) the electron-rich ring repels nucleophiles and blocks backside attack.
Dow process: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm gives sodium phenoxide, which is acidified to phenol.

Electron-withdrawing groups like –NO₂ at ortho and para positions make substitution much easier (1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene, then 2,4-dinitro, then 2,4,6-trinitro react under progressively milder conditions); a meta –NO₂ has no such effect.

Electrophilic substitution: the halogen is deactivating (–I effect) but ortho/para directing (+R effect). Chlorination, nitration, sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts alkylation/acylation of chlorobenzene give mainly the para product with some ortho.
Wurtz–Fittig: Ar–X + R–X + 2Na → Ar–R + 2NaX (dry ether). Fittig: 2Ar–X + 2Na → Ar–Ar + 2NaX, e.g. diphenyl from chlorobenzene.

ex.q: Why does 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene react with NaOH much more easily than chlorobenzene?
st: OH⁻ attacks the carbon bearing Cl
The negative charge of the intermediate is delocalised onto the para –NO₂ group
This stabilises the intermediate and lowers the activation energy
ex.a: The para nitro group withdraws electrons and stabilises the intermediate

topics.rl: Dyes and pesticides made in Indian chemical hubs such as Ankleshwar often start from nitrochlorobenzenes, which react easily because of their activating nitro groups.

topics.t: Polyhalogen compounds: dichloromethane, chloroform and iodoform
topics.h: Chloroform was once the anaesthetic of choice in operating rooms. Then doctors noticed something deadly could form from it if bottles were left in the light.
p: Dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂): used as a solvent (paint remover), aerosol propellant, process solvent in drug manufacture and for metal cleaning and finishing. It harms the central nervous system: low exposure can slightly impair hearing and vision; higher levels cause dizziness, nausea and tingling or numbness in fingers and toes; on the skin it causes intense burning, and it can burn the cornea.

Trichloromethane (chloroform, CHCl₃): solvent for fats, alkaloids and iodine; used to make the refrigerant R-22; once a general anaesthetic, now replaced by safer ones. Breathing its vapour depresses the central nervous system; chronic exposure can damage the liver and kidneys.

In air and light, chloroform is slowly oxidised to the extremely poisonous gas phosgene: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ →(light) 2COCl₂ + 2HCl. So it is stored in closed, dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim to keep out air.

Triiodomethane (iodoform, CHI₃) was used as an antiseptic; its action is due to the free iodine it releases, not iodoform itself. Because of its objectionable smell it has been replaced by other iodine-based preparations.
Lab safety: handle these volatile liquids only in a fume hood, with gloves and goggles, and never sniff them directly.

ex.q: Why is chloroform stored in closed dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim?
st: Light and air oxidise chloroform: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ → 2COCl₂ + 2HCl
Dark glass blocks light and a full bottle leaves no air
ex.a: To prevent its oxidation to poisonous phosgene

topics.rl: Industrial safety rules under India's Factories Act require proper ventilation where solvents like dichloromethane are used, for example in paint-stripping and pharma units.

topics.t: CCl₄, freons and DDT: uses and environmental effects
topics.h: The Montreal Protocol, which India signed, phased out CFCs to heal the ozone hole. The same chlorine chemistry that made freons useful made them dangerous up in the stratosphere.
p: Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄): used to make refrigerants, aerosol propellants and CFCs, in pharmaceutical manufacture and as a solvent; earlier used as a cleaning fluid, spot remover and fire extinguisher. Exposure can cause liver cancer, nerve damage, dizziness and nausea. Released into air, it rises to the stratosphere and depletes the ozone layer.

Freons are chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) of methane and ethane: stable, unreactive, non-toxic, non-corrosive and easily liquefied. Freon-12 (CCl₂F₂) is the most common, made from CCl₄ by the Swarts reaction; used in refrigeration, air conditioning and aerosols.

In the stratosphere, UV light breaks CFCs into chlorine radicals that start chain reactions destroying ozone, letting more harmful UV reach Earth (risk of skin cancer, eye disease and weakened immunity).

DDT (p,p′-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) was the first chlorinated organic insecticide. It was first made in 1873; its insecticidal power was discovered by Paul Müller in 1939 (Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1948). It was widely used against mosquitoes spreading malaria and lice carrying typhus.

Problems with DDT: insects developed resistance; it is highly toxic to fish; it is chemically stable and fat-soluble, so it is not metabolised quickly, gets stored in fatty tissues and builds up along food chains. It was banned in the USA in 1973.

ex.q: Why does DDT become more concentrated in animals higher up a food chain?
st: DDT is chemically stable and fat-soluble
It is not broken down quickly and is stored in fatty tissue
Each predator eats many contaminated organisms, accumulating more
ex.a: Because it is persistent and fat-soluble, it accumulates along the food chain

topics.rl: Under the Montreal Protocol, India completed its CFC phase-out ahead of the Protocol's 2010 deadline and is now phasing out HCFCs used in air conditioners; DDT use in India is restricted to public-health vector control.

topics.t: Classification, nomenclature and structures
topics.h: The sanitiser on your hands (ethanol or propan-2-ol), the glycerol in your soap and the phenol-based disinfectant in a hospital corridor all carry an –OH group. Naming them right is half the battle.
p: By number of –OH groups: monohydric (ethanol), dihydric (ethane-1,2-diol, glycol), trihydric (propane-1,2,3-triol, glycerol) and polyhydric compounds.

Alcohols with sp³ C–OH: 1°, 2°, 3° (by the carbon bearing OH), allylic (CH₂=CH–CH₂OH, prop-2-en-1-ol) and benzylic (C₆H₅CH₂OH, phenylmethanol). With sp² C–OH: vinylic alcohols (CH₂=CH–OH) and phenols (OH on a benzene ring).

IUPAC: replace -e of the alkane by -ol: (CH₃)₂CHOH is propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Phenols: o-cresol is 2-methylphenol; catechol, resorcinol and quinol (hydroquinone) are benzene-1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-diol.

Ethers R–O–R′ are simple (symmetrical, same groups: C₂H₅OC₂H₅, ethoxyethane) or mixed (unsymmetrical: CH₃OC₂H₅, methoxyethane). IUPAC names them as alkoxyalkanes; C₆H₅OCH₃ is methoxybenzene (anisole).

Structures: C–O–H angle in methanol is 108.9° (lone pair repulsion); C–O–C in methoxymethane is 111.7° (bulky groups). In phenol the C–O bond (136 pm) is shorter than in methanol (142 pm) because of partial double bond character from resonance and the sp² carbon.

ex.q: Name (CH₃)₂CH–CH(OH)–CH₃ and classify it.
st: Longest chain with C–OH: 4 carbons, numbered so OH gets the lower number
OH on C-2, CH₃ on C-3
The C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons

topics.rl: Hand sanitisers approved in India contain ethanol or propan-2-ol (isopropyl alcohol), and glycerol is added to keep skin moist.

topics.t: Preparation of alcohols
topics.h: Propene can give two different alcohols depending on the route: acid-catalysed hydration or hydroboration–oxidation. Your choice of reagent decides the product.
p: Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes follows Markovnikov's rule: CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O →(H⁺) CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Mechanism: (1) protonation of the alkene by H₃O⁺ to form a carbocation; (2) nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation; (3) loss of a proton to give the alcohol.

Hydroboration–oxidation: diborane adds to the alkene, and the trialkylborane is oxidised by H₂O₂ in aqueous NaOH. The product looks like anti-Markovnikov addition of water: propene → propan-1-ol, in excellent yield.

Reduction of carbonyl compounds with H₂ (Pt, Pd or Ni), NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄: aldehydes give 1° alcohols and ketones give 2° alcohols. Carboxylic acids are reduced to 1° alcohols by LiAlH₄; industrially, acids are first converted to esters, which are then hydrogenated catalytically.
Grignard reagents add to carbonyl compounds, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives alcohols: methanal → 1° alcohol, other aldehydes → 2° alcohols, ketones → 3° alcohols.

ex.q: Which carbonyl compound and Grignard reagent would you use to make 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
ex.a: Propanone with methylmagnesium bromide, followed by hydrolysis

topics.rl: Propan-2-ol used in Indian sanitiser factories is made mainly by hydration of propene from refinery cracking units.

topics.t: Preparation of phenols and physical properties
topics.h: Most of the world's phenol comes from cumene, and the same process gives acetone as a valuable bonus. Two products for the price of one!
p: From haloarenes: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm → sodium phenoxide → acidify → phenol.
From benzenesulphonic acid: sulphonate benzene with oleum, fuse the sulphonic acid with molten NaOH to get sodium phenoxide, then acidify.
From diazonium salts: aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K gives benzenediazonium chloride, which on warming with water (or dilute acid) gives phenol.
From cumene (isopropylbenzene): air oxidation gives cumene hydroperoxide, which with dilute acid gives phenol and acetone (propanone). Most phenol worldwide is made this way.

Physical properties: alcohols and phenols have much higher boiling points than hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of similar mass because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Boiling point rises with more carbon atoms and falls with branching. Lower alcohols are miscible with water (H-bonding); solubility falls as the alkyl group grows.

ex.q: Outline the cumene process for making phenol.
ex.a: Phenol, with acetone as a co-product

topics.rl: Phenol from Indian petrochemical plants goes into making bakelite switches, epoxy resins and the antiseptic 'carbolic' soaps once common in Indian homes.

topics.t: Reactions with metals and acidity of alcohols and phenols
topics.h: Phenol (carbolic acid) is about a million times more acidic than ethanol, yet it still can't fizz with baking soda. Resonance explains both facts.
p: Alcohols and phenols react with active metals to give H₂: 2R–OH + 2Na → 2R–O⁻Na⁺ + H₂; phenol also reacts with aqueous NaOH to form sodium phenoxide (alcohols do not react appreciably with NaOH).

Alcohols are very weak Brønsted acids, weaker than water: R–O⁻ + H₂O → R–OH + OH⁻ (alkoxide is a stronger base than hydroxide). Acidity order: 1° > 2° > 3°, because electron-releasing alkyl groups increase electron density on oxygen.

Phenol is more acidic (pKa ≈ 10.0) than ethanol (pKa ≈ 15.9): the OH is on an electron-withdrawing sp² carbon, and the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its negative charge over the ring.
Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. –NO₂) increase phenol's acidity, especially at ortho and para positions: p-nitrophenol pKa 7.1, o-nitrophenol 7.2, m-nitrophenol 8.3, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol 0.5.
Electron-releasing groups (e.g. –CH₃) decrease acidity: o-, m- and p-cresols have pKa about 10.1–10.2. Phenol is too weak to react with NaHCO₃.

ex.q: Arrange phenol, p-nitrophenol, p-cresol and ethanol in increasing order of acidity.

topics.rl: Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol), as acidic as a strong acid, was historically used as an explosive and in burn ointments; today it is handled only under strict safety rules.

topics.t: Esterification, C–O cleavage and dehydration
topics.h: Turn salicylic acid into aspirin, find whether an alcohol is 1°, 2° or 3° in five minutes, or turn ethanol into ethene: three reactions every Class 12 student must know.
p: Esterification: R–OH + R′COOH ⇌(conc. H₂SO₄) R′COOR + H₂O (water is removed as it forms to shift the equilibrium). With acid anhydrides (H⁺) or acid chlorides (in pyridine, which neutralises HCl). Acetylation of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride gives aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid).
With HX: R–OH + HX → R–X + H₂O. Lucas test (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂): tertiary alcohols give turbidity immediately, secondary after a few minutes, primary not at room temperature.
With phosphorus trihalides: 3R–OH + PBr₃ → 3R–Br + H₃PO₃.

Dehydration to alkenes with conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ (or anhydrous ZnCl₂, alumina): ethanol at 443 K with conc. H₂SO₄ gives ethene; 2° alcohols need 85% H₃PO₄ at 440 K; 3° alcohols only 20% H₃PO₄ at 358 K. Ease: 3° > 2° > 1°.
Mechanism of dehydration: (1) protonation of the alcohol (fast); (2) loss of water to form a carbocation (slow, rate-determining); (3) loss of H⁺ from an adjacent carbon to form the alkene.

ex.q: Why do tertiary alcohols give the Lucas test immediately while primary alcohols do not at room temperature?
st: The test involves forming an alkyl chloride via a carbocation
Tertiary carbocations are very stable and form quickly
The insoluble alkyl chloride makes the solution cloudy (turbid) at once
ex.a: Because 3° alcohols form stable carbocations rapidly, giving insoluble chlorides immediately

topics.rl: Aspirin, made by acetylating salicylic acid, is among the most widely produced drugs in India's pharmaceutical sector.

topics.t: Oxidation of alcohols and distinguishing tests
topics.h: Breathalysers used by traffic police once relied on orange dichromate turning green as it oxidised ethanol. Oxidation is also how we tell 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols apart.
p: Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids. Strong oxidants (acidified KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇) give acids; to stop at the aldehyde use CrO₃ in anhydrous medium or PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate, a complex of CrO₃ with pyridine and HCl).
Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones (e.g. by CrO₃). Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation; under strong conditions (KMnO₄, heat) they break into a mixture of acids with fewer carbon atoms.
Dehydrogenation over hot copper at 573 K: 1° alcohol → aldehyde; 2° alcohol → ketone; 3° alcohol → alkene (dehydration), e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol → 2-methylpropene.

Distinguishing tests: neutral FeCl₃ gives a violet colour with phenol (alcohols do not); bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol with phenol; Lucas test classifies alcohols; alcohols with CH₃CH(OH)– (e.g. ethanol, propan-2-ol) give a yellow iodoform precipitate with I₂/NaOH.

ex.q: How would you distinguish between ethanol and phenol?
st: Add neutral FeCl₃ solution to each
Ethanol gives no such colour (also, ethanol gives the iodoform test, phenol does not)
ex.a: Phenol gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃; ethanol does not

topics.rl: Modern breath-analysers mostly use fuel-cell sensors, but the classic dichromate test is still a favourite Class 12 demonstration of alcohol oxidation.

topics.t: Reactions of phenol: electrophilic substitution and named reactions
topics.h: Aspirin starts from salicylic acid, which comes from phenol by Kolbe's reaction. Phenol's super-activated ring makes such chemistry easy.
p: The –OH group strongly activates the ring and directs electrophiles to ortho and para positions.

Nitration: dilute HNO₃ at 298 K gives o- and p-nitrophenol, separated by steam distillation (o-nitrophenol is steam volatile because of intramolecular H-bonding; p-nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonding). Concentrated HNO₃ gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid), better made via phenol-2,4-disulphonic acid.
Halogenation: Br₂ in CS₂ or CHCl₃ at low temperature gives mono-bromophenols (mainly para) without a Lewis acid; bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

Kolbe's reaction: sodium phenoxide + CO₂, then acid → 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid). Reimer–Tiemann reaction: phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH, then acid → 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde).
Phenol heated with zinc dust gives benzene. Oxidation with chromic acid gives benzoquinone (a conjugated diketone); on standing in air, phenols slowly form dark coloured mixtures containing quinones.

ex.q: How are o- and p-nitrophenol separated after nitration of phenol?
st: o-Nitrophenol has an intramolecular H-bond (between –OH and –NO₂ on adjacent carbons)
So it does not associate and is steam volatile
p-Nitrophenol forms intermolecular H-bonds and is not steam volatile
ex.a: By steam distillation: o-nitrophenol distils over

topics.rl: Methyl salicylate (from salicylic acid) gives many Indian pain-relief balms their wintergreen smell; salicylic acid itself is made from phenol by Kolbe's reaction.

topics.t: Commercially important alcohols: methanol and ethanol
topics.h: India's E20 petrol blends ethanol from sugarcane molasses into fuel. Its cousin methanol, however, is a deadly poison if swallowed.
p: Methanol (wood spirit) was once made by destructive distillation of wood. Today it is made by catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide: CO + 2H₂ →(ZnO–Cr₂O₃, 200–300 atm, 573–673 K) CH₃OH.
Methanol is highly poisonous: drinking even small amounts can cause blindness, and larger amounts cause death. It is used as a solvent for paints and varnishes and to make formaldehyde.

Ethanol is made by fermentation of sugars (from molasses, sugarcane or fruits like grapes) using yeast enzymes: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O →(invertase) C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose); C₆H₁₂O₆ →(zymase) 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Fermentation is anaerobic; if air enters, ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid, making the product sour.
Commercial ethanol is made unfit for drinking by adding copper sulphate (to colour it) and pyridine (a foul-smelling liquid): this is denatured alcohol.
Uses of ethanol: solvent in the paint industry, in making many carbon compounds, and as a fuel blended with petrol.

ex.q: Write the two enzyme-catalysed steps in making ethanol from sucrose.
st: Both enzymes come from yeast; conditions are anaerobic
ex.a: Invertase hydrolyses sucrose; zymase ferments the hexoses to ethanol and CO₂

topics.rl: Sugar mills in Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh run distilleries that turn molasses into fuel ethanol for blending with petrol under India's ethanol-blending programme.

topics.t: Ethers: preparation and physical properties
topics.h: Diethyl ether was first publicly demonstrated as a surgical anaesthetic in 1846. Making ethers looks easy, but choosing the wrong alkyl halide gives you an alkene instead.
p: Dehydration of alcohols: 2C₂H₅OH →(conc. H₂SO₄, 413 K) C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. It proceeds by SN2 attack of an alcohol molecule on a protonated alcohol. It works for primary alcohols; secondary and tertiary alcohols give alkenes. Temperature matters: at 443 K ethanol gives ethene.
Williamson synthesis: R–X + R′–O⁻Na⁺ → R–O–R′ + NaX. It makes both symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers, and works by SN2.

The alkyl halide must be primary. With a tertiary halide, the alkoxide acts as a base and elimination gives an alkene: (CH₃)₃CBr + CH₃ONa → (CH₃)₂C=CH₂. Correct route: (CH₃)₃C–ONa + CH₃Br → (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃.
Alkyl aryl ethers are made from phenoxide and an alkyl halide: C₆H₅O⁻Na⁺ + CH₃I → C₆H₅OCH₃ (anisole).

Ethers have a bent, weakly polar C–O–C group. Their boiling points are close to alkanes of similar mass (n-pentane 309.1 K, ethoxyethane 307.6 K) and far below alcohols (butan-1-ol 390 K), because ethers cannot H-bond with each other. Their water solubility is similar to alcohols of similar mass because the ether oxygen can H-bond with water.

ex.q: Which pair of reagents should be used to make 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane by Williamson synthesis?
st: Option 2: (CH₃)₃CONa + CH₃Br → SN2 on a methyl halide works well

topics.rl: Diethyl ether is a common solvent in college labs across India; it is kept away from flames because it is extremely flammable and its vapour is heavier than air.

topics.t: Reactions of ethers
topics.h: Ethers are famously unreactive, which makes them great solvents. Yet hot concentrated HI can split them apart, and anisole's ring is eager for electrophiles.
p: Ethers are cleaved by hydrogen halides: R–O–R + HX → R–X + R–OH; with excess HX the alcohol is also converted to R–X. Reactivity: HI > HBr > HCl, following the nucleophilicity of the halide ion.

For mixed dialkyl ethers with primary/methyl groups, the halide attacks the smaller group by SN2: CH₃–O–C₂H₅ + HI → CH₃I + C₂H₅OH. If one group is tertiary, the reaction goes by SN1 and the tertiary halide forms: (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃ + HI → (CH₃)₃C–I + CH₃OH.

Alkyl aryl ethers are cleaved at the alkyl–oxygen bond: C₆H₅–O–CH₃ + HI → C₆H₅OH + CH₃I. The O–aryl bond has partial double bond character, and the sp² carbon cannot undergo SN1 or SN2, so phenol does not turn into an aryl halide.

The –OCH₃ group activates the ring and directs ortho/para. Anisole + Br₂ in ethanoic acid (no FeBr₃ needed) → mainly p-bromoanisole; Friedel–Crafts with CH₃Cl/AlCl₃ → 2- and 4-methoxytoluene; with CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ → 2- and 4-methoxyacetophenone; nitration (conc. HNO₃ + H₂SO₄) → 2- and 4-nitroanisole (para major).

ex.q: Predict the products of heating anisole with HI.
st: I⁻ attacks the methyl carbon (SN2); the phenyl–O bond is stronger and cannot be attacked

topics.rl: Anethole, a methoxybenzene derivative, gives saunf (fennel) and aniseed their sweet flavour; the methoxy group's ortho/para directing power helps chemists build such molecules.

topics.t: Nomenclature and structure of the carbonyl group
topics.h: The vanilla in kulfi, the cinnamon in garam masala and the sharp smell of camphor (kapur) all come from aldehydes and ketones. They share one star: the C=O group.
p: Aldehydes have –CHO (carbonyl bonded to at least one H); ketones have C=O bonded to two carbon groups.

IUPAC: aldehydes end in -al, ketones in -one. HCHO methanal (formaldehyde), CH₃CHO ethanal (acetaldehyde), (CH₃)₂CHCHO 2-methylpropanal, CH₃CH=CHCHO but-2-enal, C₆H₅CHO benzenecarbaldehyde (benzaldehyde).
Ketones: CH₃COCH₃ propanone (acetone), CH₃COCH₂CH₃ butan-2-one (ethyl methyl ketone), C₆H₅COCH₃ 1-phenylethan-1-one (acetophenone), C₆H₅COC₆H₅ diphenylmethanone (benzophenone).
The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised and forms three σ bonds in one plane at about 120°; its unhybridised p orbital overlaps with oxygen's p orbital to form a π bond.
Oxygen is more electronegative, so the C=O bond is polar: the carbon is electrophilic (Lewis acid site) and the oxygen nucleophilic (Lewis base site). This is shown by the resonance C=O ↔ C⁺–O⁻.

ex.q: Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂COCH₃.
st: Number from the end nearer C=O: C=O at C-2, CH₃ at C-4

topics.rl: Vanillin (an aldehyde) is the flavour in vanilla ice cream, and cinnamaldehyde gives dalchini (cinnamon) its aroma in Indian cooking.

topics.t: Preparation of aldehydes and ketones: general methods and aldehyde-specific routes
topics.h: The Rosenmund catalyst is deliberately 'poisoned' with barium sulphate so the reaction stops at the aldehyde. Sometimes chemists want a lazier catalyst!
p: Oxidation of alcohols: 1° alcohols → aldehydes and 2° alcohols → ketones (e.g. with PCC or K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ under controlled conditions). Dehydrogenation of alcohol vapours over heavy-metal catalysts (Ag or Cu) is used industrially.
Ozonolysis of alkenes followed by Zn dust and water gives aldehydes, ketones or both, depending on the alkene's substituents.
Hydration of alkynes: ethyne + H₂O (HgSO₄, dilute H₂SO₄) gives ethanal; other alkynes give ketones.
Rosenmund reduction: R–COCl + H₂ →(Pd on BaSO₄) R–CHO + HCl. BaSO₄ poisons the palladium so that the aldehyde is not reduced further to an alcohol.

From nitriles: Stephen reaction — R–CN + SnCl₂ + HCl → imine → hydrolysis → R–CHO. Nitriles and esters can also be reduced selectively to aldehydes by DIBAL-H [diisobutylaluminium hydride, AlH(i-Bu)₂] followed by hydrolysis; DIBAL-H leaves C=C bonds untouched.

ex.q: How would you convert benzoyl chloride into benzaldehyde?
st: BaSO₄ poisons Pd so the aldehyde is not reduced to benzyl alcohol
ex.a: Rosenmund reduction with H₂ over Pd–BaSO₄

topics.rl: Indian bulk-drug makers use DIBAL-H in flavour and drug synthesis because it can stop at the aldehyde stage without disturbing other double bonds in the molecule.

topics.t: Aromatic aldehydes from hydrocarbons; preparation of ketones
topics.h: Bitter-almond aroma in sweets and badam-flavoured drinks often comes from benzaldehyde made from toluene. Chemists have several neat ways to stop the oxidation right at the aldehyde.
p: Etard reaction: toluene + chromyl chloride (CrO₂Cl₂) in CS₂ forms a chromium complex, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde.

Toluene + CrO₃ in acetic anhydride gives benzylidene diacetate, which is hydrolysed by aqueous acid to benzaldehyde. Side-chain chlorination of toluene (Cl₂, light) gives benzal chloride (C₆H₅CHCl₂), which on hydrolysis at 373 K gives benzaldehyde (a commercial method).
Gatterman–Koch reaction: benzene (or a derivative) + CO + HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ or CuCl gives benzaldehyde.
Ketones from acyl chlorides: 2R–MgX + CdCl₂ → R₂Cd + 2Mg(X)Cl; then 2R′–COCl + R₂Cd → 2R′–CO–R + CdCl₂.
Ketones from nitriles: R–CN + R′MgX, then hydrolysis → R–CO–R′ (e.g. CH₃CH₂CN + C₆H₅MgBr → propiophenone, C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃). Friedel–Crafts acylation: benzene + R–COCl (anhydrous AlCl₃) → C₆H₅COR.

ex.q: How can acetophenone be prepared from benzene?
ex.a: Benzene + ethanoyl chloride with anhydrous AlCl₃

topics.rl: Benzaldehyde is used in Indian food and fragrance industries to give an almond-like flavour to sweets and syrups.

topics.t: Physical properties, nucleophilic addition and relative reactivity
topics.h: Acetone in nail-polish remover evaporates fast, yet boils higher than butane of similar mass. Its dipoles explain that — and its chemistry too.
p: Methanal is a gas; ethanal is a volatile liquid; other members are liquids or solids. Boiling points are higher than hydrocarbons and ethers of similar mass (dipole–dipole attraction) but lower than alcohols (no H-bonding between molecules). For M ≈ 58–60: n-butane 273 K < methoxyethane 281 K < propanal 322 K < acetone 329 K < propan-1-ol 370 K.

Lower members (methanal, ethanal, propanone) are miscible with water because they form H-bonds with water; solubility falls with longer chains. Lower aldehydes have sharp, pungent smells; larger ones are more fragrant.

Nucleophilic addition: the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon from a direction roughly perpendicular to the plane of the sp² orbitals; carbon changes from sp² to sp³, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which takes up a proton to give the product.
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones: sterically, ketones have two bulky groups hindering attack; electronically, two alkyl groups reduce the positive character of the carbonyl carbon more.
Benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal because the benzene ring's resonance reduces the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.

ex.q: Arrange ethanal, propanone and methanal in increasing order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition.
st: Methanal: two H atoms, least hindered, most electrophilic
Propanone: two CH₃ groups — most hindered and least electrophilic

topics.rl: Acetone is the main solvent in many nail-polish removers sold in India; its mixing with water comes from hydrogen bonding with water molecules.

topics.t: Addition of HCN, NaHSO₃, Grignard reagents and alcohols
topics.h: Chemists sometimes need to 'hide' a ketone while they work on another part of a molecule. Turning it into a ketal with ethylene glycol does the trick.
p: HCN adds to aldehydes and ketones to give cyanohydrins: >C=O + HCN → >C(OH)CN. The reaction is slow with pure HCN but is catalysed by a base, which generates the stronger nucleophile CN⁻. Cyanohydrins are useful synthetic intermediates.

Sodium hydrogensulphite (NaHSO₃) adds to give crystalline hydrogensulphite addition compounds. The equilibrium lies to the right for most aldehydes and to the left for most ketones (steric reasons). The adducts can be decomposed back by dilute acid or alkali, so this is used to separate and purify aldehydes.
Grignard reagents add to give alcohols after hydrolysis (methanal → 1°, other aldehydes → 2°, ketones → 3°).

Aldehydes + one equivalent of a monohydric alcohol in dry HCl give hemiacetals (alkoxy alcohols), and then acetals (gem-dialkoxy compounds). Ketones with ethylene glycol in dry HCl give cyclic ketals. Dry HCl protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon more electrophilic.
Acetals and ketals are hydrolysed back to the carbonyl compound by aqueous mineral acid, so they are used to protect carbonyl groups.

ex.q: What is the product when ethanal reacts with HCN, and what type of compound is it?

topics.rl: Protecting groups like ketals are routine in India's drug-synthesis labs, letting chemists build complex medicines one step at a time.

topics.t: Addition of ammonia derivatives and reduction
topics.h: An orange-red precipitate in the 2,4-DNP test tells a lab technician 'carbonyl group present' within seconds — a favourite of CBSE practical examiners.
p: Ammonia derivatives (H₂N–Z) add to aldehydes and ketones and then lose water, forming >C=N–Z. The reaction is reversible and catalysed by acid.

Products: hydroxylamine (Z = OH) → oxime; hydrazine (Z = NH₂) → hydrazone; phenylhydrazine → phenylhydrazone; 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) → 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (yellow, orange or red solid, used to identify carbonyl compounds); semicarbazide → semicarbazone.
Reduction to alcohols: NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ or catalytic hydrogenation reduce aldehydes to 1° alcohols and ketones to 2° alcohols.

Reduction to hydrocarbons: Clemmensen reduction (zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl) and Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazine, then heating with KOH in a high-boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol) convert >C=O into >CH₂.

ex.q: How would you convert propanone into propane?
st: Alternatively, Wolff–Kishner: NH₂NH₂, then KOH/ethylene glycol, heat

topics.rl: The 2,4-DNP test is used in Class 12 practicals across India to detect aldehydes and ketones in unknown organic samples.

topics.t: Oxidation, Tollens' and Fehling's tests, and the haloform reaction
topics.h: A silver mirror on the inside of a test tube is one of the prettiest results in a chemistry lab — and a sure sign of an aldehyde.
p: Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids by HNO₃, KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇ and even mild oxidising agents. Ketones are oxidised only by strong oxidants at high temperature, with C–C bond cleavage, giving acids with fewer carbon atoms.
Tollens' test: warming an aldehyde with freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate (Tollens' reagent) gives a silver mirror: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 2H₂O + 4NH₃.

Fehling's test: Fehling's A (aqueous CuSO₄) and Fehling's B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate, Rochelle salt) are mixed; aliphatic aldehydes give a reddish-brown precipitate of Cu₂O: RCHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + Cu₂O + 3H₂O. Aromatic aldehydes do not give this test.

Haloform reaction: compounds with a CH₃CO– group (methyl ketones and ethanal) are oxidised by sodium hypohalite to the sodium salt of an acid with one carbon less, plus haloform (CHX₃). With NaOI a yellow precipitate of iodoform forms (iodoform test). C=C bonds are not affected.
Distinguishing: Tollens'/Fehling's separate aldehydes from ketones; the iodoform test picks out methyl ketones and ethanal (e.g. pentan-2-one vs pentan-3-one, ethanal vs propanal).

ex.q: How would you distinguish between pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one?
st: Pentan-2-one is CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, a methyl ketone
Pentan-3-one is CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃, not a methyl ketone
Warm each with I₂ and NaOH: only pentan-2-one gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform
ex.a: Iodoform test: positive for pentan-2-one only

topics.rl: Mirror makers deposit a silver layer on glass by reducing silver ions with a mild reducing agent such as a sugar — the same chemistry as Tollens' test.

topics.t: α-Hydrogen reactions: aldol and Cannizzaro; ring substitution
topics.h: Two molecules of ethanal can join hands to make a bigger molecule with a C–C bond — the aldol reaction, one of organic chemistry's most powerful tools.
p: Hydrogens on the carbon next to C=O (α-hydrogens) are acidic because the carbonyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and the resulting carbanion (enolate) is resonance stabilised.

Aldol reaction: aldehydes/ketones with at least one α-H, in dilute alkali, give β-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols) or β-hydroxy ketones (ketols), which lose water on heating to give α,β-unsaturated compounds. 2CH₃CHO →(dil. NaOH) CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO (3-hydroxybutanal) →(heat, −H₂O) CH₃CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal). 2CH₃COCH₃ →(Ba(OH)₂) 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one → 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one.

Cross aldol condensation between two different compounds that both have α-H gives a mixture of four products. A ketone can be one partner: benzaldehyde + acetophenone (dilute NaOH) gives 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-one (benzalacetophenone).

Cannizzaro reaction: aldehydes without α-H, heated with concentrated alkali, undergo self oxidation–reduction (disproportionation): 2HCHO + conc. KOH → CH₃OH + HCOOK; 2C₆H₅CHO + conc. NaOH → C₆H₅CH₂OH + C₆H₅COONa.
Electrophilic substitution: the –CHO/–COR group is deactivating and meta-directing; benzaldehyde with conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄ at 273–283 K gives 3-nitrobenzaldehyde.

ex.q: Which of these undergo aldol condensation and which undergo Cannizzaro reaction: ethanal, methanal, benzaldehyde, propanone?
ex.a: Aldol: ethanal, propanone; Cannizzaro: methanal, benzaldehyde

topics.rl: Chalcones (made by cross aldol of benzaldehyde and acetophenone) are being studied in Indian research labs as starting points for anti-inflammatory and anticancer drugs.

topics.t: Uses of carbonyl compounds; naming and structure of carboxylic acids
topics.h: Red ants sting with formic acid, vinegar gets its tang from acetic acid, and rancid butter smells of butyric acid. Many common names come from these natural sources.
p: Uses of carbonyl compounds: formalin (40% aqueous methanal) preserves biological specimens and is used to make bakelite (phenol–formaldehyde resin) and urea–formaldehyde glues; ethanal is a starting material for acetic acid, ethyl acetate, vinyl acetate, polymers and drugs; benzaldehyde is used in perfumery and dyes; acetone and ethyl methyl ketone are common industrial solvents; vanillin, acetophenone and camphor are prized for odour and flavour.

Carboxylic acids (–COOH): HCOOH formic acid (methanoic acid, from Latin formica, ant); CH₃COOH acetic acid (ethanoic acid, from acetum, vinegar); CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH butyric acid (butanoic acid, from butyrum, butter).

More names: HOOC–COOH oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid); HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH adipic acid (hexanedioic acid); C₆H₅COOH benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid); C₆H₄(COOH)₂ phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid).

In the carboxyl group, the bonds to the carbon lie in one plane about 120° apart. The carbonyl carbon is less electrophilic than in aldehydes and ketones because the lone pair on the –OH oxygen is delocalised onto the C=O (resonance).

ex.q: Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂COOH.
st: Longest chain including COOH: 4 carbons; COOH carbon is C-1

topics.rl: Formalin is used in Indian medical colleges to preserve specimens, and bakelite from formaldehyde made the classic black electric switches in Indian homes.

topics.t: Methods of preparation of carboxylic acids
topics.h: Need benzoic acid for a food preservative? Start from toluene, from bromobenzene with dry ice, or from benzonitrile. Chemistry offers many roads to the same –COOH.
p: From primary alcohols and aldehydes by oxidation: KMnO₄ (neutral, acidic or alkaline), K₂Cr₂O₇ or CrO₃ in acidic medium (Jones reagent). Aldehydes are oxidised even by mild oxidants.

From alkylbenzenes: vigorous oxidation with chromic acid or acidic/alkaline KMnO₄ converts the entire side chain (primary or secondary alkyl, whatever its length) into –COOH: toluene, ethylbenzene and propylbenzene all give benzoic acid. A tertiary alkyl group is not oxidised.
From nitriles and amides: hydrolysis with H⁺ or OH⁻; nitriles first give amides (under mild conditions the reaction can be stopped there), then acids.
From Grignard reagents: R–MgX + CO₂ (dry ice), then H₃O⁺ → R–COOH, an acid with one more carbon than the alkyl halide.
From acyl halides and anhydrides by hydrolysis with water (with aqueous base they give carboxylate ions); from esters by acidic hydrolysis (acids) or basic hydrolysis (carboxylates, then acidified).

ex.q: Convert bromobenzene into benzoic acid.
ex.a: Via the Grignard reagent and CO₂

topics.rl: Sodium benzoate, the preservative in many Indian sauces and squashes, comes from benzoic acid made industrially by oxidising toluene.

topics.t: Physical properties and acidity of carboxylic acids
topics.h: Acetic acid boils at 391 K, way above ethanol, even though their masses are similar. And it fizzes with baking soda, which phenol cannot do.
p: Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than aldehydes, ketones and even alcohols of similar mass, because of extensive hydrogen bonding. Many exist as hydrogen-bonded dimers in the vapour phase and in aprotic solvents.

Simple aliphatic acids up to four carbons are miscible with water (H-bonding); solubility falls as the chain grows. Benzoic acid is nearly insoluble in cold water. Acids also dissolve in less polar solvents like benzene, ether and chloroform.

Acids react with metals (giving H₂), with alkalis (salt + water), and with weak bases such as NaHCO₃, giving brisk effervescence of CO₂ — a test that phenols do not pass: R–COOH + NaHCO₃ → R–COONa + H₂O + CO₂.

Acid strength: Ka = [H₃O⁺][RCOO⁻]/[RCOOH], pKa = −log Ka; smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4–5, e.g. CH₃COOH 4.76, C₆H₅COOH 4.19, HCOOH 3.75) are weaker than mineral acids but stronger than phenols (≈10) and alcohols (≈16), because the carboxylate ion has two equivalent resonance structures with the negative charge on two electronegative oxygen atoms.

Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity (CCl₃COOH > CHCl₂COOH > CH₂ClCOOH > CH₃COOH; FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > BrCH₂COOH), with a smaller effect the farther they are from –COOH. Electron-donating groups (alkyl) decrease acidity; a phenyl or vinyl group directly attached increases it relative to acetic acid.

ex.q: An acid has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is its pKa, and is it stronger or weaker than acetic acid (pKa 4.76)?
st: A larger pKa means a weaker acid
ex.a: pKa = 5; it is slightly weaker than acetic acid

topics.rl: Vinegar used in Indian kitchens for pickles and chutneys is about 5% acetic acid; a pinch of baking soda makes it fizz with CO₂ — the classic acid test.

topics.t: Reactions involving C–OH cleavage and the –COOH group
topics.h: Fruity smells of esters, the pain-relief paracetamol (an amide) and the nylon in your schoolbag straps all come from reactions where the –OH of an acid is replaced.
p: Anhydride formation: heating with a dehydrating agent such as P₂O₅ or conc. H₂SO₄ gives acid anhydrides: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O.

Esterification: R–COOH + R′–OH ⇌(H⁺) R–COOR′ + H₂O. Mechanism: (1) protonation of the carbonyl oxygen; (2) nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the carbonyl carbon; (3) proton transfer in the tetrahedral intermediate, making –OH₂⁺ a good leaving group; (4) loss of water; (5) loss of H⁺ from the protonated ester.
Acid chlorides: R–COOH + PCl₅ → R–COCl + POCl₃ + HCl; 3R–COOH + PCl₃ → 3R–COCl + H₃PO₃; R–COOH + SOCl₂ → R–COCl + SO₂ + HCl (preferred: gaseous by-products).
Amides: R–COOH + NH₃ ⇌ RCOO⁻NH₄⁺ →(heat) R–CONH₂ + H₂O. Phthalic acid with NH₃ gives phthalamide, and on strong heating, phthalimide.

Reduction: LiAlH₄ or diborane (B₂H₆) reduce –COOH to –CH₂OH (diborane does not easily reduce esters, nitro or halo groups; NaBH₄ does not reduce –COOH). Decarboxylation: sodium carboxylates heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO, 3 : 1) lose CO₂ to give an alkane with one carbon fewer; Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous salts gives an alkane with twice the carbons of the alkyl group.

ex.q: What product is obtained when sodium ethanoate is (i) heated with soda lime and (ii) electrolysed in aqueous solution?

topics.rl: Esters such as ethyl butanoate give pineapple and other fruity flavours to Indian sweets and soft drinks; they are made by acid-catalysed esterification.

topics.t: HVZ reaction, ring substitution, uses and multi-step conversions
topics.h: Board exams love 'Convert A into B in not more than two steps'. Knowing a handful of key reactions — HVZ, Rosenmund, Grignard, oxidation — unlocks most of them.
p: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction: acids with an α-hydrogen, treated with Cl₂ or Br₂ and a small amount of red phosphorus, then water, give α-halo acids: R–CH₂–COOH → R–CH(X)–COOH.

The –COOH group is deactivating and meta-directing: benzoic acid gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄) and 3-bromobenzoic acid (Br₂/FeBr₃). Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions because –COOH deactivates the ring and the AlCl₃ catalyst binds to the carboxyl group.

Uses: methanoic acid in rubber, textile, dyeing, leather and electroplating industries; ethanoic acid as a solvent and as vinegar; hexanedioic acid for nylon-6,6; esters of benzoic acid in perfumery; sodium benzoate as a food preservative; higher fatty acids for soaps and detergents.

Common conversions: toluene → benzoic acid (KMnO₄); benzoic acid → benzaldehyde (SOCl₂, then Rosenmund); ethanoic acid → 2-chloroethanoic acid (HVZ); ethanol → 3-hydroxybutanal (oxidise to ethanal, then aldol); benzene → m-nitroacetophenone (Friedel–Crafts acylation, then nitration).

ex.q: Convert ethanoic acid into 2-hydroxyethanoic acid.
st: Step 1 (HVZ): CH₃COOH + Cl₂ (red P), then H₂O → ClCH₂COOH
ex.a: HVZ chlorination, then hydrolysis of the C–Cl bond

topics.rl: Nylon-6,6 made from hexanedioic acid goes into the tyre cords and ropes produced in Indian factories, and sodium benzoate preserves bottled pickles and sauces.

topics.t: Structure, classification and nomenclature of amines
topics.h: The fishy smell of a fish market, the adrenaline rush before a board exam and the dyes in a Banarasi saree all trace back to amines.
p: Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more H atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
Nitrogen is sp³ hybridised; three orbitals bond to H or C and the fourth holds a lone pair, so amines are pyramidal. The C–N–E angle (E = C or H) is less than 109.5°, e.g. 108° in trimethylamine.
Primary (1°) R–NH₂, secondary (2°) R₂NH and tertiary (3°) R₃N amines, by the number of H atoms replaced. Simple amines have all groups the same; mixed amines have different groups.
Common names: alkylamine (methylamine, dimethylamine). IUPAC: alkanamine — CH₃NH₂ methanamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ propan-1-amine, (CH₃)₂CHNH₂ propan-2-amine, H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ hexane-1,6-diamine.

For 2° and 3° amines, the largest group gives the parent name and others are N-prefixes: (CH₃)₂NH is N-methylmethanamine, (CH₃)₃N is N,N-dimethylmethanamine, CH₃NHC₂H₅ is N-methylethanamine. Aniline is benzenamine; C₆H₅N(CH₃)₂ is N,N-dimethylbenzenamine.

ex.q: Name and classify CH₃–NH–CH₂CH₃.
st: Two groups on N: methyl and ethyl, one H left → secondary amine
Largest group (ethyl) gives the parent: ethanamine

topics.rl: The fishy smell of stale fish is largely due to volatile amines such as trimethylamine; squeezing nimbu (lemon) on fish works because the acid turns them into odourless salts.

topics.t: Preparation of amines: reduction and ammonolysis
topics.h: India's dye and drug industries make tonnes of aniline every year by reducing nitrobenzene with scrap iron and a little acid — a reaction you can write in one line.
p: Reduction of nitro compounds: H₂ with finely divided Ni, Pd or Pt, or metal + acid (Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl). C₆H₅NO₂ → C₆H₅NH₂. Fe scrap with HCl is preferred because the FeCl₂ formed is hydrolysed to release HCl, so only a small amount of acid is needed.

Ammonolysis of alkyl halides: R–X + NH₃ → R–NH₃⁺X⁻; the primary amine can react further, giving a mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and the quaternary salt R₄N⁺X⁻. With a large excess of ammonia, the primary amine is the main product. The free amine is liberated with a strong base: R–NH₃⁺X⁻ + NaOH → R–NH₂ + H₂O + NaX.
Order of reactivity of halides with amines: RI > RBr > RCl.
Reduction of nitriles with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni gives primary amines with one more carbon than the starting alkyl halide (ascent of the series): R–C≡N → R–CH₂–NH₂.
Reduction of amides with LiAlH₄ gives amines with the same number of carbons: R–CONH₂ → R–CH₂–NH₂.

ex.q: Convert bromoethane into propan-1-amine.
st: One carbon is added by the cyanide group

topics.rl: Aniline from Indian chemical plants goes into making paracetamol, rubber chemicals and many dyes.

topics.t: Gabriel and Hoffmann methods; physical properties
topics.h: Gabriel's method is the only clean way to get a pure primary amine from an alkyl halide, and Hoffmann's trick removes a carbon atom on the way.
p: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: phthalimide + ethanolic KOH → potassium phthalimide; heating with R–X gives N-alkylphthalimide; alkaline hydrolysis gives the pure primary amine. It cannot make aromatic primary amines because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.

Hoffmann bromamide degradation: R–CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → R–NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O. The amine has one carbon fewer than the amide (the alkyl or aryl group migrates from the carbonyl carbon to nitrogen).

Physical state and smell: lower aliphatic amines are gases with a fishy odour; primary amines with three or more carbons are liquids; higher ones are solids. Aniline is colourless when pure but darkens on storage due to atmospheric oxidation.

Lower aliphatic amines are water-soluble (H-bonding with water); solubility falls with larger alkyl groups. Amines are less polar than alcohols, so their H-bonds and water solubility are weaker than those of comparable alcohols.
Boiling points of isomeric amines: 1° > 2° > 3°. Tertiary amines have no H on nitrogen, so they cannot H-bond among themselves.

ex.q: How many carbon atoms does the amine have when propanamide undergoes Hoffmann bromamide degradation?
st: Hoffmann degradation removes the carbonyl carbon as carbonate

topics.rl: Aqueous solutions of amines such as ethanolamine are used in Indian fertiliser plants and refineries to scrub CO₂ from gas streams; their water solubility comes from the same H-bonding studied here.

topics.t: Basic character of amines
topics.h: Is dimethylamine a stronger base than trimethylamine? In the gas phase, no; in water, yes. Three competing effects decide the winner.
p: Amines are Lewis and Brønsted bases because of the lone pair on N: R–NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ R–NH₃⁺ + OH⁻; they react with acids to form salts, R–NH₂ + HX → R–NH₃⁺X⁻. Kb = [RNH₃⁺][OH⁻]/[RNH₂] and pKb = −log Kb: a smaller pKb means a stronger base.
Alkanamines are stronger bases than ammonia (pKb 4.75) because alkyl groups release electrons (+I). In the gas phase the order is 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃.

In water, the order also depends on solvation of the ammonium ion (more N–H bonds → better H-bonding with water → more stable) and steric hindrance. Methyl amines: (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃. Ethyl amines: (C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃.
pKb values: CH₃NH₂ 3.38, (CH₃)₂NH 3.27, (CH₃)₃N 4.22, C₂H₅NH₂ 3.29, (C₂H₅)₂NH 3.00, (C₂H₅)₃N 3.25, C₆H₅NH₂ 9.38, C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ 4.70.

Aryl amines are much weaker bases than ammonia: the lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring (aniline has five resonance structures, the anilinium ion only two). Electron-donating groups (–CH₃, –OCH₃) increase and electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂, –SO₃H, –COOH, –X) decrease the basicity of aniline.

ex.q: Arrange C₆H₅NH₂, C₂H₅NH₂, (C₂H₅)₂NH and NH₃ in decreasing order of basic strength in water.

topics.rl: Many medicines (like the antihistamines in cold tablets) are amines sold as hydrochloride salts, because the salts dissolve better in water — a direct use of amine basicity.

topics.t: Alkylation, acylation, carbylamine, nitrous acid and Hinsberg tests
topics.h: Is your unknown amine 1°, 2° or 3°? One sulphonyl chloride reagent and a little alkali can answer — Hinsberg's elegant test.
p: Alkylation: amines react with alkyl halides to form higher amines and finally quaternary ammonium salts. Acylation: 1° and 2° amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides or esters to form amides, usually in the presence of a base such as pyridine (stronger than the amine) to remove HCl: C₂H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → C₂H₅NHCOCH₃ + HCl. Benzoylation uses benzoyl chloride: CH₃NH₂ + C₆H₅COCl → C₆H₅CONHCH₃ (N-methylbenzamide) + HCl.

Carbylamine (isocyanide) test: 1° amines (aliphatic or aromatic) heated with chloroform and ethanolic KOH give foul-smelling isocyanides: R–NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → R–NC + 3KCl + 3H₂O. 2° and 3° amines do not respond.

Nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + HCl): 1° aliphatic amines give unstable diazonium salts that decompose to alcohols with quantitative evolution of N₂ (used to estimate amino acids and proteins). 1° aromatic amines at 273–278 K give stable diazonium salts.

Hinsberg's reagent (benzenesulphonyl chloride, C₆H₅SO₂Cl): 1° amines give N-alkylbenzenesulphonamides, which have an acidic H on N and dissolve in alkali; 2° amines give N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamides with no H on N, insoluble in alkali; 3° amines do not react. (p-Toluenesulphonyl chloride is now often used instead.)
Lab safety: chloroform and isocyanides are toxic and foul-smelling; do the carbylamine test only in small amounts in a fume hood.

ex.q: How would you distinguish ethanamine, N-ethylethanamine and N,N-diethylethanamine using Hinsberg's reagent?
st: Ethanamine (1°) → sulphonamide with acidic N–H → dissolves in KOH
N-Ethylethanamine (2°) → sulphonamide with no N–H → insoluble in KOH
ex.a: 1° dissolves in alkali, 2° gives an alkali-insoluble product, 3° does not react

topics.rl: Hinsberg and carbylamine tests are part of CBSE organic qualitative analysis; Indian forensic and quality-control labs use similar functional-group tests.

topics.t: Electrophilic substitution in aniline
topics.h: Add bromine water to aniline and you instantly get a white precipitate with three bromines on the ring. Want just one? You must first tame the –NH₂ group.
p: –NH₂ is a strongly activating, ortho/para-directing group. Aniline with bromine water at room temperature gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

To get a monosubstituted product, protect –NH₂ by acetylation with acetic anhydride to form acetanilide; the lone pair on N is partly delocalised onto the acetyl oxygen, reducing activation. Bromination then gives mainly 4-bromoacetanilide, and hydrolysis gives 4-bromoaniline.

Direct nitration of aniline gives tarry oxidation products along with nitro derivatives. In strongly acidic medium aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing, so a large amount of m-nitroaniline forms (about 51% para, 47% meta, 2% ortho). Acetylation first gives mainly p-nitroaniline after hydrolysis.
Sulphonation: aniline + conc. H₂SO₄ forms anilinium hydrogensulphate, which on heating at 453–473 K gives p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid (sulphanilic acid), existing as a zwitterion.
Aniline does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions: it forms a salt with the Lewis acid AlCl₃, and the positively charged nitrogen strongly deactivates the ring.

ex.q: How would you prepare 4-bromoaniline from aniline?
ex.a: Protect by acetylation, brominate, then hydrolyse

topics.rl: Sulpha drugs, among the first antibacterial medicines and still made in India, are built on sulphanilic acid chemistry from aniline.

topics.t: Diazonium salts: preparation, properties and replacement reactions
topics.h: Benzenediazonium chloride is a chemist's Swiss army knife: one intermediate that can become a halide, a nitrile, a phenol or plain benzene.
p: Diazotisation: C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl →(273–278 K) C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H₂O. Arenediazonium salts are stable for a short time in the cold because the positive charge is dispersed over the ring by resonance; aliphatic diazonium salts are highly unstable. They are used immediately.

Benzenediazonium chloride is a colourless crystalline solid, readily soluble in water, stable in the cold but reacting with water on warming; it decomposes easily when dry. Benzenediazonium fluoroborate is water-insoluble and stable at room temperature.
Sandmeyer reaction: CuCl/HCl, CuBr/HBr or CuCN/KCN replace –N₂⁺ by Cl, Br or CN. Gattermann reaction: copper powder with HCl or HBr does the same for Cl/Br (yields are usually better in Sandmeyer).

Other replacements: KI → iodobenzene; HBF₄ → fluoroborate, which on heating gives fluorobenzene + BF₃ + N₂ (Balz–Schiemann); H₃PO₂ or ethanol → benzene (reduction); warming with water (when the temperature rises to about 283 K) → phenol; fluoroborate + NaNO₂ with Cu, heat → nitrobenzene.

ex.q: How would you convert aniline into benzonitrile?
st: Diazotise: aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻
ex.a: Diazotisation followed by Sandmeyer reaction with CuCN

topics.rl: Indian manufacturers of dyes and agrochemicals use diazonium chemistry daily, always keeping the reaction vessels ice-cold for safety.

topics.t: Coupling reactions and diazonium salts in synthesis
topics.h: The orange of a traditional bandhani dupatta may well come from an azo dye — made when a diazonium salt couples with a phenol.
p: In coupling reactions the diazo group is retained (–N=N–). Benzenediazonium chloride (a weak electrophile) attacks the para position of activated rings.

With phenol in alkaline medium: p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye. With aniline in mildly acidic medium: p-aminoazobenzene, a yellow dye. These are electrophilic substitution reactions, and the products are azo compounds with extended conjugation, hence coloured.

Diazonium salts let us introduce groups that cannot be put on a benzene ring directly: F, I, CN, OH (and H to remove a group), e.g. iodo and fluoro compounds cannot be made easily by direct halogenation, and CN cannot be introduced by nucleophilic substitution of chlorobenzene.

Classic conversions: aniline → 1,3,5-tribromobenzene (Br₂ water, then diazotise, then H₃PO₂); nitrobenzene → benzoic acid (reduce, diazotise, CuCN, hydrolyse); ethanoic acid → methanamine (via ethanamide and Hoffmann degradation).

Distinguishing tests: aniline vs benzylamine — with HNO₂ in the cold, aniline gives a diazonium salt that couples with β-naphthol to an orange dye, while benzylamine releases N₂; methylamine vs dimethylamine — only methylamine gives the carbylamine test.

ex.q: Convert aniline into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.
st: Treat with H₃PO₂ to replace –N₂⁺ by H → 1,3,5-tribromobenzene
ex.a: Brominate, diazotise, then reduce with H₃PO₂

topics.rl: Azo dyes make up a large share of the dyes used by India's textile industry, from Surat to Tiruppur; regulators restrict certain azo dyes that can break down into harmful amines.

topics.t: Carbohydrates: definition and classification
topics.h: Roti, rice, gur, the cotton of your kurta and the paper of your notebook: all carbohydrates. Chemically they are far more interesting than 'just sugar'.
p: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give such units on hydrolysis. Many fit Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ, but not all (rhamnose, C₆H₁₂O₅, is a carbohydrate; acetic acid, C₂H₄O₂, fits the formula but is not).
Sugars are sweet, crystalline and water-soluble (monosaccharides, oligosaccharides); polysaccharides like starch and cellulose are non-sugars — not sweet.

Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further (glucose, fructose, ribose). Oligosaccharides give 2–10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose) give two. Polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen, gums) give a large number.
Reducing sugars reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent: all monosaccharides, and disaccharides with a free aldehyde or ketone group (maltose, lactose). Sucrose is non-reducing.
Monosaccharides are aldoses (with –CHO) or ketoses (with C=O), named by carbon count: triose, tetrose, pentose, hexose. Glucose is an aldohexose; fructose is a ketohexose.

ex.q: Classify glucose, sucrose and starch, and say which are reducing sugars.
st: Starch: polysaccharide (many glucose units) — non-reducing, not a sugar

topics.rl: India is one of the world's biggest producers of sugarcane; the sucrose from it goes into sugar, gur and khandsari, while its fibre is cellulose.

topics.t: Glucose: preparation and open-chain structure
topics.h: Glucose drips at every hospital, glucose biscuits in school tiffins — but how did chemists work out its structure without modern instruments? With a few clever reactions.
p: Preparation: boiling sucrose with dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ in alcoholic solution gives glucose and fructose. Commercially, starch is hydrolysed by boiling with dilute H₂SO₄ at 393 K under 2–3 atm pressure: (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ + nH₂O → nC₆H₁₂O₆.
Molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆. Prolonged heating with HI gives n-hexane, so the six carbons are in a straight chain.

Glucose forms an oxime with hydroxylamine and a cyanohydrin with HCN, so it has a carbonyl group. Bromine water (a mild oxidant) converts it into gluconic acid, a six-carbon acid, so the carbonyl is an aldehyde group.
Acetylation with acetic anhydride gives glucose pentaacetate: five –OH groups, on different carbons since the compound is stable.
Nitric acid oxidises glucose (and gluconic acid) to saccharic acid, a dicarboxylic acid, showing a primary alcohol (–CH₂OH) group. Open-chain structure: CHO–(CHOH)₄–CH₂OH.

ex.q: Which reaction of glucose shows that it contains an aldehyde group rather than a ketone group?
st: Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent
It oxidises glucose to gluconic acid, a carboxylic acid with six carbons
Only an aldehyde can be oxidised to an acid without losing carbon
ex.a: Oxidation by bromine water to gluconic acid

topics.rl: Glucose for India's ORS sachets and hospital drips is made mostly by hydrolysing maize or tapioca starch.

topics.t: Configuration and cyclic structure of glucose
topics.h: Glucose crystallises in two different forms with different melting points. The open-chain formula cannot explain this — a ring can.
p: D and L describe configuration relative to glyceraldehyde: if the –OH on the lowest asymmetric carbon (C-5 in glucose) is on the right in the Fischer projection, the sugar is D (like (+)-glyceraldehyde). D/L has no link to the sign of rotation, (+) or (−). Natural glucose is D-(+)-glucose.

Facts the open-chain structure cannot explain: glucose does not give Schiff's test or form a hydrogensulphite addition product with NaHSO₃; glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine (no free –CHO); and glucose exists in two crystalline forms, α and β.
α-D-glucose (m.p. 419 K) crystallises from a concentrated solution at 303 K; β-D-glucose (m.p. 423 K) from a hot saturated solution at 371 K.

The –OH at C-5 adds to the –CHO group, forming a cyclic hemiacetal with a six-membered ring (pyranose form, like pyran). C-1 becomes a new asymmetric centre: the anomeric carbon. The α and β forms, differing only at C-1, are called anomers.
Haworth projections draw the pyranose ring as a flat hexagon; in α-D-glucopyranose the C-1 –OH points down (opposite side to the –CH₂OH), and in β it points up.

ex.q: Why does glucose not react with NaHSO₃ although it is an aldehyde?
st: In solution, glucose exists almost entirely as a cyclic hemiacetal
The aldehyde group is tied up in the ring (C-1 bonded to the C-5 oxygen)
So typical aldehyde reactions like NaHSO₃ addition and Schiff's test do not occur
ex.a: Because its –CHO group is locked in the cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose) form

topics.rl: Diabetes test strips used across India detect glucose through enzyme reactions that work on its cyclic β form in blood.

topics.t: Fructose and disaccharides
topics.h: Table sugar turns 'left-handed' when you boil it with a little acid. That's why honey-like syrup made from sugar is called invert sugar.
p: Fructose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is a ketohexose with the ketone at C-2; it belongs to the D-series and is laevorotatory: D-(−)-fructose. It forms a five-membered ring (furanose, like furan) by addition of the C-5 –OH to the C-2 carbonyl, giving α and β anomers.
In disaccharides, two monosaccharides are joined by a glycosidic linkage (an oxide bridge formed with loss of water).

Sucrose: α-D-glucose (C-1) linked to β-D-fructose (C-2); both reducing groups are used, so it is non-reducing. Sucrose is dextrorotatory, but hydrolysis gives D-(+)-glucose (+52.5°) and D-(−)-fructose (−92.4°), and the mixture is laevorotatory. This change of sign is inversion; the product is invert sugar.
Maltose: two α-D-glucose units joined C-1 to C-4; the second unit has a free aldehyde at C-1 (in solution), so maltose is reducing.
Lactose (milk sugar): β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose joined C-1 (galactose) to C-4 (glucose); it is a reducing sugar.

ex.q: Why is sucrose called a non-reducing sugar, while maltose is reducing?
st: Sucrose: C-1 of glucose bonds to C-2 of fructose — both reducing groups are used up
Maltose: C-1 of one glucose bonds to C-4 of the other — C-1 of the second glucose stays free
A free C-1 (hemiacetal) can open to –CHO and reduce Fehling's solution
ex.a: Sucrose has no free reducing group; maltose has one

topics.rl: Indian sweet-makers use 'invert syrup' made by heating sugar with a little citric acid (nimbu) to stop sweets from crystallising.

topics.t: Polysaccharides and importance of carbohydrates
topics.h: Cows thrive on grass but we cannot digest it, though both grass (cellulose) and rice (starch) are made of glucose. The difference is a tiny twist at one carbon.
p: Starch, the main storage polysaccharide of plants, is a polymer of α-glucose with two components: amylose (15–20%), water-soluble, an unbranched chain of 200–1000 α-D-(+)-glucose units joined C-1 to C-4; and amylopectin (80–85%), water-insoluble and branched, with C-1 to C-4 chains and C-1 to C-6 branch points.

Cellulose, the main component of plant cell walls and the most abundant organic substance in the plant kingdom, is a straight-chain polymer of β-D-glucose joined C-1 to C-4. Humans cannot digest it; ruminants can, with the help of microbes in their gut.

Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide of animals (animal starch), found in liver, muscles and brain. Its structure resembles amylopectin but is more highly branched; it is broken down to glucose when the body needs energy.

Importance: carbohydrates are essential food and energy sources; they store energy as starch (plants) and glycogen (animals); cellulose builds plant cell walls. Wood and cotton (cellulose) are used for furniture, clothes, paper, lacquers and in breweries. Honey has long been used in Ayurveda. D-ribose and 2-deoxy-D-ribose are parts of nucleic acids.

ex.q: Why can cattle digest cellulose while humans cannot, though both starch and cellulose are made of glucose?
st: Starch has α-glycosidic links; cellulose has β-glycosidic links
Human digestive enzymes break α-links but not β-links
Microbes in the gut of ruminants produce enzymes that break β-links
ex.a: Because of the β-glycosidic linkage, which only microbial enzymes in ruminants can break

topics.rl: Cricketers 'carbo-load' with rice and roti before long matches so that their muscles store extra glycogen for energy late in the innings.

topics.t: Amino acids
topics.h: Dal, paneer, eggs and soya chunks are prized for protein — but your body really wants the amino acids inside, especially the ones it cannot make itself.
p: α-Amino acids have –NH₂ and –COOH on the same carbon: R–CH(NH₂)–COOH. The side chain R decides the amino acid (glycine R = H, alanine R = CH₃).

Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from food (e.g. valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, arginine, histidine); non-essential ones (e.g. glycine, alanine) can be made by the body.
Neutral amino acids have equal numbers of amino and carboxyl groups; acidic ones have more carboxyl groups (aspartic acid, glutamic acid); basic ones have more amino groups (lysine, arginine).
In water, the –COOH loses a proton and –NH₂ gains it, forming a zwitterion H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻. Amino acids are therefore amphoteric, crystalline, water-soluble, high-melting solids that behave like salts.
All α-amino acids except glycine are optically active, because the α-carbon is asymmetric; most naturally occurring ones have the L-configuration.

ex.q: Why is glycine optically inactive while alanine is optically active?
st: Glycine: H₂N–CH₂–COOH — the α-carbon carries two H atoms
Alanine: H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COOH — the α-carbon has four different groups
Only alanine has an asymmetric carbon
ex.a: Glycine has no asymmetric carbon; alanine does

topics.rl: India's Poshan Abhiyaan and the PM POSHAN mid-day meal scheme add pulses and eggs to diets so children get enough essential amino acids such as lysine.

topics.t: Peptides and levels of protein structure
topics.h: Hair, silk and muscle are fibrous proteins; insulin and egg albumin are globular. The difference begins with how chains fold.
p: A peptide bond (–CO–NH–) forms when the –COOH of one amino acid reacts with the –NH₂ of another, with loss of water. Two amino acids make a dipeptide (e.g. glycylalanine, Gly-Ala). More than ten make a polypeptide; a polypeptide with more than a hundred residues and molar mass above 10,000 u is called a protein.

Fibrous proteins have long parallel chains held by hydrogen and disulphide bonds; they are usually water-insoluble (keratin in hair, wool and silk; myosin in muscles). Globular proteins have chains coiled into spheres; they are usually water-soluble (insulin, albumins).
Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids. Any change in it creates a different protein.

Secondary structure is the shape of the chain: α-helix (a right-handed coil in which each –NH group is H-bonded to a C=O of an adjacent turn) or β-pleated sheet (chains stretched almost fully and laid side by side, held by intermolecular H-bonds).

Tertiary structure is the overall folding of the chain, held by hydrogen bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals forces and electrostatic attractions. Quaternary structure is the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits).

ex.q: Draw the dipeptide glycylalanine and mark the peptide bond.
st: The –COOH of glycine reacts with the –NH₂ of alanine, losing H₂O
Product: H₂N–CH₂–CO–NH–CH(CH₃)–COOH; the –CO–NH– link is the peptide bond

topics.rl: Silk from Mysuru and Kanchipuram owes its strength to β-pleated sheets of the protein fibroin, while keratin's α-helices give wool its stretch.

topics.t: Denaturation of proteins and enzymes
topics.h: Boil an egg and the clear white turns opaque forever; add nimbu to hot milk and it curdles into paneer. Both are proteins losing their shape.
p: Denaturation: a change in temperature or pH disturbs the hydrogen bonds of a native protein, so the globules unfold and helices uncoil; the protein loses its biological activity. Secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed, but the primary structure stays intact.
Examples: coagulation of egg white on boiling; curdling of milk, caused by lactic acid formed by bacteria (or by added acids like lemon juice).

Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins. They are very specific to their substrate and reaction and are usually named after the substrate or reaction with the suffix -ase: maltase converts maltose into glucose; invertase converts sucrose into glucose and fructose; enzymes catalysing oxidation–reduction are oxidoreductases.

Enzymes work by lowering the activation energy of the reaction. For example, the hydrolysis of sucrose has a much lower activation energy with invertase than with acid alone, so it happens fast at body temperature.
Being proteins, enzymes are denatured by high temperatures and extreme pH; this is why fever or strong acids disrupt their action.

ex.q: Why does a boiled egg not become raw again on cooling?
st: Heating breaks the H-bonds holding the albumin's folded secondary and tertiary structures
The chains unfold and tangle irreversibly (coagulation)
The primary sequence remains, but the native shape is lost for good
ex.a: Because heat denatures the protein irreversibly, destroying its secondary and tertiary structures

topics.rl: Paneer is made in Indian homes by curdling hot milk with lemon juice or vinegar — a delicious denaturation of milk proteins.

topics.t: Vitamins: classification, sources and deficiency diseases
topics.h: Sailors once died of scurvy on long voyages; a few amlas or lemons would have saved them. Vitamins are needed in tiny amounts, but missing them causes real disease.
p: Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small amounts in the diet for normal growth and health; their deficiency causes specific diseases. Most cannot be made by our bodies (plants can make almost all).

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) dissolve in fats and oils and are stored in the liver and adipose (fat-storing) tissue. Water-soluble vitamins (B group and C) must be supplied regularly, because they are excreted in urine and cannot be stored (except vitamin B₁₂).

A: fish liver oil, carrots, butter, milk → xerophthalmia (hardening of the cornea) and night blindness. D: sunlight, fish, egg yolk → rickets (children) and osteomalacia (soft bones and joint pain in adults). E: vegetable oils like wheat germ and sunflower oil → fragile red blood cells and muscular weakness. K: green leafy vegetables → increased blood clotting time.

B₁ (thiamine): yeast, milk, green vegetables, cereals → beri-beri (loss of appetite, retarded growth). B₂ (riboflavin): milk, egg white, liver, kidney → cheilosis (cracks at the corners of the mouth and lips), digestive disorders, burning skin. B₆ (pyridoxine): yeast, milk, egg yolk, cereals, grams → convulsions.
