B₁₂: meat, fish, egg, curd → pernicious anaemia (red blood cells deficient in haemoglobin). C (ascorbic acid): citrus fruits, amla, green leafy vegetables → scurvy (bleeding gums).

ex.q: Why must vitamin C be included in the diet every day, while vitamin A need not be?
st: Excess is excreted in urine and is not stored
Vitamin A is fat-soluble and is stored in the liver and fat tissue
ex.a: Because water-soluble vitamin C cannot be stored, but fat-soluble vitamin A can

topics.rl: Amla, rich in vitamin C, has been prized in Indian diets for centuries; the national vitamin A supplementation programme for children helps prevent night blindness.

topics.t: Nucleic acids: composition and structure
topics.h: Every one of your cells holds about two metres of DNA, coiled into a space smaller than a full stop. Its secret is a simple double helix.
p: Nucleic acids are long polymers of nucleotides (polynucleotides). Complete hydrolysis gives a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogenous bases.
DNA contains β-D-2-deoxyribose; RNA contains β-D-ribose. DNA bases: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T). RNA has A, G, C and uracil (U) in place of thymine.

A nucleoside is a base attached to C-1′ of the sugar. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with a phosphate group attached at C-5′ of the sugar. Nucleotides join by phosphodiester linkages between C-5′ and C-3′ of neighbouring sugars.
DNA (Watson–Crick model) is a double helix of two antiparallel strands held by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.
RNA is usually single-stranded (it can fold back on itself). Three main types are messenger RNA (m-RNA), ribosomal RNA (r-RNA) and transfer RNA (t-RNA).

ex.q: If one strand of DNA has the sequence A-T-G-C-C-A, what is the complementary strand?
st: A pairs with T and T with A
G pairs with C and C with G

topics.rl: India's Genome India project has sequenced the DNA of thousands of Indians to map genetic diversity — all built on reading A, T, G and C.

topics.t: Biological functions of nucleic acids and DNA fingerprinting
topics.h: Indian investigators have used DNA evidence to identify victims of disasters and to solve crimes. The idea rests on one fact: your base sequence is uniquely yours.
p: DNA is the chemical basis of heredity: it stores genetic information and is responsible for keeping the identity of a species over millions of years.
DNA can copy itself (replication) during cell division, so identical DNA passes to daughter cells.
Proteins are synthesised by the various RNA molecules in the cell, but the message for making a particular protein is present in DNA.
DNA fingerprinting: the sequence of bases in DNA is unique for each person (except identical twins), is the same in every cell and cannot be altered by any known treatment.

Uses: identifying criminals in forensic labs, settling questions of paternity, identifying bodies after accidents by comparing DNA with that of parents or children, and studying evolutionary relationships.

ex.q: How does DNA fingerprinting help identify a victim after a disaster?
st: Collect DNA from the possible parents or children
Compare the base-sequence patterns; close relatives share many of them
ex.a: By matching DNA patterns with those of close relatives

topics.rl: The Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD) in Hyderabad, set up after pioneering work by Dr Lalji Singh, provides DNA testing for courts and investigations in India.

topics.t: Hormones
topics.h: The 'adrenaline rush' before a big match and the insulin that millions of Indians with diabetes rely on are both hormones — chemical messengers in the blood.
p: Hormones are intercellular messengers produced by endocrine glands and released directly into the bloodstream, which carries them to their target sites. Chemically they are steroids (oestrogens, androgens), polypeptides (insulin, endorphins) or amino acid derivatives (epinephrine, norepinephrine).
Insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose within narrow limits: insulin is released when blood glucose rises rapidly and lowers it; glucagon raises blood glucose.
Epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine mediate responses to external stimuli. Growth hormones and sex hormones control growth and development.

Thyroxine, made by the thyroid gland, is an iodinated derivative of the amino acid tyrosine. Too little causes hypothyroidism (lethargy, obesity); too much causes hyperthyroidism. Low dietary iodine leads to hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, prevented by adding iodide to table salt.

Adrenal cortex steroids: glucocorticoids control carbohydrate metabolism, moderate inflammation and are involved in stress responses; mineralocorticoids control the kidney's excretion of water and salt. Failure of the adrenal cortex causes Addison's disease. Sex hormones: testosterone (male), estradiol (female) and progesterone (prepares the uterus for implantation of the fertilised egg).

ex.q: Why is iodised salt used throughout India?
st: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine
Low dietary iodine causes hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre)
Adding iodide to common salt ensures everyone gets enough iodine
ex.a: To prevent iodine deficiency, hypothyroidism and goitre

topics.rl: India's National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme made iodised salt widespread, sharply cutting goitre cases in hilly and other iodine-poor regions.

qa.q: A solution contains 5 g of glucose in 45 g of water. What is the mass percentage of glucose?
qa.e: Mass % = mass of solute ÷ mass of solution × 100 = 5 ÷ 50 × 100 = 10.

qa.q: Which of the following is a solid solution in which the solute is a liquid?
qa.e: In an amalgam the solvent (sodium) is a solid and the solute (mercury) is a liquid.

qa.q: 10 mL of ethanol is mixed with water to make 50 mL of solution. What is the volume percentage (V/V) of ethanol?
qa.e: V/V % = volume of ethanol ÷ volume of solution × 100 = 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20.

qa.q: A water sample of mass 2 kg contains 0.006 g of lead ions. What is the concentration of lead in ppm?
Normal saline is labelled '0.9% w/V NaCl'. How many grams of NaCl are present in 500 mL of it?
qa.e: 0.9% w/V means 0.9 g per 100 mL, so 500 mL contains 0.9 × 5 = 4.5 g.

qa.q: Which concentration term is most convenient for expressing the amount of a pollutant gas present in trace amount in air?
qa.e: When a solute is present in trace quantities, percentages become tiny and awkward, so parts per million is used.

qa.q: In a binary solution of 2 g of iodine in 100 g of carbon tetrachloride, which statement is correct?
qa.a: Iodine is the solute and CCl₄ is the solvent
qa.e: The component present in the larger amount (CCl₄) is the solvent; iodine is the solute. A binary solution simply has two components.

qa.q: A 250 g solution contains 20% by mass of sugar. How much water is in it?
qa.e: Sugar = 20% of 250 g = 50 g, so water = 250 − 50 = 200 g.

qa.q: 46 g of ethanol (C₂H₅OH, M = 46 g mol⁻¹) is mixed with 90 g of water (M = 18 g mol⁻¹). What is the mole fraction of ethanol?
qa.e: Ethanol = 1 mol, water = 5 mol. x(ethanol) = 1 ÷ (1 + 5) = 0.167.

qa.q: 4 g of NaOH (M = 40 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved to make 250 mL of solution. What is its molarity (in mol L⁻¹)?
18 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 500 g of water. What is the molality (in mol kg⁻¹)?
qa.e: Moles of glucose = 0.1; mass of solvent = 0.500 kg; m = 0.1 ÷ 0.5 = 0.2 mol kg⁻¹.

qa.q: Why does the molarity of a solution change when it is warmed, while its molality does not?
qa.a: Volume of solution changes with temperature but mass of solvent does not
qa.e: Molarity has volume in its denominator, and liquids expand on heating. Molality uses mass, which stays the same.

qa.q: A 10% (w/w) aqueous solution of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is given. What is its molality (in mol kg⁻¹, to two decimals)?
qa.e: 100 g of solution has 10 g glucose in 90 g water: m = (10/180) ÷ 0.090 = 0.62 mol kg⁻¹.

qa.q: In a binary solution the mole fraction of the solute is 0.15. What is the mole fraction of the solvent?
qa.e: In a binary solution x₁ + x₂ = 1, so x(solvent) = 1 − 0.15 = 0.85.

qa.q: A solution contains 58.5 g NaCl (1.0 mol) in 1.000 L of solution of density 1.0585 g mL⁻¹. What is its molality (in mol kg⁻¹)?
qa.e: Mass of solution = 1058.5 g; solvent = 1058.5 − 58.5 = 1000 g = 1 kg; m = 1.0 ÷ 1 = 1.0 mol kg⁻¹.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Molality is preferred over molarity for accurate physical chemistry work at varying temperatures. Reason (R): Molality is defined per kilogram of solvent, and mass does not change with temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Molality is temperature independent precisely because it uses mass of solvent, so R explains A.

qa.q: At 298 K, K_H for CO₂ is 1.67 kbar. If the partial pressure of CO₂ over water is 3.34 bar, the mole fraction of CO₂ is n × 10⁻³. What is n?
Gas A has K_H = 34.86 kbar and gas B has K_H = 144.97 kbar in water at 293 K. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: A is more soluble than B at the same partial pressure
qa.e: x = p/K_H, so the gas with the smaller K_H (A) dissolves more at the same pressure.

qa.q: The partial pressure of a gas over a solution is doubled at constant temperature. What happens to its mole fraction in the solution?
qa.e: p = K_H x with K_H constant at fixed temperature, so x is directly proportional to p.

qa.q: Dissolving a certain salt in water is endothermic. What happens to its solubility as temperature increases?
qa.e: For Δsol H > 0, Le Chatelier's principle says raising temperature shifts the equilibrium towards more dissolution.

qa.q: Why does pressure have no significant effect on the solubility of solids in liquids?
qa.a: Solids and liquids are highly incompressible
qa.e: Because neither the solid nor the liquid changes volume noticeably with pressure, the equilibrium barely shifts.

qa.q: Which pair best illustrates 'like dissolves like'?
qa.a: Sodium chloride in water and naphthalene in benzene
qa.e: Ionic/polar NaCl dissolves in polar water; non-polar naphthalene dissolves in non-polar benzene.

qa.q: A gas has K_H = 100 kbar in water at 298 K. What partial pressure (in bar) is needed to make its mole fraction 1 × 10⁻⁵ in water?
qa.e: p = K_H x = 1.0 × 10⁵ bar × 1 × 10⁻⁵ = 1 bar.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In a saturated solution, the amount of dissolved solute stays constant. Reason (R): Dissolution has completely stopped in a saturated solution.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: The amount stays constant because dissolution and crystallisation occur at equal rates — a dynamic equilibrium, not a stop.

qa.q: Why are soda water bottles sealed under high pressure?
qa.a: To increase the solubility of CO₂
qa.e: By Henry's law, a higher partial pressure of CO₂ dissolves more CO₂ in the drink.

qa.q: The bends experienced by scuba divers are caused mainly by which gas coming out of the blood?
qa.e: Nitrogen, which dissolves at high pressure, forms bubbles when the pressure falls quickly.

qa.q: Why is air in scuba tanks diluted with helium?
qa.a: Helium is much less soluble in blood than nitrogen
qa.e: Using a poorly soluble gas reduces the amount of gas dissolved in blood at depth, lowering the risk of the bends.

qa.q: What is the main cause of anoxia in climbers at high altitudes?
qa.a: Low partial pressure of oxygen at high altitude
qa.e: The partial pressure of O₂ is lower at altitude, so less O₂ dissolves in blood and tissues.

qa.q: K_H for O₂ in water is 34.86 kbar at 293 K and 46.82 kbar at 303 K. What does this show?
qa.a: Solubility of O₂ decreases as temperature increases
qa.e: A larger K_H at higher temperature means a smaller mole fraction at the same pressure, so O₂ is less soluble when warmer.

qa.q: Why do aquatic species feel more comfortable in cold water than in warm water?
qa.a: Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen
qa.e: Gas solubility falls with rising temperature, so warm water carries less dissolved O₂.

qa.q: Dissolving a gas in a liquid is generally an exothermic process. On this basis, how does raising the temperature affect gas solubility?
qa.e: For an exothermic process, Le Chatelier's principle says heating shifts the equilibrium backwards, releasing gas.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A chilled soft drink goes flat more slowly than a warm one once opened. Reason (R): K_H for CO₂ increases with temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: At low temperature K_H is smaller, so CO₂ stays more soluble and escapes more slowly. R explains A.

qa.q: Liquids A (p_A° = 400 mm Hg) and B (p_B° = 600 mm Hg) form an ideal solution with x_A = 0.4. What is the total vapour pressure (in mm Hg)?
For the solution in which p_A = 160 mm Hg and p_total = 520 mm Hg, what is the mole fraction of A in the vapour phase (two decimals)?
qa.e: y_A = p_A ÷ p_total = 160 ÷ 520 = 0.31. The vapour is poorer in A, the less volatile component.

qa.q: At 298 K, pure chloroform and pure dichloromethane have vapour pressures of 200 and 415 mm Hg. In an ideal solution with x(dichloromethane) = 0.4, what is p_total (in mm Hg)?
qa.e: p_total = p₁° + (p₂° − p₁°)x₂ = 200 + 215 × 0.4 = 286 mm Hg.

qa.q: In an ideal binary solution, how does the vapour composition compare with the liquid composition?
qa.a: The vapour is richer in the more volatile component
qa.e: The component with higher p° contributes a larger share of the vapour pressure, so its mole fraction in the vapour is higher.

qa.q: What is the shape of the plot of total vapour pressure against mole fraction for an ideal binary solution?
qa.a: A straight line joining p₁° and p₂°
qa.e: p_total = p₁° + (p₂° − p₁°)x₂ is linear in x₂.

qa.q: Raoult's law becomes a special case of Henry's law when Henry's constant K_H is equal to:
qa.a: the vapour pressure of the pure component, p₁°
qa.e: Both laws say p ∝ x. In Raoult's law the proportionality constant is p₁°, so K_H = p₁°.

qa.q: Pure benzene and toluene have vapour pressures of 75 and 25 mm Hg at a certain temperature. For an equimolar ideal solution, what is the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour?
qa.e: p(benzene) = 37.5, p(toluene) = 12.5, total 50; y(benzene) = 37.5 ÷ 50 = 0.75.

qa.q: Assertion (A): For an ideal solution of two volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its mole fraction. Reason (R): This follows from Raoult's law.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: p₁ = p₁° x₁ is exactly Raoult's law, so R explains A.

qa.q: Which pair forms a nearly ideal solution?
qa.e: Benzene and toluene have very similar intermolecular forces, so A–B interactions match A–A and B–B and Raoult's law is obeyed.

qa.q: For a solution showing positive deviation from Raoult's law, which is true?
qa.e: Weaker A–B attractions mean energy is absorbed on mixing and the molecules spread out a little: both changes are positive.

qa.q: Why does a chloroform–acetone mixture show negative deviation?
qa.a: A hydrogen bond forms between chloroform's hydrogen and acetone's oxygen
qa.e: The new CHCl₃···O=C H-bond makes A–B attraction stronger than in the pure liquids, lowering escaping tendency.

qa.q: Ethanol mixed with acetone shows positive deviation. What is the main reason?
qa.a: Acetone gets between ethanol molecules and breaks some of their hydrogen bonds
qa.e: Pure ethanol is held together by H-bonds; acetone disrupts them, so A–B attraction is weaker overall and vapour pressure rises.

qa.q: A maximum boiling azeotrope is formed by solutions that show:
qa.a: large negative deviation from Raoult's law
qa.e: Strong A–B attraction lowers vapour pressure the most at one composition, which therefore boils at the highest temperature.

qa.q: Ethanol–water forms an azeotrope at about 95% ethanol by volume. What kind is it?
qa.e: Ethanol–water shows large positive deviation, so the azeotrope has a maximum vapour pressure and hence a minimum boiling point.

qa.q: Why can an azeotropic mixture not be separated by fractional distillation?
qa.a: Its liquid and vapour have the same composition when it boils
qa.e: Distillation relies on the vapour being richer in one component; at the azeotropic composition, it is not.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The nitric acid–water azeotrope (about 68% HNO₃ by mass) boils at 393.5 K, higher than either pure component. Reason (R): Nitric acid–water solutions show large positive deviation from Raoult's law.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: This azeotrope is maximum boiling, which comes from large negative deviation, so R is false.

qa.q: 0.5 mol of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 500 g of water (K_b = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹). What is the boiling point of the solution (in K)? Pure water boils at 373.15 K.
1.28 g of a non-volatile solute in 50 g of benzene (K_b = 2.53 K kg mol⁻¹) raises the boiling point by 0.506 K. What is the molar mass (in g mol⁻¹)?
The vapour pressure of a solvent falls from 100 mm Hg to 98 mm Hg on dissolving a non-volatile solute. What is the mole fraction of the solute?
qa.e: Relative lowering = (100 − 98) ÷ 100 = 0.02 = x₂.

qa.q: 6 g of a non-volatile solute in 90 g of water (5 mol) gives a relative lowering of vapour pressure of 0.02. Using n₂/n₁ for this dilute solution, what is the molar mass of the solute (in g mol⁻¹)?
Which of these is NOT a colligative property?
qa.e: Viscosity depends on the nature of the solute and solvent, not just the number of particles.

qa.q: Why is the boiling point of a solution of a non-volatile solute higher than that of the pure solvent?
qa.a: Its vapour pressure is lower, so it must be heated more to equal atmospheric pressure
qa.e: Boiling happens when vapour pressure equals external pressure; a lower vapour pressure needs a higher temperature.

qa.q: Equal masses of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) and urea (M = 60 g mol⁻¹) are dissolved separately in equal masses of water. Which solution has the higher boiling point?
qa.e: Equal masses of urea give three times as many moles as glucose, so molality and ΔT_b are larger.

qa.q: K_b depends on the solvent and can be expressed as K_b = R M₁ T_b² ÷ (1000 Δvap H). Which change in the solvent would give a larger K_b?
qa.a: Higher boiling point with the same Δvap H and M₁
qa.e: K_b is proportional to T_b² and M₁ and inversely proportional to Δvap H; it is a property of the solvent only.

qa.q: 62 g of ethylene glycol (M = 62 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 500 g of water (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹). What is the depression in freezing point (in K)?
qa.e: m = 1 mol ÷ 0.5 kg = 2 mol kg⁻¹; ΔT_f = 1.86 × 2 = 3.72 K.

qa.q: 2 g of a non-electrolyte in 100 g of benzene lowers its freezing point by 0.32 K. K_f for benzene is 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹. What is the molar mass of the solute (in g mol⁻¹)?
A 0.2 molal aqueous solution of urea is cooled. At what temperature (in K) does it start to freeze? (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; pure water freezes at 273.15 K.)
Why is salt spread on icy roads in winter?
qa.a: It lowers the freezing point of water so ice melts
qa.e: Dissolved salt makes a solution whose freezing point is below that of pure water, so the ice melts at sub-zero temperatures.

qa.q: The cryoscopic constant K_f of a solvent can be written as K_f = R M₁ T_f² ÷ (1000 Δfus H). On what does K_f depend?
qa.a: Only on the nature of the solvent
qa.e: All quantities in the expression (M₁, T_f, Δfus H) belong to the solvent.

qa.q: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point? (All solutes are non-electrolytes.)
qa.e: For non-electrolytes, ΔT_f = K_f m, so the highest molality gives the largest depression and the lowest freezing point.

qa.q: The freezing point of a solution is lower than that of the pure solvent. Which statement explains this best?
qa.a: The solution's vapour pressure equals that of the solid solvent at a lower temperature
qa.e: Freezing occurs when liquid and solid phases have equal vapour pressure. Lowering the liquid's vapour pressure shifts this point to a lower temperature.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Kulfi makers mix salt with ice to cool their moulds below 0 °C. Reason (R): Salt solution has a lower freezing point than pure water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The ice–salt mixture can stay liquid and keep melting below 0 °C, absorbing heat from the moulds; this is because of freezing point depression.

qa.q: What is the osmotic pressure (in bar) of a 0.1 M solution of a non-electrolyte at 300 K? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
2 g of a polymer in 0.25 L of solution shows π = 0.00166 bar at 300 K. What is its molar mass (in g mol⁻¹)? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Why is osmotic pressure preferred over other colligative properties for finding molar masses of proteins?
qa.a: It is measured at room temperature and gives a large value even for dilute solutions
qa.e: Proteins often decompose on heating, and their dilute solutions give tiny ΔT values; osmotic pressure avoids both problems.

qa.q: Red blood cells are placed in 2% (w/V) NaCl solution. What happens?
qa.a: They shrink as water flows out
qa.e: 2% NaCl is hypertonic compared with 0.9% saline, so water leaves the cells by osmosis.

qa.q: In reverse osmosis used for desalination, which condition must be met?
qa.a: Pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied on the sea water side
qa.e: Only a pressure exceeding π reverses the natural flow, pushing pure water out of the salt solution.

qa.q: Two solutions are isotonic. What does this mean?
qa.a: They have the same osmotic pressure at the same temperature
qa.e: Isotonic means equal osmotic pressure, so there is no net osmosis between them.

qa.q: A solution of glucose at 300 K has an osmotic pressure of 4.98 bar. What is its molar concentration (in mol L⁻¹)? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Assertion (A): Raw mangoes shrivel when kept in concentrated salt solution for pickling. Reason (R): The salt solution is hypotonic with respect to the cell sap.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Mangoes shrivel because the brine is hypertonic, drawing water out. Calling it hypotonic is false.

qa.q: What is the depression in freezing point (in K) of a 0.1 m aqueous NaCl solution, assuming complete dissociation? (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
qa.e: NaCl gives 2 ions, so i = 2: ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 0.1 = 0.372 K.

qa.q: Ethanoic acid in benzene gives a van't Hoff factor of 0.6. What is its degree of association (as a fraction), assuming dimer formation?
A weak monobasic acid HA in water has i = 1.2. What is its degree of dissociation?
The experimentally found molar mass of a solute is half its normal molar mass. What is i?
qa.e: i = normal molar mass ÷ abnormal molar mass = M ÷ (M/2) = 2: the solute has dissociated into two particles.

qa.q: Which 0.1 m aqueous solution has the highest boiling point? (Assume complete dissociation.)
qa.e: Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives 5 ions (i = 5), the most particles, so the largest ΔT_b.

qa.q: Why does ethanoic acid show a molar mass close to 120 g mol⁻¹ in benzene instead of 60 g mol⁻¹?
qa.a: It forms dimers through hydrogen bonding in benzene
qa.e: In a non-polar solvent, two acid molecules hydrogen-bond into a dimer, halving the number of particles and doubling the apparent molar mass.

qa.q: A 0.1 M aqueous solution of K₂SO₄ is fully dissociated. What is its osmotic pressure (in bar) at 300 K? (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
qa.e: i = 3 for K₂SO₄, so π = iCRT = 3 × 0.1 × 0.083 × 300 = 7.47 bar.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The van't Hoff factor for KCl in very dilute aqueous solution is close to 2. Reason (R): KCl dissociates into K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Each KCl gives two ions, doubling the particle count, so i approaches 2 at infinite dilution.

qa.q: What is the overall reaction in a Daniell cell?
qa.e: Zinc, the stronger reducing agent, is oxidised and Cu²⁺ is reduced to copper.

qa.q: A Daniell cell is opposed by an external voltage of 0.8 V. In which direction do electrons flow in the outer circuit?
qa.a: From the zinc rod to the copper rod
qa.e: 0.8 V is less than 1.1 V, so the cell still works normally: electrons leave zinc and go to copper.

qa.q: What is the main function of a salt bridge?
qa.a: It completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality of the two solutions
qa.e: Ions migrate through the bridge to balance charges building up in the half-cells, keeping the current flowing.

qa.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a galvanic cell from an electrolytic cell?
qa.a: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy; an electrolytic cell does the reverse
qa.e: Galvanic cells run on spontaneous reactions; electrolytic cells need external electricity to drive non-spontaneous ones.

qa.q: When the opposing external voltage on a Daniell cell is raised above 1.1 V, which process takes place at the copper electrode?
qa.e: The reaction reverses: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the copper electrode while Zn²⁺ is reduced at the zinc electrode.

qa.q: Which industrial process is an application of electrolytic cells?
qa.a: Production of sodium hydroxide and chlorine from brine
qa.e: The chlor-alkali process electrolyses brine to give NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.

qa.q: At what external opposing voltage does a standard Daniell cell stop delivering current?
qa.e: Current stops when the external voltage exactly equals the cell potential of 1.1 V.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A Daniell cell can be made to work as an electrolytic cell. Reason (R): Applying an external voltage greater than 1.1 V in opposition reverses the cell reaction.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Above 1.1 V the reaction is driven backwards using external electricity, which is exactly what an electrolytic cell does.

qa.q: What is E°cell for Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq)||Ag⁺(aq)|Ag(s)? E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V (in V).
qa.e: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Doubling for 2Ag⁺ does not change E°.

qa.q: In a galvanic cell, where does oxidation take place and what is its polarity?
qa.a: At the anode, which is negative
qa.e: Oxidation releases electrons at the anode, making it the negative terminal of a galvanic cell.

qa.q: What potential is assigned to the standard hydrogen electrode?
qa.e: By convention, E°(H⁺/½H₂) = 0 at all temperatures; other potentials are measured against it.

qa.q: A cell is written Pt(s)|H₂(g, 1 bar)|H⁺(aq, 1 M)||Cu²⁺(aq, 1 M)|Cu(s) and its emf is 0.34 V. What does this tell us?
qa.a: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, and Cu²⁺ is reduced more easily than H⁺
qa.e: With SHE on the left as anode, E°cell = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − 0 = +0.34 V, so copper is the cathode.

qa.q: Which is the correct representation of the cell with the reaction Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)?
qa.e: The anode (Mg, oxidised) is written on the left, the cathode (Ag⁺/Ag) on the right, with || for the salt bridge.

qa.q: A cell made of Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V) and SHE: which electrode is the cathode?
qa.e: Zinc has the lower reduction potential, so it is oxidised (anode); H⁺ is reduced at the SHE (cathode).

qa.q: Why can the absolute potential of a single electrode not be measured?
qa.a: Only a potential difference between two electrodes can be measured
qa.e: A voltmeter needs two terminals, so potentials are measured relative to a reference like SHE.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In a galvanic cell the cathode is the positive electrode. Reason (R): Electrons are consumed at the cathode by the reduction half-reaction.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Electrons flow towards the cathode where they are used up in reduction, making it positive relative to the anode.

qa.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent among these? E°: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V.
qa.e: The species with the highest reduction potential is most easily reduced, i.e. it is the strongest oxidising agent.

qa.q: Which metal is the strongest reducing agent? E°: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.36 V, Al³⁺/Al −1.66 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V.
qa.e: The most negative E° means the metal is most easily oxidised, so it is the best reducing agent.

qa.q: Can a solution of CuSO₄ be stored in a silver vessel? E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V.
qa.a: Yes, because Ag cannot reduce Cu²⁺
qa.e: For Ag + Cu²⁺ → Ag⁺ + Cu, E°cell = 0.34 − 0.80 = −0.46 V, so no reaction occurs.

qa.q: Will Fe³⁺ oxidise I⁻ to I₂ under standard conditions? E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V, E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V. What is E°cell (in V)?
qa.e: E°cell = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V; positive, so the reaction is feasible.

qa.q: Why does copper not liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
qa.a: Its standard reduction potential is positive, higher than that of H⁺/H₂
qa.e: With E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, the reaction Cu + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂ has E°cell = −0.34 V.

qa.q: Why is platinum used as the electrode in the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ half-cell?
qa.a: It is inert and only provides a surface for electron transfer
qa.e: There is no solid metal in this couple, so an inert conductor like Pt is needed to carry electrons without reacting.

qa.q: Arrange the metals in increasing order of reducing power: Ag (+0.80 V), Zn (−0.76 V), Cu (+0.34 V), Mg (−2.36 V).
qa.e: Reducing power increases as E° becomes more negative.

qa.q: Assertion (A): F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent. Reason (R): F₂/F⁻ has the highest standard reduction potential in the electrochemical series.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The highest E° means F₂ has the greatest tendency to be reduced, so it oxidises others most strongly.

qa.q: Calculate E_cell at 298 K for Zn|Zn²⁺(0.01 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu, given E°cell = 1.10 V (answer in V).
What is the electrode potential (in V) of Cu²⁺(0.01 M)/Cu at 298 K? E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
What is the potential (in V) of a hydrogen electrode in a solution of pH 3 at 298 K (H₂ at 1 bar)?
In the Daniell cell, how can E_cell be increased above 1.10 V?
qa.e: E_cell = 1.10 − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]); a smaller ratio makes log Q negative and E_cell larger.

qa.q: For Mg(s)|Mg²⁺(0.001 M)||Cu²⁺(0.1 M)|Cu(s), E°cell = 2.70 V. What is E_cell at 298 K (in V)?
Why are concentrations of Zn(s) and Cu(s) not written in the Nernst equation for the Daniell cell?
qa.a: Pure solids have constant activity taken as 1
qa.e: The activity of a pure solid is unity, so it does not appear in Q.

qa.q: For Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s), E° = 0.80 V. What is E (in V) at 298 K when [Ag⁺] = 0.1 M?
Assertion (A): The emf of a cell changes when the concentrations of ions are changed. Reason (R): E°cell depends on the concentrations of the ions.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: E_cell changes with concentration through the log Q term, but E° is fixed (defined at 1 M), so R is false.

qa.q: What is Δr G° (in kJ mol⁻¹) for the Daniell cell with E°cell = 1.10 V? Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.
A cell reaction with n = 2 has E°cell = 0.295 V at 298 K. What is log K_c?
What is the sign of Δr G for a reaction whose E_cell is positive?
qa.e: Δr G = −nFE_cell, so a positive E_cell gives a negative Δr G.

qa.q: What is E_cell for a galvanic cell whose reaction has reached equilibrium?
qa.e: At equilibrium Δr G = 0, so E_cell = 0; the battery is 'dead'.

qa.q: For a reaction with n = 1 and E°cell = 0.118 V at 298 K, what is K_c?
Calculate Δr G° (in kJ mol⁻¹) for a cell with n = 1 and E°cell = 0.46 V. Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.
A cell reaction has a very large positive E°cell. What can you say about its equilibrium constant?
qa.a: It is very large; the reaction goes nearly to completion
qa.e: log K = nE°/0.059, so a large positive E° gives a very large K.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Electrical work done by a galvanic cell equals the decrease in its Gibbs energy. Reason (R): Δr G = −nFE_cell.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The maximum electrical work obtainable is nFE_cell, which equals −Δr G; R states this relation.

qa.q: A conductivity cell with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹) has resistance 100 Ω. What is the cell constant (in cm⁻¹)?
What is Λm (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of 0.1 M KCl with κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹?
The same cell (G* = 1.29 cm⁻¹) filled with a 0.02 M electrolyte shows R = 520 Ω. Its conductivity is n × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹. What is n (two decimals)?
Why is alternating current (AC) used to measure the resistance of an electrolytic solution?
qa.a: To prevent electrolysis and polarisation at the electrodes
qa.e: DC would decompose the electrolyte and change its composition at the electrodes; AC avoids this.

qa.q: How does the conductivity of a metal and of an electrolyte change on heating?
qa.e: Heating increases vibrations of metal ions, hindering electrons; in solutions it lowers viscosity and speeds up ions.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of molar conductivity?
qa.e: Λm = κ/c = (S m⁻¹) ÷ (mol m⁻³) = S m² mol⁻¹.

qa.q: A solution has resistivity 50 Ω cm. What is its conductivity (in S cm⁻¹)?
Assertion (A): The cell constant of a conductivity cell is found using a KCl solution of known conductivity. Reason (R): G* = κ × R, so knowing κ and measuring R gives G*.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because l and A are hard to measure directly, a standard KCl solution is used with G* = κR.

qa.q: What is Λ°m (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of MgCl₂? λ°(Mg²⁺) = 106.0, λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹.
What is Λ°m (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of Na₂SO₄? λ°(Na⁺) = 50.1, λ°(SO₄²⁻) = 160.0 S cm² mol⁻¹.
Why does the conductivity (κ) of a solution decrease on dilution?
qa.a: The number of ions per unit volume decreases
qa.e: κ measures conductance of a unit volume (1 cm³); dilution leaves fewer ions in that volume.

qa.q: Why does molar conductivity increase on dilution?
qa.a: Λm = κV, and the volume V containing one mole increases more than κ decreases
qa.e: Although κ falls, the volume containing 1 mol of electrolyte rises faster, so their product Λm increases.

qa.q: For a strong electrolyte, a graph of Λm against √c is a straight line. What does its intercept give?
qa.e: From Λm = Λ°m − A√c, the intercept at √c = 0 is Λ°m and the slope is −A.

qa.q: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
qa.a: Λ°m of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion
qa.e: At infinite dilution each ion moves independently and contributes its own λ°, so Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.

qa.q: Which electrolyte would have the largest constant A in Λm = Λ°m − A√c, in water at the same temperature?
qa.e: A depends on the charges of the ions; MgSO₄ is a 2-2 electrolyte, giving the strongest interionic effects.

qa.q: Assertion (A): H⁺ has a much higher limiting molar conductivity than Na⁺. Reason (R): According to Kohlrausch's law, each ion contributes a definite share to Λ°m.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but Kohlrausch's law does not explain why H⁺ moves so fast; that is due to its special proton-hopping mechanism in water.

qa.q: Λ°m values: HCl 425.9, NaCl 126.4, CH₃COONa 91.0 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is Λ°m of CH₃COOH (in S cm² mol⁻¹)?
qa.e: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹: the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ contributions cancel.

qa.q: 0.01 M acetic acid has Λm = 39.05 S cm² mol⁻¹ and Λ°m = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is its degree of dissociation?
For 0.01 M acetic acid with α = 0.1, Ka = n × 10⁻⁴. What is n (two decimals)?
Why can Λ°m of acetic acid not be found by extrapolating its Λm vs √c graph?
qa.a: Λm rises very steeply at low concentrations, so the curve cannot be extrapolated reliably
qa.e: For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation keeps increasing sharply on dilution, so the curve is steep near zero concentration.

qa.q: Why does the molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte increase sharply on dilution?
qa.a: Its degree of dissociation increases a lot on dilution
qa.e: On dilution more molecules ionise, greatly increasing the number of ions per mole.

qa.q: Using λ°(H⁺) = 349.6 and λ°(HCOO⁻) = 54.6 S cm² mol⁻¹, what is Λ°m of formic acid (in S cm² mol⁻¹)?
qa.e: Λ°m(HCOOH) = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2 S cm² mol⁻¹.

qa.q: A 0.001 M solution of a weak acid HA has Λm = 78.1 S cm² mol⁻¹ and Λ°m = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is α?

Assertion (A): Kohlrausch's law helps find the dissociation constant of a weak acid from conductivity data. Reason (R): It allows Λ°m of the weak acid to be calculated from Λ°m values of strong electrolytes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With Λ°m known, α = Λm/Λ°m and then Ka = cα²/(1 − α); R is exactly why A works.

qa.q: A current of 2 A flows through CuSO₄ solution for 965 s. What mass of Cu (in g) is deposited? (Cu = 63.5 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
qa.e: Q = 1930 C = 0.02 mol e⁻; Cu needs 2 e⁻, so 0.01 mol Cu = 0.635 g.

qa.q: How much charge (in C) is needed to deposit 1.08 g of silver from AgNO₃ solution? (Ag = 108 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
How long (in s) must a 5 A current flow to deposit 2.7 g of aluminium from molten Al₂O₃? (Al = 27 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
The same charge deposits 1.08 g of Ag in one cell and some copper in a second cell connected in series. What mass of Cu (in g) is deposited? (Ag = 108, Cu = 63.5)
qa.e: 1.08 g Ag means 0.01 mol e⁻ passed; Cu²⁺ needs 2e⁻, so 0.005 mol Cu = 0.3175 g.

qa.q: In the electrolysis of CuSO₄ solution using copper electrodes, what happens at the anode?
qa.e: The copper anode is oxidised, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, replacing the Cu²⁺ deposited at the cathode.

qa.q: In electrorefining of copper, which is made the anode?
qa.e: Impure copper dissolves at the anode, and pure copper deposits on the cathode; impurities settle as anode mud.

qa.q: How many faradays are needed to reduce 1 mol of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺?
qa.e: Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons per ion, so 5 F per mole.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In an electrolytic cell the anode is the positive electrode. Reason (R): Oxidation always occurs at the anode.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true. The anode is positive because it is connected to the positive terminal of the external source; the fact that oxidation happens there holds in all cells and does not explain the sign.

qa.q: What is obtained at the cathode when molten NaCl is electrolysed?
qa.e: In the melt there is no water, so Na⁺ is the only species reduced: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na.

qa.q: Why is H₂ and not Na formed at the cathode during electrolysis of aqueous NaCl?
qa.a: Water has a higher (less negative) reduction potential than Na⁺
qa.e: E°(H₂O/H₂) = −0.83 V is less negative than E°(Na⁺/Na) = −2.71 V, so water is reduced preferentially.

qa.q: Why is chlorine rather than oxygen liberated at the anode in the electrolysis of brine?
qa.a: Oxygen evolution has a high overpotential
qa.e: Thermodynamics favours O₂ slightly (1.23 V vs 1.36 V), but the extra voltage needed for O₂ makes Cl₂ formation faster in practice.

qa.q: Which substance is left in the solution after electrolysis of aqueous NaCl?
qa.e: Na⁺ ions remain and OH⁻ forms at the cathode, giving NaOH in solution.

qa.q: Which product forms at the anode on electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid with platinum electrodes?
qa.e: In dilute acid water is oxidised: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

qa.q: At higher concentrations of H₂SO₄, what is the anode product?
qa.e: With more sulphate ions available, 2SO₄²⁻ → S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻ becomes the anode reaction.

qa.q: Aqueous CuSO₄ is electrolysed with platinum electrodes. What forms at the anode?
qa.e: Pt is inert, so water is oxidised to O₂; copper deposits at the cathode.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The products of electrolysis can differ for the same electrolyte. Reason (R): Products depend on whether the electrolyte is molten or aqueous and on the electrode material.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Molten vs aqueous NaCl, and Pt vs Cu electrodes with CuSO₄, give different products, as R explains.

qa.q: What is the anode in a dry (Leclanché) cell?
qa.e: Zinc is oxidised (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), so the zinc container is the anode.

qa.q: What is the cathode reaction of a dry cell?
qa.e: MnO₂ is reduced (Mn from +4 to +3) at the carbon cathode in the presence of NH₄⁺.

qa.q: Why does a mercury cell give a constant voltage during its life?
qa.a: Its overall reaction involves no ions whose concentration changes
qa.e: Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l) has only solids and a liquid, so Q stays constant.

qa.q: What is the overall discharge reaction of a lead storage battery?
qa.e: Both electrodes turn into PbSO₄ while sulphuric acid is used up during discharge.

qa.q: Why is the density of the acid in a lead storage battery a measure of its charge?
qa.a: H₂SO₄ is consumed during discharge, so the acid becomes less dense
qa.e: Discharge uses up H₂SO₄ and forms water, lowering density; charging restores it.

qa.q: What is the cathode reaction in an H₂–O₂ fuel cell with alkaline electrolyte?
qa.e: Oxygen is reduced at the cathode in alkaline medium, giving hydroxide ions.

qa.q: What is the approximate efficiency of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
qa.e: Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electricity at about 70%, compared with about 40% for thermal power plants.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A nickel–cadmium cell is a secondary cell. Reason (R): Its cell reaction can be reversed by passing current through it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Secondary cells are rechargeable, i.e. their reaction can be reversed by an external current, which is true for Ni–Cd cells.

qa.q: What is E°cell (in V) for 2Fe + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + 2H₂O? E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V, E°(O₂/H₂O) = +1.23 V.
Which reaction occurs at the anodic spot during rusting of iron?
qa.e: Iron is oxidised at the anodic spot; oxygen is reduced at the cathodic spot.

qa.q: What is the chemical formula of rust?
qa.e: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

qa.q: Why does iron rust faster near the sea coast?
qa.a: Salt in the moist air makes the surface water a better electrolyte
qa.e: Dissolved salts increase ionic conduction between anodic and cathodic spots, speeding the electrochemical reaction.

qa.q: How does galvanising protect iron?
qa.a: Zinc is more reactive and gets oxidised in preference to iron
qa.e: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V is more negative than Fe's, so zinc corrodes first even if the coating is scratched.

qa.q: A magnesium block is connected to an underground iron pipeline. What is it called?
qa.e: Magnesium is oxidised instead of iron, so it is sacrificed to protect the pipe.

qa.q: Why does corrosion of iron need both moisture and oxygen?
qa.a: Water acts as the electrolyte and O₂ is reduced at the cathodic spot
qa.e: Without an electrolyte the electrochemical cell cannot work, and without O₂ there is no cathode reaction.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A scratch on a galvanised iron sheet does not lead to rusting of the exposed iron. Reason (R): Zinc has a lower (more negative) reduction potential than iron and corrodes preferentially.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Even when exposed, iron is protected because zinc acts as the anode and is oxidised first.

qa.q: The concentration of a reactant falls from 0.50 M to 0.30 M in 4 minutes. What is the average rate (in mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹)?
For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, −d[H₂]/dt = 0.03 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is d[NH₃]/dt (in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)?
qa.e: Rate = −(1/3) d[H₂]/dt = 0.01 = (1/2) d[NH₃]/dt, so d[NH₃]/dt = 0.02.

qa.q: For 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂, which expression correctly gives the rate of reaction?
qa.e: Each rate is divided by its stoichiometric coefficient so they all become equal; reactants carry a minus sign.

qa.q: How is the instantaneous rate found from a concentration–time graph?
qa.a: From the slope of the tangent at that instant
qa.e: Instantaneous rate is d[R]/dt, the gradient of the tangent at that point.

qa.q: What is the unit of rate for a gaseous reaction when concentration is expressed as pressure?
qa.e: Rate = change in pressure ÷ time, so the unit is atm s⁻¹ (or bar s⁻¹).

qa.q: Why does a reaction that is thermodynamically feasible sometimes not occur noticeably?
qa.a: Thermodynamics shows feasibility but not speed; the rate may be extremely slow
qa.e: ΔG < 0 says the reaction can occur; kinetics (activation energy) decides how fast. Diamond to graphite is very slow.

qa.q: For 2A → B, the product forms at 0.15 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the rate of disappearance of A (in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)?
Assertion (A): The rate of a reaction usually decreases with time. Reason (R): Reactant concentrations decrease as the reaction proceeds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Rate depends on reactant concentrations, which fall as they are consumed, so the rate generally slows.

qa.q: For rate = k[NO]²[O₂], by what factor does the rate change if [NO] is doubled and [O₂] is halved?
For rate = k[A][B]², by what factor does the rate change if [B] is tripled at constant [A]?
qa.e: Rate ∝ [B]², so tripling [B] multiplies the rate by 3² = 9.

qa.q: Which statement about the rate law is correct?
qa.e: Exponents in the rate law come from experiment; for example CHCl₃ + Cl₂ has an order of ½ in Cl₂.

qa.q: What is the physical meaning of the rate constant k?
qa.a: The rate of reaction when every reactant concentration is 1 mol L⁻¹
qa.e: Putting [A] = [B] = 1 M in rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ gives rate = k.

qa.q: Which change will NOT change the rate constant of a reaction?
qa.a: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
qa.e: Concentration changes the rate but not k; k changes only with temperature or catalyst.

qa.q: For CH₃CHO → CH₄ + CO, rate = k[CH₃CHO]^(3/2). By what factor does the rate change if [CH₃CHO] is made 4 times?
For a reaction A + B → C, the rate law is rate = k[A]. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Changing [B] does not affect the rate
qa.e: The rate law shows no dependence on [B], though B is still consumed; its order is zero.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The rate of a gaseous reaction increases when the reaction mixture is compressed. Reason (R): Compression increases the concentration (partial pressure) of the gaseous reactants.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Higher pressure means more molecules per unit volume, i.e. higher concentration, which raises the rate.

qa.q: In an experiment, doubling [A] at constant [B] doubles the rate, and doubling [B] at constant [A] increases the rate 4 times. What is the overall order?
qa.e: Order in A = 1 and in B = 2, so overall order = 1 + 2 = 3.

qa.q: The rate constant of a reaction is 2.0 × 10⁻³ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the order of the reaction?
qa.e: L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−2) s⁻¹, which matches n = 2.

qa.q: What is the unit of the rate constant of a zero order reaction?
qa.e: For n = 0, unit = (mol L⁻¹)¹ s⁻¹ — the same as the unit of rate.

qa.q: Initial rates: [A] = 0.1 M gives 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; [A] = 0.2 M gives 8.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹. What is the order with respect to A?
qa.e: Doubling [A] increases the rate 4 times: 2ˣ = 4, so x = 2.

qa.q: For CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl, rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½. What is the overall order?
qa.e: Order = 1 + ½ = 1.5; orders can be fractional.

qa.q: The rate of a reaction is unchanged when the concentration of reactant X is tripled. What is the order with respect to X?
qa.e: If 3ˣ = 1, x = 0: the rate does not depend on [X].

qa.q: Which of these values is possible for the order of a reaction but impossible for the molecularity of an elementary step?
qa.e: Order is experimental and can be fractional; molecularity counts colliding species, so it must be a whole number (1, 2 or 3).

qa.q: Assertion (A): The unit of k for a first order reaction does not involve concentration. Reason (R): For n = 1, (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) becomes (mol L⁻¹)⁰.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: For first order the concentration unit cancels, leaving s⁻¹.

qa.q: What is the molecularity of the elementary reaction 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g)?
qa.e: Two HI molecules collide simultaneously, so it is bimolecular.

qa.q: Which statement about molecularity is correct?
qa.a: It cannot be zero or fractional
qa.e: Molecularity counts colliding species in an elementary step, which must be a whole number of 1, 2 or 3.

qa.q: Why are reactions with molecularity greater than three very rare?
qa.a: The chance of more than three molecules colliding at once with the right orientation is extremely small
qa.e: Simultaneous effective collisions of many species are statistically very unlikely.

qa.q: In a complex reaction, which step determines the overall rate?
qa.e: The overall rate can be no faster than its slowest step, the rate-determining step.

qa.q: For 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (catalysed by I⁻ in alkaline medium), the rate law is rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]. What is the order with respect to H₂O₂?
qa.e: The power of [H₂O₂] in the experimental rate law is 1, even though its coefficient in the overall equation is 2.

qa.q: Which reaction is unimolecular?
qa.e: A single species (NH₄NO₂) decomposes in this elementary step.

qa.q: The order of a reaction is 1.5. What can you conclude?
qa.a: It is a complex reaction, not an elementary one
qa.e: A fractional order cannot arise from a single elementary step, so the reaction must have a multi-step mechanism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Order and molecularity are the same for every reaction. Reason (R): Molecularity has meaning only for elementary reactions.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: Order and molecularity often differ (and molecularity is meaningless for complex reactions), so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: A zero order reaction has [R]₀ = 0.8 mol L⁻¹ and k = 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is its half-life (in s)?
For a zero order reaction with [R]₀ = 0.6 M and k = 0.01 M s⁻¹, what is [R] (in M) after 20 s?
What is obtained when [R] is plotted against t for a zero order reaction?
qa.a: A straight line with slope −k and intercept [R]₀
qa.e: From [R] = −kt + [R]₀, the graph is linear with slope −k.

qa.q: Why is the decomposition of NH₃ on a hot platinum surface at high pressure zero order?
qa.a: The metal surface is saturated with NH₃, so more gas cannot increase the rate
qa.e: Once all active sites are covered, the rate is fixed by the surface, not by the gas concentration.

qa.q: How does the half-life of a zero order reaction depend on the initial concentration?
qa.e: t½ = [R]₀/2k, so doubling [R]₀ doubles t½.

qa.q: A first order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. What is its half-life (in min)?
How long (in s) will a zero order reaction with [R]₀ = 0.5 M and k = 0.025 M s⁻¹ take to go to completion?
qa.e: At completion [R] = 0, so t = [R]₀/k = 0.5 ÷ 0.025 = 20 s.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface is a zero order reaction. Reason (R): For zero order reactions, the rate depends on the concentration of the reactant.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: HI decomposition on gold is zero order, but zero order means the rate does NOT depend on concentration, so R is false.

qa.q: A first order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. How long (in min) does it take for 75% completion?
qa.e: 75% completion = 2 half-lives; t½ = 0.693/0.0231 = 30 min, so t = 60 min.

qa.q: The concentration of a reactant in a first order reaction falls from 0.1 M to 0.01 M in 46.06 s. What is k (in s⁻¹)?
What fraction of a first order reactant remains after 4 half-lives?
qa.e: Each half-life halves the amount: (½)⁴ = 1/16.

qa.q: Which plot gives a straight line for a first order reaction?
qa.e: ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt is linear in t with slope −k.

qa.q: Why is the half-life of a first order reaction independent of the initial concentration?
qa.a: Because t½ = 0.693/k, which contains no concentration term
qa.e: Substituting [R] = [R]₀/2 into k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R]) gives t½ = 2.303 log 2/k = 0.693/k.

qa.q: A first order reaction is 50% complete in 30 minutes. How long (in min) will it take to be 87.5% complete?
qa.e: 87.5% complete means 12.5% = (½)³ remains, so 3 half-lives = 90 min.

qa.q: The half-life of a first order reaction is 10 min. What is k (in min⁻¹)?
Assertion (A): All natural radioactive decays follow first order kinetics. Reason (R): The rate of radioactive decay is proportional to the number of nuclei present.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Decay rate ∝ N is the first order rate law, so R explains A.

qa.q: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), pᵢ = 0.5 atm and pₜ = 0.95 atm after 100 s. k is n × 10⁻² s⁻¹. What is n?
For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), what is the partial pressure of A in terms of pᵢ and the total pressure pₜ?
qa.e: If x atm of A reacts, pₜ = pᵢ + x, so p_A = pᵢ − x = 2pᵢ − pₜ.

qa.q: Why is the acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate called a pseudo first order reaction?
qa.a: Water is in large excess, so its concentration remains almost constant
qa.e: Rate = k[ester][H₂O] becomes k′[ester] because [H₂O] barely changes.

qa.q: What are the products of the acid-catalysed inversion of cane sugar?
qa.e: Sucrose + water → glucose + fructose (in the presence of H⁺).

qa.q: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g) at constant volume, what happens to the total pressure as the reaction proceeds?
qa.e: One mole of gas gives two moles, so total pressure rises towards 2pᵢ.

qa.q: A pseudo first order reaction has rate = k′[ester], where k′ = k[H₂O]. If k′ = 0.0050 min⁻¹ and [H₂O] = 50 M, what is the true rate constant k (in L mol⁻¹ min⁻¹)?
Which reaction is a standard example of a first order gas-phase decomposition followed by pressure measurements?
qa.e: Decomposition of N₂O₅ is first order and changes the total pressure, which makes it easy to follow.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Inversion of cane sugar is a pseudo first order reaction. Reason (R): Its rate law is rate = k[C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁] because water is present in large excess.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The large excess of water makes its concentration constant, so the rate depends only on sucrose.

qa.q: A reaction's rate doubles for every 10 K rise. By what factor does the rate increase when temperature rises from 300 K to 340 K?
qa.e: 40 K = 4 steps of 10 K, so the factor is 2⁴ = 16.

qa.q: In the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT), what does e^(−Ea/RT) represent?
qa.a: The fraction of molecules with kinetic energy equal to or greater than Ea
qa.e: The exponential term gives the fraction of collisions energetic enough to cross the barrier.

qa.q: What is the activated complex?
qa.a: An unstable, high-energy arrangement of atoms at the top of the energy barrier
qa.e: It forms when reactants gain energy equal to Ea and exists only momentarily before giving products or reactants.

qa.q: How does the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve change when temperature increases?
qa.a: It broadens and shifts towards higher energies
qa.e: Higher temperature spreads energies more widely, with more molecules at high energy; total area stays constant.

qa.q: Why does a small rise in temperature increase the rate of reaction so much?
qa.a: The fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases greatly
qa.e: Because of the exponential term, a modest temperature rise sharply increases the number of molecules that can cross the barrier.

qa.q: Two reactions have the same A at the same temperature, but reaction X has a higher Ea than reaction Y. Which is faster?
qa.e: k = A e^(−Ea/RT): a lower Ea gives a larger k.

qa.q: If the rate constant increases from k to 3k for a 10 K rise, what is the temperature coefficient?
qa.e: Temperature coefficient = k(T + 10)/k(T) = 3k/k = 3.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Increasing temperature increases the rate of a reaction. Reason (R): Increasing temperature decreases the activation energy of the reaction.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true, but temperature does not change Ea; it increases the fraction of molecules having energy ≥ Ea. R is false.

qa.q: A reaction's rate constant doubles when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K. What is Ea (in kJ mol⁻¹)? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, log 2 = 0.3010)
A plot of ln k against 1/T has a slope of −6000 K. What is Ea (in kJ mol⁻¹)? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
qa.e: Slope = −Ea/R, so Ea = 6000 × 8.314 = 49884 J mol⁻¹ ≈ 49.88 kJ mol⁻¹.

qa.q: A plot of log k against 1/T has a slope of −5000 K. What is Ea (in kJ mol⁻¹)? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
qa.a: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
qa.e: The catalyst forms a different route (often via an intermediate) with a lower energy barrier.

qa.q: What effect does a catalyst have on the equilibrium constant of a reversible reaction?
qa.e: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so K is unchanged; equilibrium is just reached sooner.

qa.q: Can a catalyst make a reaction with positive ΔG occur spontaneously?
qa.a: No; it only speeds up reactions that are already spontaneous
qa.e: A catalyst does not change ΔG, so it cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction spontaneous.

qa.q: In the Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T, what does the intercept on the ln k axis give?
qa.e: From ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T), the intercept at 1/T = 0 is ln A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A catalyst does not alter the equilibrium constant of a reaction. Reason (R): A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and backward reactions by the same amount.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Equal lowering of both barriers speeds both directions equally, so the equilibrium position and K stay the same.

qa.q: According to collision theory, which two factors decide whether a collision is effective?
qa.e: Molecules must have at least the threshold energy and collide in the right orientation to form products.

qa.q: In the expression rate = P Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT), what does P represent?
qa.a: The probability or steric factor for proper orientation
qa.e: P accounts for the fraction of energetic collisions that also have correct orientation.

qa.q: What is collision frequency (Z)?
qa.a: The number of collisions per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture
qa.e: Z counts all collisions, effective or not, per unit time per unit volume.

qa.q: What is the main limitation of collision theory?
qa.a: It treats atoms and molecules as hard spheres and ignores their structure
qa.e: Real molecules have shapes and internal structure that the hard-sphere model ignores.

qa.q: For CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻, why do many energetic collisions still fail to give products?
qa.a: OH⁻ must attack carbon from the side opposite to Br, and many collisions are wrongly oriented
qa.e: Proper orientation is needed; only attack opposite to Br leads to the product.

qa.q: Why does an increase in temperature increase the number of effective collisions?
qa.a: More molecules possess energy equal to or greater than the threshold energy
qa.e: Higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with sufficient energy; Ea and P are unchanged.

qa.q: Who proposed the collision theory of reaction rates?
qa.e: Collision theory was developed by Max Trautz and William Lewis (1916–18).

qa.q: Assertion (A): All collisions between reactant molecules do not lead to the formation of products. Reason (R): Only collisions with sufficient energy and proper orientation are effective.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Effective collisions need both energy and orientation, which explains why most collisions fail.

qa.q: What is the ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
qa.e: A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d.

qa.q: Why are Zn, Cd and Hg not regarded as transition elements?
qa.a: They have completely filled d¹⁰ orbitals in the ground state and in their common oxidation states
qa.e: Zn²⁺, Cd²⁺ and Hg²⁺ are all d¹⁰, so these elements never have a partly filled d subshell in common states.

qa.q: Which series of transition elements starts with lanthanum?
qa.e: La and then Hf to Hg make up the 5d series.

qa.q: What is the general outer electronic configuration of the d-block elements?
qa.e: The d orbitals of the penultimate shell, (n−1)d, are being filled.

qa.q: How many unpaired electrons are present in Cu²⁺ (Z of Cu = 29)?
qa.e: Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹, which has one unpaired electron.

qa.q: Which element of the d-block has the configuration 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰?
qa.e: Pd is the notable exception with an empty 5s orbital.

qa.q: Silver has the configuration [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s¹. Why is it considered a transition element?
qa.a: In its +2 oxidation state it has an incomplete 4d⁹ subshell
qa.e: Ag²⁺ (4d⁹) has an incompletely filled d subshell, satisfying the definition.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Copper has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s². Reason (R): A completely filled d subshell has extra stability.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Moving one electron from 4s to 3d gives the more stable full 3d¹⁰ subshell.

qa.q: Why do transition metals have high melting points and enthalpies of atomisation?
qa.a: Strong metallic bonding involving both (n−1)d and ns electrons
qa.e: Unpaired d electrons add to metallic bonding, which is strongest around the middle of a series.

qa.q: Which 3d metal has the lowest melting point?
qa.e: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell and no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weakest.

qa.q: Why are the atomic radii of Zr (160 pm) and Hf (159 pm) almost equal?
qa.e: The poorly shielding 4f electrons filled before Hf cause a contraction that cancels the expected size increase.

qa.q: Why is the second ionisation enthalpy of chromium unusually high?
qa.a: Removing the second electron breaks the stable 3d⁵ configuration of Cr⁺
qa.e: Cr⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, a stable half-filled subshell; removing another electron needs extra energy.

qa.q: Why is the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese unusually high?
qa.a: Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
qa.e: Removing a third electron from Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) destroys the extra-stable half-filled subshell.

qa.q: How does atomic radius generally change across the 3d series?
qa.a: It decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant
qa.e: Increasing nuclear charge contracts the atom, but poor shielding by d electrons soon balances the effect.

qa.q: Which property increases from titanium to copper in the 3d series?
qa.e: Atoms get slightly smaller while atomic mass increases, so density rises from Ti to Cu.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Reason (R): Mercury has no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weak.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With a full 5d¹⁰ 6s² configuration, Hg has weak metallic bonding and a very low melting point.

qa.q: What is the oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇?
Which 3d element shows the largest number of oxidation states?
qa.e: Mn has the most electrons available in 3d and 4s and shows +2 to +7.

qa.q: Why is the highest oxidation state of a metal often found in its oxide rather than its fluoride?
qa.a: Oxygen can form multiple bonds with the metal
qa.e: Multiple M=O bonding lets oxygen stabilise very high oxidation states, e.g. Mn₂O₇ versus MnF₄.

qa.q: Why does CuI₂ not exist while CuCl₂ and CuBr₂ do?
qa.a: Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is reduced to Cu(I)
qa.e: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂: iodide is a good reducing agent.

qa.q: Why is Cu⁺ unstable in aqueous solution?
qa.a: It disproportionates to Cu²⁺ and Cu because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy
qa.e: The large hydration energy of the smaller, more highly charged Cu²⁺ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy.

qa.q: What is the oxidation state of nickel in Ni(CO)₄?
qa.e: CO is a neutral ligand, so nickel is in the zero oxidation state.

qa.q: Which is the highest oxidation state shown by vanadium?
qa.e: V has 3d³ 4s², so it can use all five electrons, as in V₂O₅.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Transition elements show variable oxidation states. Reason (R): The energies of (n−1)d and ns orbitals are very close.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the two sets of electrons are close in energy, varying numbers can be used in bonding.

qa.q: Why does copper not liberate hydrogen from dilute HCl?
qa.e: A positive reduction potential means Cu is a weaker reducing agent than H₂, so it cannot reduce H⁺.

qa.q: What is the main reason for the positive E°(Cu²⁺/Cu)?
qa.a: High enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation of Cu are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy
qa.e: Turning solid Cu into hydrated Cu²⁺ costs more energy than hydration returns.

qa.q: Why is Mn³⁺ a strong oxidising agent?
qa.a: It readily gains an electron to form the stable d⁵ Mn²⁺
qa.e: E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) = +1.57 V: reduction to half-filled d⁵ Mn²⁺ is highly favourable.

qa.q: Why is Cr²⁺ a strong reducing agent?
qa.a: It is oxidised to Cr³⁺, which has a stable t₂g³ (d³) configuration
qa.e: E°(Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺) = −0.41 V; Cr²⁺ gives up an electron to become stable Cr³⁺.

qa.q: Why is E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) comparatively low among the M³⁺/M²⁺ couples of the 3d series?
qa.a: Fe³⁺ has the extra-stable d⁵ configuration
qa.e: Because Fe³⁺ (d⁵) is stable, it is less eager to be reduced, so the potential is lower than for Mn or Co.

qa.q: Which ion is the strongest oxidising agent in aqueous solution? E°: Co³⁺/Co²⁺ +1.97 V, Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V, Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V.
qa.e: The highest reduction potential (+1.97 V) means Co³⁺ is most easily reduced.

qa.q: Why is E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) more negative than expected from the general trend?
qa.a: Zn²⁺ has a stable, completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration
qa.e: The stability of d¹⁰ Zn²⁺ makes oxidation of Zn especially favourable.

qa.q: Assertion (A): E°(Mn²⁺/Mn) is more negative than expected from the trend across the 3d series. Reason (R): Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled d⁵ configuration.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The stability of d⁵ Mn²⁺ makes its formation from Mn more favourable, giving a more negative E°.

qa.q: What is the spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of Mn²⁺ (Z of Mn = 25)?
qa.e: Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons: μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 = 5.92 BM.

qa.q: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of Cr³⁺ (Z of Cr = 24).
qa.e: Cr³⁺ is 3d³ with 3 unpaired electrons: μ = √15 = 3.87 BM.

qa.q: A divalent ion of the 3d series has a magnetic moment of 2.83 BM. How many unpaired electrons does it have?
Why is Zn²⁺ colourless in aqueous solution?
qa.a: It has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration, so no d–d transition is possible
qa.e: A full d subshell leaves no vacancy for an electron to jump into.

qa.q: Which ion is diamagnetic?
qa.e: Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰ with all electrons paired.

qa.q: What causes the colour of most transition-metal ions in solution?
qa.a: Absorption of visible light that promotes a d electron to a higher-energy d orbital
qa.e: d–d transitions absorb certain wavelengths, and the complementary colour is observed.

qa.q: Which ion has the highest spin-only magnetic moment: Ti³⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺ or Ni²⁺?
qa.e: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons; Ti³⁺ has 1, Cu²⁺ 1 and Ni²⁺ 2.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sc³⁺ compounds are colourless. Reason (R): Sc³⁺ has no electrons in its 3d orbitals.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A d⁰ ion has no d electrons to undergo d–d transitions, so it is colourless.

qa.q: Why do transition metal ions form a large number of complexes?
qa.a: Small size, high charge and availability of vacant d orbitals
qa.e: These features let them attract and accept electron pairs from ligands.

qa.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process for making sulphuric acid?
qa.e: V₂O₅ catalyses the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃.

qa.q: What is the main reason transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts?
qa.a: Their ability to show multiple oxidation states and form complexes
qa.e: Variable oxidation states let them form and break intermediates; surfaces also adsorb reactants.

qa.q: In the Fe³⁺-catalysed reaction of I⁻ with S₂O₈²⁻, what is the role of Fe²⁺?
qa.a: It reduces S₂O₈²⁻ and is oxidised back to Fe³⁺
qa.e: 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻ regenerates the catalyst.

qa.q: Which statement about interstitial compounds is correct?
qa.a: They are very hard and have high melting points
qa.e: Small atoms in the lattice holes make the solid harder and higher melting, while metallic conductivity stays.

qa.q: Which of these is an interstitial compound?
qa.e: In TiC, small carbon atoms occupy the holes of the titanium lattice.

qa.q: Why do transition metals readily form alloys with one another?
qa.a: Their atomic radii are very similar
qa.e: Atoms of similar size (within about 15%) can replace each other in the crystal lattice.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Finely divided iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process. Reason (R): Transition metals provide a surface on which reactant molecules can be adsorbed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Finely divided iron has a large surface area that adsorbs N₂ and H₂, weakening their bonds and speeding up the reaction.

qa.q: What happens when an alkali is added to an orange solution of potassium dichromate?
qa.a: It turns yellow as chromate ions form
qa.e: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O; chromate is yellow.

qa.q: Which is the correct balanced equation for the oxidation of Fe²⁺ by acidified dichromate?
qa.e: Each Cr gains 3 electrons (6 for two Cr), so 6 Fe²⁺ are oxidised; charges and atoms balance.

qa.q: What is the Cr–O–Cr bond angle in the dichromate ion?
qa.e: Two CrO₄ tetrahedra share one oxygen at the corner, with a Cr–O–Cr angle of 126°.

qa.q: Why is K₂Cr₂O₇ made from Na₂Cr₂O₇ by adding KCl?
qa.a: K₂Cr₂O₇ is less soluble, so it crystallises out
qa.e: Sodium dichromate is more soluble; the potassium salt separates as orange crystals.

qa.q: Which oxide is the most acidic?
qa.e: Mn is in its highest oxidation state (+7); acidity increases with oxidation state.

qa.q: How many electrons are gained by one dichromate ion when it is reduced to Cr³⁺ in acid?
qa.e: Each of the two Cr atoms goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons: total 6.

qa.q: What happens when H₂S is passed through acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ solution?
qa.a: Sulphur is precipitated and the solution turns green
qa.e: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3H₂S + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3S + 7H₂O; Cr³⁺ is green and S is a pale yellow precipitate.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An orange dichromate solution turns yellow on adding NaOH. Reason (R): The oxidation state of chromium changes from +6 to +3.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: The colour change is due to dichromate converting to chromate; Cr stays +6 in both, so R is false.

qa.q: How many electrons does MnO₄⁻ gain when it is reduced in acidic medium?
qa.e: Mn goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, a gain of 5 electrons.

qa.q: What is the product of reduction of MnO₄⁻ in neutral or faintly alkaline medium?
qa.e: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻; Mn goes from +7 to +4.

qa.q: Why is dilute H₂SO₄ and not HCl used to acidify KMnO₄ in titrations?
qa.a: KMnO₄ would oxidise HCl to chlorine
qa.e: Permanganate is a strong enough oxidant to oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂, which would consume extra titrant.

qa.q: Which is the correctly balanced equation for MnO₄⁻ oxidising Fe²⁺ in acid?
qa.e: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻ and each Fe²⁺ loses 1, so 5 Fe²⁺ react per MnO₄⁻; charges balance (+17 on each side).

qa.q: What is the shape and magnetic nature of the permanganate ion?
qa.e: In MnO₄⁻, Mn(+7) is d⁰ with no unpaired electrons, and the ion is tetrahedral.

qa.q: What is formed when acidified KMnO₄ reacts with a nitrite?
qa.e: 5NO₂⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5NO₃⁻ + 3H₂O.

qa.q: In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, KMnO₄ oxidises iodide to:
qa.e: 2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O + I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻ + IO₃⁻; in acid the product would be I₂.

qa.q: Assertion (A): No separate indicator is needed in titrations with KMnO₄. Reason (R): The intensely coloured MnO₄⁻ gives a pink colour as soon as it is in slight excess, while Mn²⁺ is nearly colourless.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: At the end point the first excess drop of purple permanganate tints the solution pink, so it acts as a self-indicator.

qa.q: What is the most common oxidation state of the lanthanoids?
qa.e: All lanthanoids show +3; +2 and +4 occur only where they give f⁰, f⁷ or f¹⁴.

qa.q: What is the main cause of lanthanoid contraction?
qa.a: Imperfect shielding of one 4f electron by another
qa.e: Diffuse 4f orbitals shield poorly, so effective nuclear charge rises steadily and the size shrinks.

qa.q: Why is Ce⁴⁺ a strong oxidising agent in aqueous solution?
qa.a: It tends to return to the common +3 state by gaining an electron
qa.e: E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V, so Ce⁴⁺ is readily reduced to Ce³⁺.

qa.q: Which lanthanoid ion is a strong reducing agent?
qa.e: Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) is readily oxidised to the common Eu³⁺ state.

qa.q: How does the basic strength of lanthanoid hydroxides change from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃?
qa.e: Smaller Ln³⁺ ions polarise OH⁻ more and hold it more covalently, so basicity falls.

qa.q: What is misch metal mainly composed of?
qa.a: About 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al
qa.e: Misch metal is a lanthanoid-rich alloy used in magnesium alloys for bullets, shells and lighter flints.

qa.q: What is formed when a lanthanoid reacts with water?
qa.e: Lanthanoids are reactive metals; they form hydroxides and release hydrogen.

qa.q: Assertion (A): It is difficult to separate lanthanoids from one another. Reason (R): Due to lanthanoid contraction, their ionic radii and chemical properties are very similar.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Similar size and charge make their chemistry nearly identical, so separation is hard.

qa.q: What is the general electronic configuration of the lanthanoids?
qa.e: Lanthanoids fill the 4f subshell, with 6s² and 0 or 1 electron in 5d. 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s² is the actinoid pattern.

qa.q: Why is actinoid contraction greater than lanthanoid contraction?
qa.a: 5f electrons shield the nuclear charge more poorly than 4f electrons
qa.e: Poorer shielding by 5f electrons means effective nuclear charge rises more sharply across the series.

qa.q: Which element marks the beginning of the actinoid series?
qa.e: The 14 actinoids run from Th (90) to Lr (103).

qa.q: What is the highest oxidation state shown by neptunium?
qa.e: The maximum oxidation state rises from +4 (Th) to +7 at Np and then falls.

qa.q: Why do actinoids show a wide range of oxidation states?
qa.e: Close energy levels let different numbers of electrons be used in bonding.

qa.q: Which property is common to all actinoids?
qa.e: Every actinoid is radioactive; early ones have long half-lives and later ones very short.

qa.q: Which lanthanoid is radioactive?
qa.e: Pm is the only radioactive lanthanoid; all actinoids are radioactive.

qa.q: How do actinoids behave with nitric acid?
qa.a: Nitric acid has little effect because a protective oxide layer forms
qa.e: Like some passive metals, actinoids are protected by an oxide film in HNO₃, while HCl attacks them.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The chemistry of actinoids is less smooth and predictable than that of lanthanoids. Reason (R): Actinoids show a wide range of oxidation states and are radioactive.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Many oxidation states and radioactivity (making study difficult) give actinoid chemistry its complexity.

qa.q: Thorium (Z = 90) is the first actinoid. What is its ground-state configuration?
qa.e: Because 5f and 6d are close in energy, thorium places its two outer electrons in 6d and has no 5f electron. Such irregularities are typical of the early actinoids (general pattern 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s²).

qa.q: Which compound is used as a white pigment in paints?
qa.e: Titanium dioxide is a brilliant white, stable pigment.

qa.q: Which metals are known as coinage metals?
qa.e: The group 11 metals copper, silver and gold have been used for coins.

qa.q: What is the Ziegler catalyst used for making polythene?
qa.e: The titanium–aluminium catalyst system polymerises ethene.

qa.q: Why is AgBr used in photographic films?
qa.e: Light decomposes AgBr locally, forming the latent image.

qa.q: Give reason: Transition metals have high enthalpies of atomisation.
qa.a: They have many unpaired d electrons that strengthen metallic bonding
qa.e: More unpaired electrons give stronger interatomic metallic bonds, which need more energy to break.

qa.q: Which component of a dry cell is a compound of a transition element?
qa.e: Manganese dioxide is the depolariser at the cathode.

qa.q: Give reason: The 3d metals Sc and Zn form colourless compounds in their common oxidation states.
qa.a: Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transitions are possible
qa.e: Empty or full d subshells cannot undergo d–d excitation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Iron is used in the Haber process. Reason (R): Iron is the most abundant transition metal in the Earth's crust.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but iron catalyses the Haber process because of its surface and variable oxidation states, not because it is abundant.

qa.q: How many moles of AgCl are precipitated when 1 mol of [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ is treated with excess AgNO₃?
qa.e: All three chlorides are outside the coordination sphere and are ionisable.

qa.q: CoCl₃·4NH₃ gives 1 mol AgCl per mol with excess AgNO₃. What is its Werner formula?
qa.e: Only one Cl⁻ is ionisable; the other two Cl and four NH₃ complete the coordination number of 6.

qa.q: According to Werner, the secondary valence of a metal corresponds to its:
qa.e: Secondary valence (non-ionisable) equals the coordination number; primary valence equals the oxidation state.

qa.q: Which statement distinguishes a double salt from a complex?
qa.a: A double salt dissociates completely into simple ions in water; a complex ion does not
qa.e: Mohr's salt gives Fe²⁺, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻, but K₄[Fe(CN)₆] gives K⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, not Fe²⁺ and CN⁻.

qa.q: How many ions does [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ produce in aqueous solution?
qa.e: It gives one [CoCl(NH₃)₅]²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions.

qa.q: Which of these is a double salt?
qa.e: Mohr's salt dissociates completely into Fe²⁺, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ in water.

qa.q: What shapes did Werner propose for groups bound by secondary valence?
qa.e: He postulated definite spatial arrangements, explaining isomerism such as the green and violet forms of CoCl₃·4NH₃.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An aqueous solution of K₄[Fe(CN)₆] does not give tests for Fe²⁺ ions. Reason (R): [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is a stable complex ion that does not dissociate into Fe²⁺ and CN⁻.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The complex ion stays intact in water, so free Fe²⁺ is not available to react.

qa.q: Which of these biologically important substances is a coordination compound of magnesium?
qa.e: In chlorophyll, Mg²⁺ is held by four nitrogen donor atoms of a ring ligand. Haemoglobin (Fe) and vitamin B₁₂ (Co) are other natural coordination compounds.

qa.q: What is the coordination number of Co in [Co(en)₃]³⁺?
qa.e: Each ethane-1,2-diamine is didentate, so 3 × 2 = 6 nitrogen atoms bind cobalt.

qa.q: What is the coordination number of Fe in K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃]?
qa.e: Each oxalate binds through two oxygen atoms: 3 × 2 = 6.

qa.q: How many donor atoms does EDTA⁴⁻ use to bind a metal ion?
qa.e: EDTA⁴⁻ binds through two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms, so it is hexadentate.

qa.q: Which ligand is ambidentate?
qa.e: Thiocyanate can bind through S or through N.

qa.q: What is a chelate?
