qa.a: A ring complex formed when a ligand binds the same metal through two or more donor atoms
qa.e: Chelating ligands like en or oxalate wrap around the metal, forming a ring.

qa.q: In K₄[Fe(CN)₆], what are the counter ions?
qa.e: Ions outside the square bracket that balance its charge are counter ions.

qa.q: In a coordination entity, the central metal ion acts as a:
qa.e: Ligands donate lone pairs to the metal, which accepts them.

qa.q: Assertion (A): NO₂⁻ is an ambidentate ligand. Reason (R): It can coordinate to a metal through either its nitrogen or one of its oxygen atoms.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Binding through N gives nitrito-N and through O gives nitrito-O; this is the definition of ambidentate.

qa.q: What is the oxidation state of Fe in K₄[Fe(CN)₆]?
qa.e: Complex ion is [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: x + 6(−1) = −4, so x = +2.

qa.q: What is the oxidation state of Cu in [Cu(CN)₄]³⁻?
What is the oxidation state of Co in [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂?
qa.e: The complex ion is [CoCl(NH₃)₅]²⁺: x + (−1) + 0 = +2, so x = +3.

qa.q: What is the geometry of [Ni(CO)₄]?
qa.e: Ni(CO)₄ is a tetrahedral complex with Ni in the zero oxidation state.

qa.q: Which complex is heteroleptic?
qa.e: It has two kinds of ligands, NH₃ and Cl⁻.

qa.q: What are the oxidation state and coordination number of Pt in [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]?
qa.e: x + 0 + 2(−1) = 0 gives +2; four donor atoms are bonded, so CN = 4.

qa.q: What is the oxidation state of Cr in [Cr(en)₃]Cl₃?
qa.e: en is neutral, so x = +3 to balance three Cl⁻ counter ions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is a homoleptic complex. Reason (R): The metal is bound to only one kind of donor group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Only NH₃ ligands are present, which is the meaning of homoleptic.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂?
qa.e: Ligands alphabetical (ammine before chlorido); Co is +3; the complex is a cation, so no -ate.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of K₃[Fe(CN)₆]?
qa.e: The complex anion takes the Latin -ate form ferrate; x + 6(−1) = −3 gives Fe(III).

qa.q: What is the formula of tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride?
qa.e: Co(III) with one Cl⁻ ligand gives a +2 complex ion, which needs two Cl⁻ counter ions.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of [CoCl₂(en)₂]Cl?
qa.e: 'bis' is used because the ligand name contains 'di'; chlorido comes before ethane-1,2-diamine alphabetically; Co is +3.

qa.q: What is the formula of potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II)?
qa.e: Zn(II) with four OH⁻ gives [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻, which needs two K⁺; the cation is written first.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name for the ligand H₂O in a complex?
qa.e: Neutral ligands keep their names except aqua, ammine, carbonyl and nitrosyl.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of [Ag(NH₃)₂][Ag(CN)₂]?
qa.e: The cation is named first without -ate; the anionic complex uses the Latin name argentate.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the name of an anionic complex, the metal name ends in -ate. Reason (R): Anionic ligands in a complex end in -o.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both rules are true, but the -o ending of anionic ligands does not explain why the metal takes -ate.

qa.q: How many geometrical isomers does square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] have?
qa.e: The two Cl can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans).

qa.q: How many stereoisomers does [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ have?
qa.e: trans (one, optically inactive) + cis (d and l) = 3.

qa.q: Which complex shows fac–mer isomerism?
qa.e: Octahedral MA₃B₃ complexes show fac and mer forms.

qa.q: Why do tetrahedral complexes not show geometrical isomerism?
qa.a: All four positions in a tetrahedron are adjacent to one another
qa.e: Any two positions are equivalent and adjacent, so no cis–trans distinction exists.

qa.q: Which complex is optically active?
qa.e: With three didentate en ligands, the complex and its mirror image are non-superimposable.

qa.q: What are optical isomers of a complex called?
qa.e: Non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers (d and l forms).

qa.q: Which type of isomerism does [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ show?
qa.e: Two Cl can be cis or trans; neither form is chiral, so there is no optical isomerism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): trans-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ is optically inactive. Reason (R): It has a plane of symmetry.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A molecule with a plane of symmetry is superimposable on its mirror image, so it cannot be optically active.

qa.q: [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ exists as red and yellow forms. What type of isomerism is this?
qa.e: NO₂⁻ binds through O in one form and through N in the other.

qa.q: [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆] are examples of:
qa.e: The ligands NH₃ and CN⁻ are interchanged between the cationic and anionic complexes.

qa.q: Which pair shows ionisation isomerism?
qa.e: A ligand and a counter ion exchange places, giving different ions in solution.

qa.q: [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) and [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O (dark green) are:
qa.e: Water moves between the coordination sphere and the crystal lattice.

qa.q: In the yellow isomer of [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂, through which atom is the NO₂⁻ ligand bound?
qa.e: The yellow form is the nitrito-N isomer; the red form is nitrito-O.

qa.q: How many moles of AgCl are precipitated by 1 mol of [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O with excess AgNO₃?
qa.e: Only the two Cl⁻ outside the bracket are ionisable.

qa.q: Which test distinguishes [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ from [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br?
qa.a: BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate only with [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄
qa.e: Only the isomer with SO₄²⁻ outside the bracket releases free sulphate to form BaSO₄.

qa.q: Assertion (A): [Co(NH₃)₅(SCN)]²⁺ can show linkage isomerism. Reason (R): SCN⁻ is an ambidentate ligand.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: SCN⁻ can bind through S or N, giving two linkage isomers.

qa.q: What is the hybridisation of Co in [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺?
qa.e: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶; electrons pair up in three 3d orbitals, leaving two 3d orbitals free for d²sp³ hybridisation.

qa.q: How many unpaired electrons are present in [CoF₆]³⁻?
qa.e: Weak-field F⁻ does not cause pairing: Co³⁺ 3d⁶ keeps 4 unpaired electrons (sp³d², high spin).

qa.q: What is the shape and magnetic nature of [NiCl₄]²⁻?
qa.e: Cl⁻ does not pair Ni²⁺'s two unpaired 3d electrons; sp³ gives a tetrahedral, paramagnetic complex.

qa.q: [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ has a magnetic moment of about 1.73 BM. What does this indicate?
qa.a: One unpaired electron; inner orbital d²sp³ complex
qa.e: 1.73 BM = √3 corresponds to n = 1: Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) electrons are paired by CN⁻, using d²sp³.

qa.q: What is the spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of [NiCl₄]²⁻?
qa.e: Two unpaired electrons: μ = √(2 × 4) = √8 = 2.83 BM.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of valence bond theory?
qa.a: It cannot explain the colour of coordination compounds
qa.e: VBT has no account of d–d transitions or colour; it also fails to distinguish weak and strong ligands quantitatively.

qa.q: Why is [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ called an inner orbital complex?
qa.a: It uses the inner (n−1)d, i.e. 3d, orbitals in hybridisation
qa.e: d²sp³ uses 3d orbitals of the penultimate shell; sp³d² would use the outer 4d orbitals.

qa.q: Assertion (A): [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is diamagnetic. Reason (R): It is a square planar complex with dsp² hybridisation in which all 3d electrons are paired.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: CN⁻ pairs the 3d⁸ electrons of Ni²⁺, freeing one d orbital for dsp²; no unpaired electrons remain.

qa.q: In an octahedral crystal field, which orbitals form the higher-energy eg set?
qa.e: dx²−y² and dz² point directly at the ligands along the axes, so they are raised in energy.

qa.q: What is the configuration of a d⁴ ion in a strong octahedral field (Δo > P)?
qa.e: When Δo exceeds the pairing energy, the fourth electron pairs in t₂g.

qa.q: How many unpaired electrons does a d⁴ ion have in a weak octahedral field?
qa.e: Weak field: t₂g³eg¹, all four electrons unpaired.

qa.q: Which ligand produces the largest crystal field splitting?
qa.e: CO is at the strong-field end of the spectrochemical series.

qa.q: What is the relation between Δt and Δo for the same metal, ligands and metal–ligand distance?
qa.e: Tetrahedral splitting is smaller, about four-ninths of octahedral splitting.

qa.q: Why are low-spin tetrahedral complexes rarely observed?
qa.a: Δt is small and usually less than the pairing energy
qa.e: With small splitting, it costs less energy to put electrons in higher orbitals than to pair them.

qa.q: Arrange in increasing order of crystal field strength: NH₃, Cl⁻, H₂O, CN⁻.
qa.e: From the spectrochemical series: Cl⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < CN⁻.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In an octahedral field, the t₂g orbitals are lowered in energy relative to the barycentre. Reason (R): t₂g orbitals point between the axes, away from the ligands.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Less repulsion from the approaching ligands lowers t₂g by 0.4Δo.

qa.q: Why is [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ coloured?
qa.a: A d electron absorbs visible light and moves from t₂g to eg
qa.e: This d–d transition absorbs blue-green light, so the solution appears violet.

qa.q: Why is anhydrous CuSO₄ white while CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue?
qa.a: Without water ligands there is no crystal field splitting for d–d transitions
qa.e: Water ligands split the d orbitals; removing them removes the visible d–d absorption.

qa.q: A complex absorbs orange light. What colour does it appear?
qa.e: We see the complementary colour of the absorbed light; the complement of orange is blue.

qa.q: What happens to the colour when en is gradually added to green [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
qa.a: It changes towards violet as [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ forms
qa.e: en is a stronger field ligand than H₂O, so Δo increases and the absorbed wavelength shifts.

qa.q: What gives ruby its red colour?
qa.e: About 0.5–1% Cr³⁺ replaces Al³⁺ in corundum, and the crystal field gives the red colour.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of crystal field theory?
qa.a: It treats ligands as point charges and ignores covalent bonding
qa.e: So it cannot explain why anionic ligands such as I⁻ are weak-field ligands.

qa.q: Which metal ion is responsible for the colours of both ruby and emerald?
qa.e: Cr³⁺ gives red in ruby (Al₂O₃) and green in emerald (beryl) because the crystal fields differ.

qa.q: Assertion (A): According to CFT, anionic ligands should cause the greatest splitting. Reason (R): In practice, anionic ligands such as I⁻ and Br⁻ are found at the weak-field end of the spectrochemical series.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true. R describes the observation that contradicts A's prediction — it shows a limitation of CFT rather than explaining A.

qa.q: What is the shape of Fe(CO)₅?
qa.e: Five CO ligands around Fe(0) give a trigonal bipyramid.

qa.q: What is the shape of Ni(CO)₄?
qa.e: Ni(CO)₄ is a tetrahedral, diamagnetic molecule.

qa.q: Which carbonyl contains a metal–metal bond bridged by two CO groups?
qa.e: Co₂(CO)₈ has a Co–Co bond with two bridging CO groups; Mn₂(CO)₁₀ has an unbridged Mn–Mn bond.

qa.q: In π back-bonding in metal carbonyls, electrons move from:
qa.a: filled metal d orbitals into the vacant π* orbital of CO
qa.e: Back-donation fills CO's antibonding π* orbital, strengthening M–C and weakening C–O.

qa.q: What is meant by synergic bonding in metal carbonyls?
qa.a: σ donation from CO and π back-donation from the metal reinforce each other
qa.e: Donation to the metal raises its electron density, which favours back-donation, and vice versa.

qa.q: What is the oxidation state of Cr in Cr(CO)₆?
qa.e: CO is neutral, so chromium is in the zero oxidation state.

qa.q: What happens to the C–O bond when CO bonds to a metal through synergic bonding?
qa.e: Electrons entering CO's π* antibonding orbital reduce the C–O bond order.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The metal–carbon bond in metal carbonyls has both σ and π character. Reason (R): CO donates a lone pair to the metal and accepts electron density from filled metal d orbitals into its π* orbital.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The σ part comes from CO's donation and the π part from back-donation, exactly as R states.

qa.q: Which metal is present in chlorophyll?
qa.e: Chlorophyll is a magnesium complex; haemoglobin contains iron and vitamin B₁₂ contains cobalt.

qa.q: Which metal is present in vitamin B₁₂?
qa.e: Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) is a cobalt complex.

qa.q: How is the hardness of water estimated using coordination chemistry?
qa.a: By titration with Na₂EDTA, which complexes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
qa.e: EDTA forms stable 1:1 complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, allowing their estimation.

qa.q: What is the role of cyanide ions in extracting gold?
qa.e: Gold dissolves as [Au(CN)₂]⁻ in the presence of oxygen, and is then recovered by adding zinc.

qa.q: What is Wilkinson's catalyst used for?
qa.e: [(Ph₃P)₃RhCl] catalyses the addition of H₂ to alkenes.

qa.q: What is chelate therapy?
qa.a: Removal of excess or toxic metals from the body using chelating ligands
qa.e: For example, EDTA removes lead, and D-penicillamine and desferrioxamine B remove excess copper and iron.

qa.q: Which complex is used as an anticancer drug?
qa.e: cis-Platin inhibits the growth of tumours; the trans isomer is much less effective.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In black-and-white photography, the developed film is fixed by washing with hypo solution. Reason (R): Hypo dissolves undecomposed AgBr by forming the complex [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Removing unexposed AgBr as a soluble complex stops further darkening, fixing the image.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CBr?
qa.e: The longest chain is propane with Br and CH₃ both on C-2.

qa.q: CH₂=CH–CH₂–Cl is an example of which type of halide?
qa.e: Cl is on an sp³ carbon next to a C=C double bond.

qa.q: Which is a vinylic halide?
qa.e: In a vinylic halide, the halogen is bonded directly to an sp² carbon of C=C.

qa.q: Which dihalide is a geminal dihalide?
qa.e: Both chlorines are on the same carbon (gem = twins).

qa.q: Classify CH₃CH₂CH(Br)CH₃.
qa.e: The carbon bearing Br is bonded to two other carbons.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of C₆H₅CH₂Cl?
qa.e: The Cl is on the CH₂ group attached to the ring, named as a chloromethyl substituent.

qa.q: In which compound is the C–X carbon sp² hybridised?
qa.e: In aryl halides, X is attached to an sp² carbon of the aromatic ring.

qa.q: Assertion (A): ClCH₂CH₂Cl is a vicinal dihalide. Reason (R): Its two chlorine atoms are on adjacent carbon atoms.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: vic dihalides have halogens on neighbouring carbons, exactly as in 1,2-dichloroethane.

qa.q: Which compound has the highest dipole moment?
qa.e: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) beats CH₃F (1.847 D) because the C–F bond is very short, reducing charge × distance.

qa.q: How do C–X bond length and bond enthalpy change from C–F to C–I?
qa.a: Bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases
qa.e: Larger halogen atoms form longer, weaker bonds with carbon.

qa.q: Which has the highest boiling point?
qa.e: Boiling point increases with molar mass and polarisability: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

qa.q: Why does 2-bromo-2-methylpropane boil at a lower temperature than 1-bromobutane?
qa.a: Branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface area and van der Waals forces
qa.e: Isomers have equal mass, so the shape decides intermolecular contact.

qa.q: Why is the melting point of p-dichlorobenzene higher than that of its o- and m-isomers?
qa.a: Its symmetrical shape fits better in the crystal lattice
qa.e: The para isomer is symmetric and packs closely, so more energy is needed to melt it.

qa.q: Why are haloalkanes only slightly soluble in water even though they are polar?
qa.a: Energy released by new attractions with water is less than that needed to break water's hydrogen bonds
qa.e: Haloalkanes cannot form hydrogen bonds as strong as those between water molecules.

qa.q: Which is denser than water?
qa.e: Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives are denser than water.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Haloalkanes have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass. Reason (R): The C–X bond is polar, and haloalkanes have stronger intermolecular attractions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Dipole–dipole attractions plus greater polarisability make haloalkane molecules stick together more.

qa.q: What are the by-products when an alcohol reacts with thionyl chloride?
qa.e: R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂ + HCl; both are gases.

qa.q: What is the role of anhydrous ZnCl₂ when a primary alcohol reacts with HCl?
qa.a: It acts as a Lewis acid catalyst
qa.e: ZnCl₂ coordinates with the OH group, making it a better leaving group.

qa.q: Which reaction converts C₂H₅Br into C₂H₅I?
qa.a: Finkelstein reaction with NaI in dry acetone
qa.e: NaI swaps Br for I; NaBr is insoluble in acetone and precipitates.

qa.q: Why does the Finkelstein reaction go to completion in dry acetone?
qa.a: NaCl or NaBr formed is insoluble in acetone and precipitates out
qa.e: Removing the product salt by precipitation shifts the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier).

qa.q: Which reagent is used to prepare alkyl fluorides by the Swarts reaction?
qa.e: Heating an alkyl chloride or bromide with a metallic fluoride such as AgF gives the alkyl fluoride.

qa.q: Which alcohol reacts fastest with concentrated HCl at room temperature without ZnCl₂?
qa.e: Tertiary alcohols react readily because they form stable carbocations; reactivity 3° > 2° > 1°.

qa.q: Why are aryl halides not prepared by treating phenol with HCl or PCl₅?
qa.a: The C–O bond in phenol has partial double bond character and is difficult to break
qa.e: Resonance gives the C–O bond in phenol partial double bond character, so OH cannot be easily replaced.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Thionyl chloride is the preferred reagent for preparing alkyl chlorides from alcohols. Reason (R): Both by-products of the reaction are gases that escape easily.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Gaseous SO₂ and HCl leave the reaction, so the alkyl chloride obtained is pure.

qa.q: What is the role of anhydrous FeCl₃ in the chlorination of benzene?
qa.a: It is a Lewis acid that generates the Cl⁺ electrophile
qa.e: FeCl₃ polarises Cl₂, producing Cl⁺ (as FeCl₄⁻ forms), which attacks the ring.

qa.q: Which reagent converts benzenediazonium chloride into chlorobenzene in the Sandmeyer reaction?
qa.e: Cuprous chloride replaces the diazonium group by Cl, releasing N₂.

qa.q: How is iodobenzene prepared from benzenediazonium chloride?
qa.a: By shaking it with potassium iodide solution
qa.e: KI readily replaces the diazonium group by iodine without needing a copper catalyst.

qa.q: Why is an oxidising agent like HNO₃ needed for direct iodination of benzene?
qa.a: Iodination is reversible; the oxidising agent removes the HI formed
qa.e: HI is a strong reducing agent that would reverse the reaction; oxidising it drives iodination forward.

qa.q: Why are fluoroarenes not made by direct fluorination of benzene?
qa.a: The reaction with fluorine is too violent to control
qa.e: Fluorine is so reactive that direct reaction cannot be controlled.

qa.q: What is formed when methylbenzene (toluene) is chlorinated with Cl₂ and FeCl₃ in the dark?
qa.e: The methyl group is ortho/para directing; in the dark with a Lewis acid, substitution occurs on the ring.

qa.q: At what temperature range is benzenediazonium chloride prepared from aniline?
qa.e: Diazonium salts are unstable and must be made and used in the cold (0–5 °C).

qa.q: Assertion (A): The ortho and para isomers formed on chlorinating toluene can be separated easily. Reason (R): The para isomer has a much higher melting point than the ortho isomer.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because of the large difference in melting points, the para isomer can be crystallised out.

qa.q: What is the main product when CH₃CH₂Br reacts with alcoholic KCN?
qa.e: Ionic KCN gives CN⁻, which attacks through carbon to form propanenitrile.

qa.q: Why does AgCN give isocyanides with alkyl halides?
qa.a: AgCN is mainly covalent, so only the lone pair on nitrogen is available for attack
qa.e: With the carbon bonded to silver, the nitrogen lone pair attacks, giving R–NC.

qa.q: What forms when bromoethane reacts with AgNO₂?
qa.e: AgNO₂ attacks through nitrogen to give the nitroalkane.

qa.q: Which reagent converts an alkyl halide into an ether?
qa.e: R′O⁻ replaces X, giving R–O–R′ (Williamson synthesis).

qa.q: What is formed when an alkyl halide is treated with LiAlH₄?
qa.e: LiAlH₄ supplies hydride ions (H⁻), which replace the halogen.

qa.q: Which is an ambident nucleophile?
qa.e: Cyanide can attack through C or through N.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms does the product have when 1-chloropropane reacts with KCN?
qa.e: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CN (butanenitrile), with one extra carbon.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Alkyl halides react with KCN to form alkyl cyanides as the main product. Reason (R): The C–C bond formed is more stable than a C–N bond.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Free CN⁻ prefers to attack through carbon because the resulting C–C bond is more stable.

qa.q: What is the rate law for an SN2 reaction of R–X with OH⁻?
qa.e: Both the substrate and nucleophile are in the single rate-determining step.

qa.q: Which alkyl bromide reacts fastest by the SN2 mechanism?
qa.e: The methyl carbon is least hindered, so backside attack is easiest.

qa.q: Which alkyl bromide reacts fastest by the SN1 mechanism?
qa.e: It forms the most stable (tertiary) carbocation.

qa.q: Why are benzyl chloride and allyl chloride very reactive towards SN1?
qa.a: Their carbocations are stabilised by resonance
qa.e: The positive charge is delocalised over the ring or the double bond.

qa.q: Which solvent favours the SN1 mechanism?
qa.a: A polar protic solvent such as water or ethanol
qa.e: Polar protic solvents stabilise the carbocation and leaving halide ion by solvation.

qa.q: Arrange in decreasing order of reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution (same alkyl group): R–F, R–Cl, R–Br, R–I.
qa.e: C–I is the weakest and longest bond, so iodide leaves most easily.

qa.q: Why does the rate of SN2 reaction decrease from methyl to tertiary halides?
qa.a: Increasing steric hindrance blocks the backside attack of the nucleophile
qa.e: Bulky alkyl groups crowd the carbon, making the five-coordinate transition state harder to reach.

qa.q: Assertion (A): (CH₃)₃CBr undergoes hydrolysis mainly by the SN1 mechanism. Reason (R): The tertiary carbocation formed is highly stable, while backside attack is sterically hindered.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both factors favour SN1 for tertiary halides, so R correctly explains A.

qa.q: Which compound is chiral?
qa.e: C-2 of butan-2-ol carries H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅ — four different groups.

qa.q: What is a racemic mixture?
qa.a: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers with zero optical rotation
qa.e: The rotations of the d and l forms cancel exactly (external compensation).

qa.q: What stereochemical outcome is typical of an SN2 reaction at a chiral carbon?
qa.e: Backside attack flips the configuration, like an umbrella turning inside out.

qa.q: Why does an SN1 reaction of an optically active halide usually give a racemic product?
qa.a: The planar carbocation can be attacked equally from both sides
qa.e: Attack from either face gives both configurations in nearly equal amounts.

qa.q: Which property differs between two enantiomers?
qa.a: Direction of rotation of plane-polarised light
qa.e: Enantiomers share all physical properties except the sign of optical rotation.

qa.q: How many asymmetric carbon atoms are present in 2-chlorobutane?
qa.e: Only C-2 has four different groups: H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅.

qa.q: What does the symbol (±) before a name indicate?
qa.e: (±) or dl shows equal amounts of the + and − enantiomers.

qa.q: Assertion (A): 2-Chloropropane is optically inactive. Reason (R): It does not have any carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: C-2 carries two identical CH₃ groups, so there is no stereocentre and the molecule is achiral.

qa.q: What is the major product when 2-bromopentane is heated with alcoholic KOH?
qa.e: By Zaitsev's rule, the more substituted alkene (pent-2-ene, 81%) is the major product.

qa.q: Which reagent favours elimination over substitution for an alkyl halide?
qa.e: In alcohol, OH⁻/alkoxide acts more as a base, abstracting a β-hydrogen.

qa.q: What is formed when CH₃MgBr reacts with water?
qa.e: The carbanion-like CH₃ takes a proton from water: CH₃MgBr + H₂O → CH₄ + Mg(OH)Br.

qa.q: Why must Grignard reagents be prepared under anhydrous conditions?
qa.a: They react with water (any proton source) to form hydrocarbons
qa.e: The highly polar C–Mg bond makes R a strong base that grabs protons from water.

qa.q: What is the product of the Wurtz reaction of CH₃CH₂Br with sodium in dry ether?
qa.e: Two ethyl groups join: 2C₂H₅Br + 2Na → C₄H₁₀ + 2NaBr.

qa.q: Which type of alkyl halide is most likely to undergo elimination rather than SN2 with a strong base?
qa.e: Tertiary halides are too hindered for SN2 and give stable, substituted alkenes.

qa.q: How many different alkenes can form when 2-bromobutane undergoes dehydrohalogenation (ignoring cis–trans isomers)?
qa.e: Removal of H from C-1 gives but-1-ene; from C-3 gives but-2-ene.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Elimination from 2-bromobutane gives but-2-ene as the major product. Reason (R): The alkene with more alkyl groups on the double-bonded carbons is more stable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: This is Zaitsev's rule, which follows from the greater stability of more substituted alkenes.

qa.q: Which is NOT a reason for the low reactivity of haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution?
qa.a: The C–X bond in haloarenes is longer than in haloalkanes
qa.e: The C–X bond in haloarenes is actually shorter (169 pm vs 177 pm), making it stronger.

qa.q: What are the conditions of the Dow process for converting chlorobenzene into phenol?
qa.a: NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm, then acidification
qa.e: Drastic conditions are needed because chlorobenzene resists nucleophilic attack.

qa.q: What is the major product of nitration of chlorobenzene?
qa.e: Cl is ortho/para directing; the para product is major for steric reasons.

qa.q: Why is chlorine deactivating yet ortho/para directing in electrophilic substitution?
qa.a: Its –I effect reduces ring electron density, while its +R effect increases it at ortho and para positions
qa.e: Overall the ring is deactivated (–I wins), but resonance directs electrophiles to ortho/para.

qa.q: What is formed when chlorobenzene and methyl chloride react with sodium in dry ether?
qa.e: This is the Wurtz–Fittig reaction: C₆H₅Cl + CH₃Cl + 2Na → C₆H₅CH₃ + 2NaCl.

qa.q: What is formed when chlorobenzene alone is treated with sodium in dry ether?
qa.e: Fittig reaction: 2C₆H₅Cl + 2Na → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2NaCl.

qa.q: Which compound undergoes nucleophilic substitution with aqueous NaOH most readily?
qa.e: Three o/p nitro groups strongly stabilise the intermediate; meta nitro and methyl do not help.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Chlorobenzene does not undergo SN1 reactions easily. Reason (R): The phenyl cation formed by loss of Cl⁻ is not stabilised by resonance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: SN1 needs a stable carbocation; the phenyl cation is unstable, so the SN1 route is ruled out.

qa.q: What poisonous gas forms when chloroform is exposed to air and light?
qa.e: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ → 2COCl₂ + 2HCl in the presence of light.

qa.q: Why is chloroform stored in dark bottles filled to the brim?
qa.a: To keep out light and air that oxidise it to phosgene
qa.e: Both light and oxygen are needed for the oxidation to phosgene.

qa.q: To what is the antiseptic property of iodoform due?
qa.e: Iodoform releases iodine, which kills microbes.

qa.q: Which of these is a use of dichloromethane?
qa.a: Paint remover and process solvent in drug manufacture
qa.e: Its solvent power makes it useful for stripping paint and in pharmaceutical processes.

qa.q: Which health effect is associated with exposure to dichloromethane?
qa.a: Damage to the central nervous system, with dizziness and impaired hearing and vision
qa.e: CH₂Cl₂ harms the CNS; higher doses cause dizziness, nausea and numbness.

qa.q: Why was chloroform replaced as a general anaesthetic?
qa.a: Safer anaesthetics became available; chloroform is toxic to the liver and can form phosgene
qa.e: Toxicity and the risk of phosgene formation led to its replacement.

qa.q: Which refrigerant is manufactured from chloroform?
qa.e: Chloroform is a raw material for R-22 (a hydrochlorofluorocarbon); Freon-12 is made from CCl₄.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Iodoform was once used as an antiseptic. Reason (R): It liberates free iodine.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The antiseptic action comes from the free iodine released, which is why iodoform worked.

qa.q: What is the formula of Freon-12?
qa.e: Freon-12 is dichlorodifluoromethane, the most common freon.

qa.q: How is Freon-12 manufactured?
qa.a: From tetrachloromethane by the Swarts reaction
qa.e: Fluorine is introduced by treating CCl₄ with a metallic fluoride such as SbF₃.

qa.q: Why do CFCs cause ozone depletion although they are unreactive at ground level?
qa.a: In the stratosphere, UV light breaks them into chlorine radicals that destroy ozone
qa.e: Their stability lets them reach the stratosphere, where UV releases reactive Cl radicals.

qa.q: Who discovered the insecticidal properties of DDT?
qa.e: Paul Müller found it in 1939 and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1948.

qa.q: Why is DDT harmful to the environment?
qa.a: It is stable and fat-soluble, so it is stored in fatty tissues and builds up in food chains
qa.e: Its persistence leads to accumulation in animals, and it is highly toxic to fish.

qa.q: Which health effect is linked to exposure to CCl₄?
qa.e: CCl₄ exposure can cause liver cancer, along with nerve damage, dizziness and nausea.

qa.q: Which use of CCl₄ has largely stopped because of health and environmental concerns?
qa.a: As a household spot remover and fire extinguisher
qa.e: Until the mid-1960s, CCl₄ was a common cleaning fluid and fire extinguisher; such uses were dropped.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Insects developed resistance to DDT over time. Reason (R): DDT is highly toxic to fish.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but toxicity to fish does not explain insect resistance.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃C–OH?
qa.e: The longest chain through the C–OH carbon is propane with OH and CH₃ on C-2.

qa.q: Which is a benzylic alcohol?
qa.e: The OH is on an sp³ carbon attached directly to a benzene ring.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of resorcinol?
qa.e: Resorcinol has two OH groups meta to each other.

qa.q: Why is the C–O–C bond angle in methoxymethane (111.7°) larger than the tetrahedral angle?
qa.a: Repulsion between the two bulky methyl groups
qa.e: The bulky CH₃ groups push apart, slightly widening the angle.

qa.q: Why is the C–O bond in phenol shorter than in methanol?
qa.a: Resonance gives it partial double bond character and the carbon is sp² hybridised
qa.e: Delocalisation of oxygen's lone pair into the ring and sp² carbon both shorten the bond (136 pm vs 142 pm).

qa.q: C₂H₅–O–CH₃ is an example of a:
qa.e: The two groups on oxygen are different (ethyl and methyl).

qa.q: What is the C–O–H bond angle in methanol?
qa.e: Repulsion between oxygen's lone pairs makes it slightly less than the tetrahedral angle.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Phenols are not classified as alcohols although they contain an –OH group. Reason (R): In phenols the –OH is bonded to an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Alcohols have OH on sp³ carbon; phenols have it on an aromatic sp² carbon, which changes their properties.

qa.q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is classified as a:
qa.e: Alcohols are classified by the number of –OH groups. Glycerol has three, so it is trihydric; ethane-1,2-diol (glycol) is dihydric.

qa.q: What is the main product of acid-catalysed hydration of propene?
qa.e: Markovnikov addition puts OH on the more substituted carbon via the more stable 2° carbocation.

qa.q: What is the product of hydroboration–oxidation of propene?
qa.e: The overall result looks like anti-Markovnikov addition of water, putting OH on the terminal carbon.

qa.q: Which type of alcohol is obtained when a ketone reacts with a Grignard reagent followed by hydrolysis?
qa.e: The carbonyl carbon of a ketone already has two alkyl groups; adding a third gives a 3° alcohol.

qa.q: What is obtained when methanal reacts with CH₃CH₂MgBr followed by hydrolysis?
qa.e: Methanal gives a 1° alcohol with one more carbon than the Grignard alkyl group: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.

qa.q: Which reagent reduces a carboxylic acid directly to a primary alcohol?
qa.e: LiAlH₄ is strong enough to reduce –COOH to –CH₂OH; NaBH₄ is not.

qa.q: What is the first step in the mechanism of acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene?
qa.a: Protonation of the alkene to form a carbocation
qa.e: H₃O⁺ acts as an electrophile and protonates the double bond.

qa.q: Reduction of butan-2-one with NaBH₄ gives:
qa.e: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols at the carbonyl carbon.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Industrially, carboxylic acids are converted to esters before reduction to alcohols. Reason (R): LiAlH₄ is an expensive reagent.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because LiAlH₄ is costly, industry hydrogenates esters catalytically instead.

qa.q: Which by-product is obtained along with phenol in the cumene process?
qa.e: Cumene hydroperoxide splits into phenol and acetone on treatment with acid.

qa.q: How is phenol prepared from benzenediazonium chloride?
qa.e: Warm water replaces –N₂⁺ by –OH, releasing N₂.

qa.q: Why does ethanol have a much higher boiling point than methoxymethane, though both have M = 46?
qa.a: Ethanol molecules form intermolecular hydrogen bonds
qa.e: Ethanol has an O–H group that H-bonds between molecules; the ether has no O–H.

qa.q: How does branching affect the boiling point of isomeric alcohols?
qa.e: Branched molecules have smaller surface area and weaker van der Waals forces.

qa.q: Why does the solubility of alcohols in water decrease with increasing molar mass?
qa.a: The larger hydrophobic alkyl part hinders hydrogen bonding with water
qa.e: As the alkyl chain grows, it dominates and the molecule behaves more like a hydrocarbon.

qa.q: Which reagent is used to convert benzene into benzenesulphonic acid for making phenol?
qa.e: Sulphonation with oleum introduces the –SO₃H group, which is later replaced by –OH.

qa.q: Under what conditions does chlorobenzene give sodium phenoxide with NaOH?
qa.e: Drastic conditions are needed because aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Lower alcohols are miscible with water. Reason (R): Alcohols form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The –OH group of small alcohols forms H-bonds with water, so they dissolve completely.

qa.q: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
qa.a: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its negative charge over the ring
qa.e: Delocalisation spreads the charge in phenoxide, while ethoxide's charge stays on oxygen and is further destabilised by the ethyl group.

qa.q: Which is the most acidic?
qa.e: The NO₂ group withdraws electrons and stabilises the phenoxide ion (pKa 7.1).

qa.q: Why is m-nitrophenol (pKa 8.3) less acidic than p-nitrophenol (pKa 7.1)?
qa.a: At the meta position –NO₂ acts only by its –I effect, while at para it also withdraws electrons by resonance
qa.e: Resonance withdrawal (–R) operates only from ortho and para positions.

qa.q: Why are alcohols weaker acids than water?
qa.a: Alkyl groups release electrons, making the alkoxide ion a stronger base than hydroxide
qa.e: So R–O⁻ readily takes a proton from water: R–O⁻ + H₂O → R–OH + OH⁻.

qa.q: What is formed when ethanol reacts with sodium metal?
qa.e: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂.

qa.q: Arrange in increasing order of acidity: propan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, propan-2-ol.
qa.e: More electron-releasing alkyl groups on the carbinol carbon reduce acidity: 3° < 2° < 1°.

qa.q: What is the pKa of phenol?
qa.e: Phenol's pKa is about 10.0, between alcohols (about 16) and carboxylic acids (about 4–5).

qa.q: Assertion (A): o-Cresol is less acidic than phenol. Reason (R): The methyl group is electron releasing and destabilises the phenoxide ion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Electron donation increases negative charge density on the phenoxide oxygen, making it less stable, so acidity falls.

qa.q: What are the reagents in the Lucas test?
qa.e: Lucas reagent converts alcohols into insoluble alkyl chlorides at rates depending on their class.

qa.q: Which alcohol gives turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent?
qa.e: Tertiary alcohols react fastest because they form stable 3° carbocations.

qa.q: What is the product when ethanol is heated with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K?
qa.e: At 443 K, intramolecular dehydration gives ethene; at 413 K, ethoxyethane forms.

qa.q: Which step is rate-determining in the acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols?
qa.e: Loss of water from the protonated alcohol to form the carbocation is slow.

qa.q: Arrange in order of ease of dehydration: 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
qa.e: Dehydration goes via carbocations, and 3° carbocations are most stable.

qa.q: Why is pyridine used when an alcohol reacts with an acid chloride?
qa.a: To neutralise the HCl formed, shifting the equilibrium forward
qa.e: Removing HCl drives the esterification towards the ester.

qa.q: What is the product of acetylation of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride?
qa.e: The phenolic OH of salicylic acid is acetylated to form aspirin.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Tertiary alcohols undergo dehydration more readily than primary alcohols. Reason (R): Dehydration proceeds through a carbocation intermediate, and tertiary carbocations are the most stable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The more stable the carbocation, the faster the slow step, so 3° alcohols dehydrate under milder conditions.

qa.q: Which reagent oxidises a primary alcohol only up to the aldehyde stage?
qa.e: PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde.

qa.q: What is formed when propan-2-ol is oxidised with CrO₃?
qa.e: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.

qa.q: What happens when 2-methylpropan-2-ol vapour is passed over hot copper at 573 K?
qa.e: Tertiary alcohols have no H on the carbinol carbon, so they lose water instead of being dehydrogenated.

qa.q: Which test distinguishes phenol from ethanol?
qa.a: Neutral FeCl₃ gives a violet colour with phenol
qa.e: Phenols form a violet complex with Fe³⁺; alcohols do not.

qa.q: Which alcohol gives a positive iodoform test?
qa.e: Propan-2-ol has the CH₃CH(OH)– group, which is oxidised to CH₃CO– and then gives CHI₃.

qa.q: What is the final product when ethanol is oxidised with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇?
qa.e: Ethanol → ethanal → ethanoic acid with a strong oxidant in excess.

qa.q: How do tertiary alcohols behave towards mild oxidising agents?
qa.e: There is no H on the carbon bearing OH, so mild oxidation does not occur.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Phenol gives a white precipitate with bromine water but ethanol does not. Reason (R): The –OH group strongly activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The activated ring of phenol reacts at once with bromine water to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol; ethanol has no ring.

qa.q: What is the product of Kolbe's reaction?
qa.e: Sodium phenoxide reacts with CO₂ (a weak electrophile), and acidification gives salicylic acid.

qa.q: What is the product of the Reimer–Tiemann reaction of phenol?
qa.e: CHCl₃ and NaOH introduce a –CHO group at the ortho position after hydrolysis.

qa.q: What is formed when phenol is treated with bromine water?
qa.e: In water, bromine reacts at all three activated positions (two ortho, one para).

qa.q: Why is o-nitrophenol more volatile than p-nitrophenol?
qa.a: o-Nitrophenol forms intramolecular hydrogen bonds, while p-nitrophenol forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds
qa.e: Intramolecular H-bonding prevents association of o-nitrophenol molecules.

qa.q: What is obtained when phenol is heated with zinc dust?
qa.e: Zinc dust reduces phenol to benzene, forming ZnO.

qa.q: What is formed when phenol is oxidised with chromic acid?
qa.e: Phenol is oxidised to the conjugated diketone benzoquinone.

qa.q: Why does phenol undergo bromination even without a Lewis acid?
qa.a: The –OH group strongly activates the ring, polarising the bromine molecule
qa.e: The ring is so electron-rich that Br₂ is polarised enough without FeBr₃.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sodium phenoxide reacts with CO₂, a weak electrophile, while phenol itself does not under the same conditions. Reason (R): Phenoxide ion is more reactive than phenol towards electrophilic substitution.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The negative charge on O makes the ring of phenoxide even more electron-rich, so it can react with weak electrophiles like CO₂.

qa.q: Which catalyst is used for the industrial manufacture of methanol from CO and H₂?
qa.e: CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH over ZnO–Cr₂O₃ at 200–300 atm and 573–673 K.

qa.q: Which enzyme converts glucose into ethanol during fermentation?
qa.e: Zymase from yeast ferments glucose (and fructose) to ethanol and CO₂.

qa.q: Why does a fermented drink turn sour when air gets in?
qa.a: Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid
qa.e: Oxygen allows bacteria to oxidise ethanol to acetic acid.

qa.q: What is denatured alcohol?
qa.a: Ethanol made unfit for drinking by adding copper sulphate and pyridine
qa.e: Additives give colour and a foul smell to discourage drinking.

qa.q: What is the danger of drinking methanol?
qa.a: It can cause blindness and, in larger amounts, death
qa.e: Methanol is highly poisonous even in small quantities.

qa.q: How many moles of CO₂ are produced when 1 mol of glucose is fermented completely to ethanol?
qa.e: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.

qa.q: What is the role of invertase in making ethanol from cane sugar?
qa.a: It hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose
qa.e: Invertase breaks sucrose into the two hexoses that zymase can ferment.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fermentation of sugar to ethanol is carried out in the absence of air. Reason (R): In the presence of air, ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Keeping air out prevents the ethanol formed from being oxidised to acetic acid.

qa.q: What is the product when ethanol is heated with conc. H₂SO₄ at 413 K?
qa.e: At 413 K, two ethanol molecules lose water to form diethyl ether.

qa.q: Which reagents give the best yield of 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane?
qa.e: The alkyl halide must be primary (here methyl) for SN2; a tertiary halide would eliminate.

qa.q: What happens when (CH₃)₃CBr is treated with sodium methoxide?
qa.e: The strongly basic methoxide removes a β-hydrogen from the crowded tertiary halide.

qa.q: Why is the dehydration method unsuitable for making ethers from secondary and tertiary alcohols?
qa.a: These alcohols readily dehydrate to alkenes instead
qa.e: Elimination competes strongly with substitution for 2° and 3° alcohols.

qa.q: Why do ethers have much lower boiling points than isomeric alcohols?
qa.a: Ether molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other
qa.e: Without O–H, ethers lack intermolecular H-bonding.

qa.q: Why is ethoxyethane about as soluble in water as butan-1-ol?
qa.a: The ether oxygen can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
qa.e: Water's hydrogen atoms bond to the lone pairs on the ether oxygen.

qa.q: Which reaction is used to prepare anisole?
qa.e: Phenoxide is a good nucleophile and CH₃I a good SN2 substrate; aryl halides do not undergo SN2.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In Williamson synthesis, primary alkyl halides are preferred. Reason (R): The reaction proceeds by an SN2 mechanism, and with tertiary halides the alkoxide acts as a base causing elimination.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: SN2 needs an unhindered carbon, and tertiary halides prefer elimination with strong bases.

qa.q: What are the products when anisole is heated with HI?
qa.e: The O–CH₃ bond is cleaved; the O–phenyl bond has partial double bond character and is not attacked.

qa.q: What are the products when methoxyethane reacts with one equivalent of HI?
qa.e: By SN2, I⁻ attacks the less hindered methyl group.

qa.q: What are the products of the reaction of 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane with HI?
qa.e: With a tertiary group, the reaction goes via the stable tertiary carbocation (SN1), so the tertiary iodide forms.

qa.q: Arrange HCl, HBr and HI in increasing order of reactivity towards ether cleavage.
qa.e: Iodide is the best nucleophile and HI the strongest acid of the three.

qa.q: Why does phenol formed from anisole not react further with HI to form iodobenzene?
qa.a: The sp² carbon–oxygen bond of phenol has partial double bond character and does not undergo SN1/SN2
qa.e: The aryl C–O bond resists nucleophilic substitution.

qa.q: What is the major product of nitration of anisole?
qa.e: –OCH₃ is ortho/para directing; the para product is major.

qa.q: Why does bromination of anisole not require FeBr₃?
qa.a: The –OCH₃ group activates the ring strongly
qa.e: The electron-donating methoxy group makes the ring reactive enough for Br₂ in ethanoic acid.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ethers are commonly used as solvents for reactions. Reason (R): Ethers are relatively unreactive under ordinary conditions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Their low reactivity means they do not interfere with most reagents, such as Grignard reagents.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
qa.e: Four carbons with C=O at C-2 (numbered to give the lowest locant).

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of C₆H₅COCH₃?
qa.e: Acetophenone is an ethanone with a phenyl group on the carbonyl carbon.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCHO?
qa.e: The CHO carbon is C-1; a methyl group sits on C-2 of a propanal chain.

qa.q: What is the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon?
qa.e: It forms three σ bonds and one π bond, in a trigonal planar arrangement.

qa.q: Which statement about the carbonyl group is correct?
qa.a: The carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen is nucleophilic
qa.e: Polarisation of C=O leaves carbon partially positive and oxygen partially negative.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCHO?
qa.e: Number from the CHO carbon (C-1); the double bond starts at C-2.

qa.q: What is the approximate bond angle around the carbonyl carbon?
qa.e: sp² hybridisation gives a trigonal planar arrangement with angles near 120°.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The carbonyl carbon is attacked by nucleophiles. Reason (R): Due to the polarity of the C=O bond, the carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The electron-poor carbon attracts electron-rich nucleophiles.

qa.q: What is the role of BaSO₄ in the Rosenmund reduction?
qa.a: It poisons the Pd catalyst so the aldehyde is not reduced further to an alcohol
qa.e: A partially deactivated catalyst stops the reduction at the aldehyde stage.

qa.q: What is the product of the Stephen reaction of CH₃CN?
qa.e: SnCl₂/HCl reduces the nitrile to an imine, which hydrolyses to the aldehyde.

qa.q: Which reagent converts CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₂CN into CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₂CHO without affecting the C=C bond?
qa.e: DIBAL-H selectively reduces nitriles (and esters) to aldehydes and leaves C=C alone.

qa.q: What is formed when ethyne is hydrated with HgSO₄ and dilute H₂SO₄?
qa.e: The enol formed first tautomerises to ethanal.

qa.q: What is obtained when propyne is hydrated in the presence of HgSO₄/H₂SO₄?
qa.e: Alkynes other than ethyne give ketones (Markovnikov hydration).

qa.q: Which method converts a secondary alcohol into a ketone?
qa.e: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.

qa.q: What does ozonolysis of but-2-ene (followed by Zn/H₂O) give?
qa.e: The C=C splits in the middle, each half becoming CH₃CHO.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Esters can be converted into aldehydes using DIBAL-H. Reason (R): DIBAL-H is a strong reducing agent that always reduces esters completely to alcohols.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: DIBAL-H at controlled conditions stops at the aldehyde; R is false.

qa.q: What is the Etard reaction?
qa.a: Oxidation of toluene by chromyl chloride to benzaldehyde
qa.e: CrO₂Cl₂ forms a complex with toluene which is hydrolysed to benzaldehyde.

qa.q: Which reagents are used in the Gatterman–Koch reaction?
qa.a: CO and HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ or CuCl
qa.e: These reagents introduce a –CHO group into benzene.

qa.q: What is the product of CH₃COCl with (CH₃)₂Cd?
qa.e: The methyl group from dimethylcadmium replaces Cl, giving CH₃COCH₃.

qa.q: What is obtained when ethanenitrile (CH₃CN) reacts with CH₃MgBr followed by hydrolysis?
qa.e: R–CN + R′MgX gives R–CO–R′ after hydrolysis: CH₃COCH₃.

qa.q: Why is dialkylcadmium preferred over a Grignard reagent for making ketones from acyl chlorides?
qa.a: Dialkylcadmium is less reactive and does not attack the ketone formed
qa.e: A Grignard reagent would add further to the ketone to give a tertiary alcohol.

qa.q: What is formed when benzal chloride (C₆H₅CHCl₂) is hydrolysed at 373 K?
qa.e: Two Cl on the same carbon are replaced, and the gem-diol loses water to give –CHO.

qa.q: Which ketone is obtained when benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃?
qa.e: Friedel–Crafts acylation introduces CH₃CO– onto the ring.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the oxidation of toluene with CrO₃ in acetic anhydride, the aldehyde is protected as benzylidene diacetate. Reason (R): This prevents further oxidation of benzaldehyde to benzoic acid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Trapping the aldehyde as a diacetate stops over-oxidation; acid hydrolysis then releases benzaldehyde.

qa.q: Why do aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons of similar mass?
qa.a: Dipole–dipole attractions between polar C=O groups
qa.e: The polar carbonyl group gives strong dipole–dipole forces; there is no O–H for H-bonding among themselves.

qa.q: Why do aldehydes and ketones have lower boiling points than alcohols of similar mass?
qa.a: They cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other
qa.e: Alcohols have O–H groups that H-bond between molecules.

qa.q: Which is the most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?
qa.e: HCHO has no alkyl groups, so it is least hindered and most electrophilic.

qa.q: Why are ketones less reactive than aldehydes towards nucleophiles?
qa.a: Two alkyl groups hinder attack and reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon
qa.e: Both steric and electronic (+I) effects of two alkyl groups lower reactivity.

qa.q: Why is benzaldehyde less reactive than propanal towards nucleophilic addition?
qa.a: Resonance with the benzene ring reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
qa.e: Delocalisation of electrons from the ring into C=O makes carbon less electrophilic.

qa.q: What change in hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon occurs during nucleophilic addition?
qa.e: The trigonal planar carbon becomes tetrahedral in the alkoxide intermediate.

qa.q: Why are lower aldehydes and ketones such as propanone miscible with water?
qa.a: They form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
qa.e: The carbonyl oxygen accepts H-bonds from water.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Propanal boils at a lower temperature than propan-1-ol. Reason (R): Propan-1-ol molecules are held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: H-bonding in the alcohol is stronger than dipole–dipole attraction in the aldehyde.

qa.q: What is the product when propanone reacts with HCN?
qa.e: CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon and OH forms on the same carbon: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN.

qa.q: Why is the addition of HCN to carbonyl compounds catalysed by a base?
qa.a: The base generates CN⁻, a stronger nucleophile than HCN
qa.e: HCN is a weak acid; base produces cyanide ions which attack the carbonyl carbon readily.

qa.q: Why is the NaHSO₃ addition reaction useful?
qa.a: The crystalline adducts can be separated and then decomposed to recover pure aldehydes
qa.e: The reversible adduct formation allows separation and purification.

qa.q: What is formed when an aldehyde reacts with one equivalent of a monohydric alcohol in dry HCl?
qa.e: One equivalent gives the hemiacetal (alkoxy alcohol); a second equivalent gives the acetal.

qa.q: What is formed when propanone reacts with ethylene glycol in dry HCl?
qa.e: The diol forms a five-membered ring with the carbonyl carbon (ethylene glycol ketal).

qa.q: What is the product of the reaction of ethanal with CH₃MgBr followed by hydrolysis?
qa.e: An aldehyde other than methanal gives a secondary alcohol: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.

qa.q: Why is dry HCl used in the formation of acetals?
qa.a: It protonates the carbonyl oxygen, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon
qa.e: Acid catalysis makes the weakly nucleophilic alcohol able to attack.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ketals are used to protect the carbonyl group of ketones during synthesis. Reason (R): Ketals can be converted back into ketones by hydrolysis with aqueous mineral acid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the ketal is stable to many reagents but easily hydrolysed when needed, it serves as a protecting group.

qa.q: What is formed when an aldehyde reacts with hydroxylamine?
qa.e: R–CHO + NH₂OH → R–CH=N–OH + H₂O.

qa.q: Which reagent is used to identify aldehydes and ketones by forming coloured precipitates?
qa.e: 2,4-DNP derivatives are yellow, orange or red solids.

qa.q: What is Clemmensen reduction?
qa.a: Reduction of >C=O to >CH₂ using zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl
qa.e: Zn–Hg/HCl removes the oxygen, converting the carbonyl group into a methylene group.

qa.q: Which reduction converts a carbonyl group into CH₂ under basic conditions?
qa.e: The hydrazone is heated with KOH in ethylene glycol, giving >CH₂ and N₂.

qa.q: What is obtained when butan-2-one is reduced with NaBH₄?
qa.e: NaBH₄ reduces ketones to secondary alcohols.

qa.q: What is the general product of the reaction between a carbonyl compound and H₂N–Z?
qa.e: Addition is followed by elimination of water to form a C=N bond.

qa.q: What is the product of ethanal with semicarbazide?
qa.e: Semicarbazide (H₂NNHCONH₂) condenses with the aldehyde to form a semicarbazone.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The reaction of carbonyl compounds with ammonia derivatives is carried out in weakly acidic medium. Reason (R): Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon more electrophilic.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Mild acid activates the carbonyl group (too much acid would protonate the nucleophile).

qa.q: Which reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes?
qa.e: Aldehydes reduce [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ to metallic silver, which deposits as a mirror.

qa.q: What is the reddish-brown precipitate formed in Fehling's test?
qa.e: Cu²⁺ is reduced to copper(I) oxide by the aldehyde.

qa.q: Which compound gives a positive Tollens' test but a negative Fehling's test?
qa.e: Aromatic aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent but do not respond to Fehling's solution.

qa.q: Which compound gives a yellow precipitate with I₂ and NaOH?
qa.e: Propanone has the CH₃CO– group needed for the iodoform reaction.

qa.q: What are the products when CH₃COCH₂CH₃ reacts with NaOI?
qa.e: The CH₃ group becomes CHI₃ and the rest becomes the salt of an acid with one carbon fewer (propanoate).

qa.q: How can ethanal be distinguished from propanal?
qa.a: Iodoform test: only ethanal gives a yellow precipitate
qa.e: Ethanal has the CH₃CO– group; propanal does not. Both give Tollens' and Fehling's tests.

qa.q: Why are ketones not oxidised by Tollens' reagent?
qa.a: They have no H on the carbonyl carbon, and oxidation would need C–C bond cleavage
qa.e: Mild oxidants cannot break C–C bonds, so ketones resist them.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Benzaldehyde gives a positive Tollens' test. Reason (R): Benzaldehyde gives a positive iodoform test.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Benzaldehyde is an aldehyde and reduces Tollens' reagent, but it has no CH₃CO– group, so it gives no iodoform. R is false.

qa.q: Why are α-hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones acidic?
qa.a: The carbonyl group withdraws electrons and the resulting enolate is resonance stabilised
qa.e: Both the electron-withdrawing C=O and delocalisation of the negative charge stabilise the conjugate base.

qa.q: What is the product of aldol reaction of ethanal in dilute NaOH (without heating)?
qa.e: Two ethanal molecules combine to give the β-hydroxy aldehyde; heating would dehydrate it to but-2-enal.

qa.q: What are the products of Cannizzaro reaction of methanal with conc. KOH?
qa.e: One HCHO is reduced to CH₃OH and another is oxidised to HCOO⁻K⁺.

qa.q: Which compound does NOT undergo aldol condensation?
qa.e: Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen; it undergoes Cannizzaro reaction instead.

qa.q: How many products (ignoring stereoisomers) are possible in the cross aldol condensation of ethanal and propanal?
qa.e: Two self-condensations and two cross-condensations give four products.

qa.q: What is the product of nitration of benzaldehyde with conc. HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄ at 273–283 K?
qa.e: The –CHO group is deactivating and meta-directing.

qa.q: What is formed when benzaldehyde is heated with concentrated NaOH?
qa.e: Cannizzaro reaction: one molecule is oxidised to benzoate and another reduced to benzyl alcohol.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Methanal undergoes Cannizzaro reaction. Reason (R): Methanal has no α-hydrogen atom.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without α-H, enolate formation (aldol) is impossible, so in concentrated alkali it disproportionates.

qa.q: What is formalin?
qa.e: Formalin is used to preserve biological specimens.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of adipic acid?
qa.e: Adipic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH, has six carbons and two COOH groups.

qa.q: Which acid gets its name from the Latin word for ant?
qa.e: Formica means ant; formic acid was first obtained from red ants.

qa.q: Why is the carbonyl carbon of a carboxylic acid less electrophilic than that of an aldehyde?
qa.a: Resonance with the –OH oxygen's lone pair reduces its positive character
qa.e: Delocalisation of the lone pair from –OH onto C=O lowers the partial positive charge.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of C₆H₅COOH?
qa.e: Its common name is benzoic acid; IUPAC calls it benzenecarboxylic acid.

qa.q: Which compound is used to make bakelite?
qa.e: Phenol–formaldehyde resin is bakelite.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of HOOC–COOH?
qa.e: Two carbons, each a COOH group.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Acetone is widely used as an industrial solvent. Reason (R): Acetone is a ketone that dissolves many organic compounds and is miscible with water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Its ability to dissolve a wide range of substances (and mix with water) makes it a useful solvent.

qa.q: What is obtained when propylbenzene is oxidised vigorously with alkaline KMnO₄ followed by acidification?
qa.e: The entire side chain is oxidised to –COOH regardless of its length.

qa.q: What is formed when CH₃CH₂MgBr reacts with dry ice followed by acid hydrolysis?
qa.e: CO₂ adds one carbon: C₂H₅–COOH.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms are in the acid formed from 1-bromobutane via its Grignard reagent and CO₂?
qa.e: Butyl (4 C) + 1 C from CO₂ = pentanoic acid.

qa.q: Which intermediate forms during the hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid?
qa.e: R–CN → R–CONH₂ → R–COOH.

qa.q: Which reagent is known as Jones reagent for oxidising primary alcohols to acids?
qa.e: Chromium trioxide in acidic medium oxidises 1° alcohols to carboxylic acids.

qa.q: What are the products of alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate?
qa.e: Basic hydrolysis (saponification) gives the carboxylate salt and the alcohol.

qa.q: Which alkylbenzene is NOT oxidised to benzoic acid by hot KMnO₄?
qa.e: Oxidation needs a benzylic hydrogen; the tertiary carbon in tert-butylbenzene has none.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Toluene and ethylbenzene both give benzoic acid on vigorous oxidation. Reason (R): The entire side chain of an alkylbenzene (primary or secondary) is oxidised to –COOH regardless of its length.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Whatever the length of the side chain, only the carbon attached to the ring remains, as –COOH.

qa.q: An acid has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is its pKa?
qa.e: pKa = −log Ka = −log(10⁻⁵) = 5.

qa.q: Why do carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than alcohols of similar molar mass?
qa.a: They form more extensive hydrogen bonds, often existing as dimers
qa.e: Two H-bonds hold acid molecules in pairs, needing more energy to separate.

qa.q: Which test distinguishes a carboxylic acid from a phenol?
qa.e: Acids release CO₂ with bicarbonate; phenols are too weak to do so.

qa.q: Which is the strongest acid?
qa.e: Three highly electronegative F atoms give the strongest electron-withdrawing effect.

qa.q: Why is a carboxylic acid more acidic than phenol?
qa.a: Carboxylate has two equivalent resonance structures with the charge on two oxygen atoms, while phenoxide places charge on less electronegative carbon
qa.e: Better delocalisation over electronegative atoms makes carboxylate more stable.

qa.q: Arrange in increasing order of acidity: 4-chlorobutanoic acid, 2-chlorobutanoic acid, butanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid.
qa.e: The –I effect of Cl decreases with distance from –COOH.

qa.q: Why is benzoic acid nearly insoluble in cold water while ethanoic acid is miscible?
qa.a: The large hydrophobic benzene ring outweighs the hydrogen bonding of –COOH
qa.e: As the hydrocarbon part grows, water solubility falls.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Benzoic acid (pKa 4.19) is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76). Reason (R): A phenyl group directly attached to –COOH increases acidity compared with a methyl group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The sp² carbon of the phenyl ring is more electronegative than the methyl carbon, and CH₃ releases electrons, so benzoic acid is stronger.

qa.q: Which reagent is preferred for converting a carboxylic acid into an acid chloride?
qa.e: Its by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases, so the acid chloride is obtained pure.

qa.q: What is formed when sodium propanoate is heated with soda lime?
qa.e: Decarboxylation removes CO₂, giving an alkane with one carbon fewer.

qa.q: What is the product of Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous sodium propanoate?
qa.e: Two ethyl radicals (from CH₃CH₂COO⁻) combine: C₂H₅–C₂H₅ = butane.

qa.q: What is formed when ethanoic acid is reduced with LiAlH₄ followed by hydrolysis?
qa.e: LiAlH₄ reduces –COOH to –CH₂OH.

qa.q: Which reducing agent does NOT reduce a carboxylic acid?
qa.e: NaBH₄ is too mild to reduce –COOH.

qa.q: What is formed when phthalic acid is treated with NH₃ and then strongly heated?
qa.e: Ammonium phthalate → phthalamide → (strong heat) phthalimide.

qa.q: In acid-catalysed esterification, which group is lost from the carboxylic acid?
qa.a: The –OH group (with H from the alcohol, as water)
qa.e: The acyl–oxygen bond breaks: R–CO–OH + H–OR′ → R–CO–OR′ + H₂O.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is reversible. Reason (R): The ester formed can be hydrolysed back by water in the presence of acid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, water is often removed to drive esterification forward.

qa.q: What is the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction?
qa.a: α-Halogenation of carboxylic acids using X₂ and red phosphorus
qa.e: Acids with α-H are converted to α-halo acids.

qa.q: What is the product of nitration of benzoic acid?
qa.e: –COOH is meta directing.

qa.q: Why does benzoic acid not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions?
qa.a: –COOH deactivates the ring and AlCl₃ binds to the carboxyl group
qa.e: The deactivated ring and the loss of the catalyst to the carboxyl group stop the reaction.

qa.q: Which acid is used in making nylon-6,6?
qa.e: Adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine form nylon-6,6.

qa.q: Which sequence converts benzoic acid into benzaldehyde?
qa.e: Acid → acid chloride → Rosenmund reduction to the aldehyde.

qa.q: Which compound is the product of HVZ reaction of propanoic acid with Br₂/red P followed by water?
qa.e: Halogenation occurs at the α-carbon (C-2).

qa.q: How can benzene be converted into m-nitroacetophenone?
qa.a: Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH₃COCl/AlCl₃, then nitration
qa.e: The acetyl group is meta directing, so nitration then goes meta. Nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative. Reason (R): Benzoic acid undergoes the HVZ reaction readily.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true, but benzoic acid has no α-hydrogen (the –COOH is attached directly to the ring), so it cannot undergo the HVZ reaction; R is false.

qa.q: What is the shape of an amine molecule around nitrogen?
qa.e: N is sp³ with three bonds and a lone pair, giving a pyramidal shape.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃N?
qa.e: Parent is methanamine; the other two methyl groups are on N.

qa.q: Classify C₆H₅NHCH₃.
qa.e: Two groups (phenyl and methyl) are attached to N with one H remaining.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of aniline?
qa.e: Aniline is named benzenamine in IUPAC.

qa.q: Why is the C–N–C angle in trimethylamine (108°) less than 109.5°?
qa.a: Repulsion by the lone pair on nitrogen
qa.e: The lone pair occupies more space and compresses the bond angles.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(NH₂)CH₃?
qa.e: The NH₂ group is on C-2 of a three-carbon chain.

qa.q: Which is a mixed (unsymmetrical) tertiary amine?
qa.e: The three groups on N are not all the same.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Amines are pyramidal in shape. Reason (R): The nitrogen atom in amines is sp³ hybridised with one lone pair.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Three bonding pairs and one lone pair around sp³ N give a pyramidal geometry.

qa.q: Which reagent is preferred industrially for reducing nitrobenzene to aniline?
qa.e: Fe/HCl is cheap and FeCl₂ formed releases HCl on hydrolysis, so little acid is needed.

qa.q: What is the main drawback of ammonolysis of alkyl halides for making primary amines?
qa.a: A mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and quaternary salts forms
qa.e: The primary amine is itself a nucleophile and reacts further with the alkyl halide.

qa.q: How can the yield of primary amine be increased in ammonolysis?
qa.a: By using a large excess of ammonia
qa.e: Excess NH₃ makes it more likely that the alkyl halide reacts with ammonia than with the amine formed.

qa.q: What is obtained when ethanenitrile is reduced with LiAlH₄?
qa.e: CH₃C≡N + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂NH₂.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms are present in the amine formed when 1-bromopropane is treated with KCN and the product reduced with LiAlH₄?
qa.e: Propyl (3 C) + CN (1 C) → butanenitrile → butan-1-amine.

qa.q: What is formed when benzamide is reduced with LiAlH₄?
qa.e: C₆H₅CONH₂ → C₆H₅CH₂NH₂; the C=O becomes CH₂.

qa.q: How is a free amine obtained from its ammonium salt R–NH₃⁺Cl⁻?
qa.a: By treating the salt with a strong base such as NaOH
qa.e: The base removes the proton from the ammonium ion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Reduction of nitriles is a method of ascending the amine series by one carbon. Reason (R): The carbon of the –CN group becomes the –CH₂– attached to nitrogen in the amine.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the nitrile carbon is retained, the amine has one more carbon than the alkyl halide used to make the nitrile.

qa.q: What is the product of Hoffmann bromamide degradation of ethanamide?
qa.e: CH₃CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → CH₃NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O; one carbon is lost.

qa.q: Why can aniline not be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?
qa.a: Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion
qa.e: The aryl C–X bond resists nucleophilic attack.

qa.q: Why does Gabriel synthesis give only primary amines?
qa.a: Nitrogen in N-alkylphthalimide bears no H to react further, so over-alkylation cannot occur
qa.e: Only one alkyl group can attach to the imide nitrogen, so a single primary amine forms.

qa.q: Arrange the isomers butan-1-amine, N-ethylethanamine and N,N-dimethylethanamine in decreasing order of boiling point.
qa.e: 1° amines have two H on N for H-bonding, 2° have one and 3° none.

qa.q: Why does aniline turn brown on storage?
qa.e: Aryl amines are slowly oxidised by air, forming coloured products.

qa.q: Why are amines less soluble in water than alcohols of similar mass?
qa.a: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so amines form weaker hydrogen bonds
qa.e: Weaker N–H···O bonds give lower solubility than O–H···O bonds of alcohols.

qa.q: How many moles of NaOH are used per mole of amide in Hoffmann bromamide degradation?
qa.e: R–CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → R–NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Tertiary amines have lower boiling points than isomeric primary amines. Reason (R): Tertiary amines have no hydrogen on nitrogen and cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without N–H, tertiary amines lack H-bonding between molecules.

qa.q: Which is the strongest base in aqueous solution?
qa.e: Diethylamine has the lowest pKb (3.00); the balance of inductive, solvation and steric effects favours it.

qa.q: Why is aniline a weaker base than ammonia?
qa.a: The lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring
qa.e: Delocalisation makes the lone pair less available to accept a proton.

qa.q: Arrange in decreasing order of basicity in water: CH₃NH₂, (CH₃)₂NH, (CH₃)₃N.
qa.e: pKb: 3.27 < 3.38 < 4.22. Solvation and steric effects make (CH₃)₃N weakest in water.

qa.q: The pKb of an amine is 4.0. What is its Kb?
Which is the strongest base?
qa.e: The electron-releasing CH₃ group increases electron density on N; NO₂ and Cl decrease it.

qa.q: Why is triethylamine a weaker base than diethylamine in water, though it has more electron-releasing groups?
qa.a: Its protonated form is less solvated and the bulky ethyl groups hinder approach
qa.e: With only one N–H in (C₂H₅)₃NH⁺, H-bonding with water is weaker, and steric hindrance adds to this.

qa.q: Why is benzylamine (pKb 4.70) a much stronger base than aniline (pKb 9.38)?
qa.a: In benzylamine the NH₂ is on an sp³ CH₂, so its lone pair is not delocalised into the ring
qa.e: The CH₂ group isolates the lone pair from the ring's π system.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia. Reason (R): The electron-releasing methyl group increases electron density on nitrogen.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The +I effect of CH₃ makes the lone pair more available for protonation and stabilises the ammonium ion.

qa.q: Which amine gives the carbylamine test?
qa.e: Only primary amines form isocyanides with CHCl₃ and ethanolic KOH.

qa.q: What is the product of reaction of ethanamine with nitrous acid?
qa.e: Aliphatic diazonium salts are unstable and decompose to alcohols, releasing N₂ quantitatively.

qa.q: Why is the product of a primary amine with Hinsberg's reagent soluble in alkali?
qa.a: It has an acidic hydrogen on nitrogen, next to the strongly electron-withdrawing sulphonyl group
qa.e: The N–H is acidic enough to be removed by alkali, forming a soluble salt.

qa.q: How does a tertiary amine behave with benzenesulphonyl chloride?
qa.e: Tertiary amines have no H on N to be replaced.

qa.q: Why is pyridine added during acylation of amines?
qa.a: To remove the HCl formed and shift the equilibrium towards the amide
qa.e: Pyridine is a stronger base than the amine and neutralises HCl.

qa.q: What is formed when methanamine reacts with benzoyl chloride?
qa.e: Benzoylation replaces an N–H by C₆H₅CO–: C₆H₅CONHCH₃.

qa.q: Why is the reaction of primary aliphatic amines with nitrous acid used to estimate amino acids?
qa.e: Measuring the volume of N₂ gives the amount of –NH₂ present.

qa.q: Assertion (A): N,N-Diethylbenzenesulphonamide is insoluble in alkali. Reason (R): It has no hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without an acidic N–H, the sulphonamide cannot form a salt with alkali.

qa.q: What is formed when aniline reacts with bromine water at room temperature?
qa.e: The strongly activated ring is substituted at all available ortho and para positions.

qa.q: Why is a large amount of m-nitroaniline formed in direct nitration of aniline?
qa.a: In strongly acidic medium aniline is protonated to the meta-directing anilinium ion
qa.e: The –NH₃⁺ group deactivates the ring and directs to meta.

qa.q: Why is aniline acetylated before nitration?
qa.a: To reduce the activating effect of –NH₂ and protect it from oxidation
qa.e: Acetanilide is less activated and is not oxidised by nitric acid, giving mainly the para product.

qa.q: What is sulphanilic acid?
qa.e: It is obtained by heating anilinium hydrogensulphate at 453–473 K.

qa.q: Why does aniline not undergo Friedel–Crafts reaction?
qa.a: It forms a salt with AlCl₃, and the positive nitrogen deactivates the ring
qa.e: Aniline acts as a Lewis base towards AlCl₃.

qa.q: What is the main product when acetanilide is brominated, followed by hydrolysis?
qa.e: Acetylation controls the reaction so mainly one Br enters at para.

qa.q: Approximately what percentage of p-nitroaniline is formed in the direct nitration of aniline (in acidic medium)?
qa.e: The products are about 51% para, 47% meta and 2% ortho.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Acetanilide is less reactive than aniline towards electrophilic substitution. Reason (R): The lone pair on nitrogen in acetanilide is partly delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen of the acetyl group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Less of the lone pair is available to the ring, so activation is reduced.

qa.q: At what temperature is diazotisation of aniline carried out?
qa.e: Diazonium salts decompose on warming, so the reaction is done in ice-cold conditions (0–5 °C).

qa.q: Why are arenediazonium salts more stable than alkyldiazonium salts?
qa.a: The positive charge is dispersed over the benzene ring by resonance
qa.e: Delocalisation of the charge stabilises arenediazonium ions.

qa.q: Which reagent converts benzenediazonium chloride into benzene?
qa.e: H₃PO₂ (or ethanol) reduces the diazonium group, replacing it by H.

qa.q: How is fluorobenzene prepared from benzenediazonium chloride?
qa.a: By forming the fluoroborate with HBF₄ and then heating
qa.e: Ar–N₂⁺BF₄⁻ decomposes on heating to Ar–F + BF₃ + N₂.

qa.q: What is the Gattermann reaction?
qa.a: Replacement of –N₂⁺ by Cl or Br using copper powder and the halogen acid
qa.e: It uses Cu powder with HCl/HBr; Sandmeyer uses cuprous salts.

qa.q: Which statement about benzenediazonium chloride is correct?
qa.a: It is a colourless, water-soluble solid that is stable only in the cold
qa.e: It decomposes on warming with water and explodes easily when dry.

qa.q: What is formed when benzenediazonium chloride solution is warmed?
qa.e: Water replaces the diazonium group: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Benzenediazonium fluoroborate can be stored at room temperature. Reason (R): Unlike the chloride, it is insoluble in water and fairly stable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The fluoroborate's insolubility and stability are why it can be isolated and stored.

qa.q: What is formed when benzenediazonium chloride reacts with phenol in alkaline medium?
qa.e: Coupling at the para position of phenol gives an orange azo compound.

qa.q: What is the product of coupling benzenediazonium chloride with aniline in mildly acidic medium?
qa.e: The diazonium ion attacks the para position of aniline.

qa.q: What kind of reaction is diazo coupling?
qa.e: The diazonium ion is an electrophile that attacks the activated ring.

qa.q: How can benzylamine be distinguished from aniline?
qa.a: With HNO₂ in the cold, only aniline gives a diazonium salt that couples with β-naphthol to give an orange dye
qa.e: Benzylamine is aliphatic-type and gives N₂; aniline gives a stable diazonium salt.

qa.q: Which reagent sequence converts aniline into benzoic acid?
qa.e: The diazonium salt is converted into benzonitrile, which is hydrolysed to benzoic acid.

qa.q: Which group can be introduced on a benzene ring via a diazonium salt but not by direct electrophilic substitution?
qa.e: Direct fluorination is too violent; fluorobenzene is made via the fluoroborate.

qa.q: How can methylamine be distinguished from dimethylamine?
qa.a: Carbylamine test: only methylamine gives a foul-smelling isocyanide
qa.e: The carbylamine test is specific to primary amines.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Azo compounds are coloured. Reason (R): The –N=N– group connects two aromatic rings, creating an extended conjugated system.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Extended conjugation lets them absorb visible light, so they are coloured dyes.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-reducing sugar?
qa.e: In sucrose, the reducing groups of glucose (C1) and fructose (C2) are tied up in the glycosidic bond.

qa.q: Glucose is classified as:
qa.e: Glucose has six carbons and an aldehyde group.

qa.q: How many monosaccharide units does an oligosaccharide give on hydrolysis?
qa.e: Oligosaccharides give two to ten units; disaccharides give two.

qa.q: Which statement about the formula Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ is correct?
qa.a: Not all carbohydrates fit it, and not all compounds fitting it are carbohydrates
qa.e: Rhamnose (C₆H₁₂O₅) is a carbohydrate but does not fit; acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂) fits but is not a carbohydrate.

qa.q: Which is a ketohexose?
qa.e: Fructose has six carbons with a ketone group at C-2.

qa.q: Why is starch called a non-sugar?
qa.a: It is not sweet in taste
qa.e: Polysaccharides such as starch are not sweet, so they are called non-sugars, although they are made of glucose units.

qa.q: Which disaccharide is a reducing sugar?
qa.e: Maltose has a free aldehyde group at C-1 of its second glucose unit.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Glucose reduces Tollens' reagent. Reason (R): Glucose is a monosaccharide with a free aldehyde group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: All monosaccharides are reducing sugars; the aldehyde group of glucose is oxidised.
