qa.q: What does the formation of n-hexane on heating glucose with HI show?
qa.a: All six carbon atoms are linked in a straight chain
qa.e: HI reduces glucose completely, and the straight-chain hydrocarbon reveals the unbranched carbon skeleton.

qa.q: What is formed when glucose reacts with bromine water?
qa.e: Bromine water oxidises only the –CHO group to –COOH.

qa.q: What does the formation of saccharic acid with nitric acid show?
qa.a: Glucose contains a primary alcohol group
qa.e: Both ends (–CHO and –CH₂OH) are oxidised to –COOH, giving a dicarboxylic acid.

qa.q: How many –OH groups does glucose pentaacetate show glucose to have?
qa.e: Five acetyl groups attach, one to each –OH.

qa.q: Which reagent forms an oxime with glucose, showing a carbonyl group?
qa.e: C=O + NH₂OH → C=N–OH (oxime).

qa.q: How is glucose obtained commercially?
qa.a: By hydrolysis of starch with dilute H₂SO₄ at 393 K under pressure
qa.e: Starch from maize or potatoes is boiled with dilute acid under pressure.

qa.q: What products are obtained when sucrose is boiled with dilute HCl in alcoholic solution?
qa.e: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Glucose pentaacetate is a stable compound. Reason (R): The five –OH groups of glucose are attached to different carbon atoms.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: If two –OH groups were on the same carbon, the compound would lose water; stability shows they are on different carbons.

qa.q: Which observation cannot be explained by the open-chain structure of glucose?
qa.a: Glucose does not form a hydrogensulphite addition product with NaHSO₃
qa.e: A free aldehyde should add NaHSO₃; the ring form explains its absence.

qa.q: What are α- and β-D-glucose called?
qa.e: They differ only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon (C-1).

qa.q: Which carbon of glucose is called the anomeric carbon?
qa.e: C-1 becomes asymmetric when the ring forms.

qa.q: What does the 'D' in D-(+)-glucose indicate?
qa.a: Its configuration resembles that of D-glyceraldehyde at the lowest asymmetric carbon
qa.e: D/L is configuration; (+) separately shows dextrorotation.

qa.q: Which –OH group of glucose forms the ring with the aldehyde group?
qa.e: C-5 –OH and C-1 –CHO form a six-membered ring (five C + one O).

qa.q: What is the melting point of α-D-glucose?
qa.e: α-D-glucose melts at 419 K and β-D-glucose at 423 K.

qa.q: Why is the six-membered ring form of glucose called a pyranose?
qa.a: It resembles the ring of pyran (five carbons and one oxygen)
qa.e: The ring analogy with pyran gives the name.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine. Reason (R): In glucose pentaacetate there is no free aldehyde group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The aldehyde is locked in the cyclic structure, so it cannot form an oxime.

qa.q: Why is the hydrolysis product of sucrose called invert sugar?
qa.a: The sign of rotation changes from dextro (+) to laevo (−)
qa.e: Fructose (−92.4°) outweighs glucose (+52.5°), so the mixture becomes laevorotatory.

qa.q: Which monosaccharides are obtained by hydrolysis of lactose?
qa.e: Lactose, milk sugar, is made of galactose and glucose.

qa.q: Which linkage joins the two glucose units in maltose?
qa.a: C-1 of one α-D-glucose to C-4 of the other
qa.e: Maltose has an α(1→4) glycosidic linkage.

qa.q: What size of ring does fructose form?
qa.e: The C-5 –OH bonds to C-2, giving a ring of four carbons and one oxygen.

qa.q: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar?
qa.a: The reducing groups of both glucose (C-1) and fructose (C-2) are involved in the glycosidic bond
qa.e: No free hemiacetal or hemiketal group remains to open up.

qa.q: What is a glycosidic linkage?
qa.a: An oxide (ether-type) linkage joining two monosaccharide units, formed with loss of water
qa.e: The C–O–C bridge links monosaccharides in di- and polysaccharides.

qa.q: What is the sign of specific rotation of D-fructose?
qa.e: D-fructose is D-(−)-fructose; the D refers to configuration, not rotation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Maltose is a reducing sugar. Reason (R): Maltose is composed of two α-D-glucose units.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the reason maltose is reducing is that one glucose unit has a free C-1 (hemiacetal) group, not merely that it contains glucose (sucrose also contains glucose).

qa.q: Which component of starch is water-soluble?
qa.e: Amylose (15–20% of starch) is an unbranched, water-soluble chain.

qa.q: What type of linkage creates branches in amylopectin?
qa.e: The main chain uses C-1→C-4 links, and branches start at C-1→C-6 links.

qa.q: What is cellulose made of?
qa.a: β-D-Glucose units joined by C-1 to C-4 glycosidic links
qa.e: The β-linkage gives straight chains that pack into strong fibres.

qa.q: Why is glycogen called animal starch?
qa.a: It is the storage polysaccharide of animals with a structure similar to amylopectin
qa.e: It plays the same storage role in animals that starch plays in plants.

qa.q: Where is glycogen mainly stored in the human body?
qa.e: Glycogen is stored in the liver, muscles and brain.

qa.q: What percentage of starch is amylose?
qa.e: Amylose is the minor component; amylopectin is 80–85%.

qa.q: Which is the most abundant organic substance in the plant kingdom?
qa.e: Cellulose makes up plant cell walls.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Humans cannot digest cellulose. Reason (R): Human digestive enzymes cannot hydrolyse the β-glycosidic linkages in cellulose.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Our enzymes break α-links (in starch) but not β-links (in cellulose).

qa.q: Which amino acid is optically inactive?
qa.e: Glycine's α-carbon has two H atoms, so it is not asymmetric.

qa.q: What is a zwitterion?
qa.a: A dipolar ion with both positive and negative charges, e.g. H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻
qa.e: The acidic –COOH protonates the basic –NH₂ within the same molecule.

qa.q: Why are amino acids amphoteric?
qa.a: They contain both an acidic (–COOH or –COO⁻) and a basic (–NH₂ or –NH₃⁺) group
qa.e: They can react with both acids and bases.

qa.q: Which is an essential amino acid?
qa.e: Lysine cannot be made by the human body and must come from food.

qa.q: What configuration do most naturally occurring α-amino acids have?
qa.e: Proteins are built from L-amino acids.

qa.q: Why do amino acids have high melting points?
qa.a: They exist as zwitterions and behave like salts
qa.e: Strong electrostatic attractions between zwitterions hold the crystal together.

qa.q: Which is an acidic amino acid?
qa.e: Aspartic acid has an extra –COOH group in its side chain.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Amino acids are soluble in water. Reason (R): Amino acids exist as zwitterions in water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Their ionic, salt-like zwitterionic form interacts strongly with polar water molecules.

qa.q: What is a peptide bond?
qa.a: An amide linkage (–CO–NH–) between two amino acids
qa.e: It forms between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of another, with loss of water.

qa.q: What does the primary structure of a protein refer to?
qa.a: The sequence of amino acids in the chain
qa.e: Primary structure is simply the order of amino acids.

qa.q: What holds an α-helix together?
qa.a: Hydrogen bonds between –NH and C=O groups of nearby turns of the same chain
qa.e: Intramolecular H-bonds stabilise the right-handed helix.

qa.q: Which protein is fibrous?
qa.e: Keratin (hair, wool, silk) has long parallel chains and is water-insoluble.

qa.q: Which forces stabilise the tertiary structure of proteins?
qa.a: Hydrogen bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals forces and electrostatic attractions
qa.e: Several kinds of interactions between side chains maintain the folded shape.

qa.q: How many water molecules are eliminated when a tripeptide is formed from three amino acids?
qa.e: Each peptide bond releases one water; a tripeptide has two peptide bonds.

qa.q: What is quaternary structure?
qa.a: The spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits)
qa.e: Proteins with more than one chain have quaternary structure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Globular proteins are generally soluble in water. Reason (R): Their polypeptide chains are coiled into a spherical shape.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Folding into compact spheres (with polar groups outside) makes them soluble, unlike long fibrous chains.

qa.q: Which structure of a protein remains intact after denaturation?
qa.e: Denaturation disrupts H-bonds and folding, but peptide bonds (the sequence) are not broken.

qa.q: Which is an example of denaturation of protein?
qa.a: Coagulation of egg white on boiling
qa.e: Heat unfolds the albumin, making it opaque and solid.

qa.q: What causes the curdling of milk on standing?
qa.a: Lactic acid formed by bacteria changes the pH and denatures milk proteins
qa.e: The pH change disrupts the proteins' structure.

qa.q: What is the reaction catalysed by maltase?
qa.e: Maltase hydrolyses maltose into two molecules of glucose.

qa.q: How do enzymes speed up biochemical reactions?
qa.e: Enzymes provide an alternative path with a lower energy barrier, like other catalysts.

qa.q: Which statement about enzymes is correct?
qa.a: They are highly specific for their substrates
qa.e: Enzymes are mostly globular proteins with a specific shape that fits particular substrates.

qa.q: Which suffix is commonly used in enzyme names?
qa.e: Enzyme names usually end in -ase (maltase, invertase, lipase).

qa.q: Assertion (A): High fever can affect enzyme activity in the body. Reason (R): Enzymes are proteins that can be denatured by heat.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Heat can disturb the enzyme's 3D structure, reducing its catalytic activity.

qa.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes scurvy?
qa.e: Lack of ascorbic acid causes scurvy, with bleeding gums.

qa.q: Which vitamin's deficiency causes rickets in children?
qa.e: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets (bone deformities) in children and osteomalacia in adults.

qa.q: Which water-soluble vitamin can be stored in the body?
qa.e: Unlike other water-soluble vitamins, B₁₂ can be stored.

qa.q: Which group of vitamins is fat-soluble?
qa.e: These dissolve in fats and are stored in the liver and adipose tissue.

qa.q: Deficiency of vitamin B₁ causes:
qa.e: Thiamine deficiency causes beri-beri (loss of appetite, retarded growth).

qa.q: Which vitamin deficiency increases blood clotting time?
qa.e: Vitamin K is needed for normal blood clotting.

qa.q: Which disease is caused by deficiency of vitamin B₆?
qa.e: Pyridoxine (B₆) deficiency causes convulsions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Water-soluble vitamins must be supplied regularly in the diet. Reason (R): They are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored in the body (except vitamin B₁₂).
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since the body cannot keep reserves of them, a regular supply is needed.

qa.q: Which base is present in RNA but not in DNA?
qa.e: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.

qa.q: Which sugar is present in DNA?
qa.e: DNA contains deoxyribose, which lacks an –OH at C-2.

qa.q: What is a nucleotide?
qa.a: A base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group joined together
qa.e: A nucleoside plus a phosphate at C-5′ is a nucleotide.

qa.q: Which base pairs with guanine in DNA?
qa.e: G pairs with C and A pairs with T.

qa.q: What type of linkage joins nucleotides in a nucleic acid chain?
qa.e: Phosphate links C-5′ of one sugar to C-3′ of the next.

qa.q: If a DNA molecule has 30% adenine, what percentage of guanine does it have?
Which are the three main types of RNA?
qa.e: Messenger, ribosomal and transfer RNA each play roles in protein synthesis.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In DNA, the amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine. Reason (R): Adenine always pairs with thymine through hydrogen bonds in the double helix.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Complementary base pairing makes A and T (and G and C) equal in amount.

qa.q: Which molecule carries the genetic information of an organism?
qa.e: DNA stores hereditary information and passes it to the next generation.

qa.q: What is the main role of RNA in the cell?
qa.e: RNA molecules synthesise proteins using the message from DNA.

qa.q: What property of DNA makes fingerprinting possible?
qa.a: Each person's base sequence is unique and the same in every cell
qa.e: A unique, stable pattern identifies an individual from any tissue sample.

qa.q: What is replication of DNA?
qa.a: The process by which DNA makes an identical copy of itself
qa.e: Replication occurs during cell division so each new cell gets the same DNA.

qa.q: Which is NOT a use of DNA fingerprinting?
qa.a: Measuring a person's blood sugar level
qa.e: Blood sugar is measured chemically, not by DNA analysis.

qa.q: Where is the message for synthesising a particular protein stored?
qa.e: DNA holds the code; RNA molecules use it to build proteins.

qa.q: Why can DNA fingerprinting identify a person from a hair root or a drop of blood?
qa.a: Every cell of a person carries the same DNA sequence
qa.e: The sequence is identical in all body cells, so any sample works.

qa.q: Assertion (A): DNA fingerprinting is used to settle paternity disputes. Reason (R): A child inherits DNA from both parents.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because half of the child's DNA comes from each parent, patterns can be matched.

qa.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
qa.e: Insulin is released when blood glucose rises and brings it back down.

qa.q: Thyroxine is an iodinated derivative of which amino acid?
qa.e: Thyroxine is made from tyrosine with iodine atoms attached.

qa.q: What is the chemical nature of insulin?
qa.e: Insulin is a polypeptide hormone.

qa.q: Which disease results from failure of the adrenal cortex?
qa.e: Insufficient adrenal cortex hormones cause Addison's disease.

qa.q: What is the role of glucocorticoids?
qa.a: They control carbohydrate metabolism, moderate inflammation and respond to stress
qa.e: Glucocorticoids are adrenal cortex steroids with these roles.

qa.q: Which hormones belong to the steroid class?
qa.e: Sex hormones are steroids.

qa.q: What is the effect of deficiency of thyroxine?
qa.e: Low thyroxine slows metabolism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Hormones act at sites far from the glands that make them. Reason (R): Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The blood carries hormones to distant target organs.
